case_summary.text: Income-tax : Section 271(1)(c) - Penalty - For concealment of income : If an assessee is found owner of any money, jewellery, bullion, article or thing at time of search and investment which are not recorded in books of account maintained by him, then such undisclosed investment in assets found would be deemed as concealed income of assessee

IT : Where upon discrepancies noticed in accounts of assessee during search, assessee surrendered income on account of excess cash and stock, however later retracted from statement and did not include amount of surrender in return of income, this being a clear case of concealment, penalty had been rightly levied under section 271(1)(c)

INCOME TAX : Where assessee made bogus purchases from hawala parties, since assessee had concealed income to extent of profit element in garb of purchases which turned out to be bogus, penalty under section 271(1)(c) was leviable

IT: Where deemed income assessed under section 115JB becomes basis of assessment as it was higher than income determined under normal provision, concealment made under normal provision having no effect, penalty under section 271(1)(c) could not be levied

INCOME TAX : Where assessee filed audit report, paid due taxes, and disclosed income, but filed ITR belatedly in response to notice, there was no concealment under clause (c) of Explanation 4 to section 271; hence, penalty under section 271(1)(c) was unjustified
INCOME TAX : Where assessee made bogus purchases from hawala parties and concealed income to extent of profit element in garb of purchases, penalty under section 271(1)(c) was leviable

IT : Where assessee having made investment in properties, claimed said amount as service charges by fabricating evidence with a view to suppress its taxable profits, there being a deliberate concealment on part of assessee, a case for penalty was made out under section 271(1)(c)

IT-I : Where assessee, carrying on poultry business in a remote village, could not maintain his books of account under section 44AA on account of difficulty to get an accountant at affordable cost at such a place, it constituted a reasonable cause within meaning of section 273B IT-II : Where assessee did not furnish any return in response to notice under section 148 and it was having taxable income, there was a deemed concealment within meaning of section 271(1)(c)

IT: Where search operation led to detection of various undisclosed bank accounts wherein undisclosed income of assessee was deposited, he could not challenge penalty order passed under section 271(1)(c) on ground that he bonafidely believed that he need not disclose those particulars and, thus, was not guilty of concealment of any income

INCOME TAX : Where Assessing Officer imposed penalty under section 271(1)(c) in respect of concealment of income related to additions made under sections 68 and 69, since components of these additions were already there in bank account transactions maintained by assessee, it could not be treated as concealment of income and, thus, impugned penalty was not justified
IT-II : Where assessee did not furnish any return in response to notice under section 148 and it was having taxable income, there was a deemed concealment within meaning of section 271(1)(c)
Penalty u/s 271(1)(c) vitiated where notice u/s 274 did not specify charge of concealment or inaccurate particulars: HC

IT: Where assessee made payment to a company, which, in case of search on third party, was found to be a paper company only and since matter was old and assessee was not having supporting evidence except ledger account of said party, it offered said amount to tax, it couldn't be held beyond doubt that there was concealment of particulars of income or furnishing inaccurate particulars thereof on part of assessee to attract penalty under section 271(1)(c)

IT: Where assessee withdrew claim for depreciation on IPR in statement during search and seizure operations undertaken on assessee but nothing incriminating was found during search which was concealed by assessees, penalty could not be levied under section 271(1)(c) merely on basis of statement during search

IT: Where assessee disclosed additional income only after search of premises of another assessee by DIT (Investigations) which unearthed certain evidences indicating that certain expenditure claimed by assessee was disallowable, it would amount to concealment of income liable to penalty under section 271(1)(c)
Concealment penalty not tenable, if provisions of sec. 271 not satisfied before imposition of penalty
Concealment penalty justified as assessee filed ITR in response to notice without considering sec. 50C provisions: ITAT

IT: Where there was a search upon assessee and she subsequent to search, in pursuance of notice issued under section 153A, filed returns for relevant assessment years and amount shown in returns filed as 'other income' was not a part of her regular accounts, such amount would squarely come within purview of concealed income liable to penalty under section 271(1)(c)
INCOME TAX : Penalty under section 271(1)(c) may be imposed only on occurrence of concealment and not on under-disclosure
Pre amended Expl 5A to sec. 271(1)(c)- no deemed concealment on income offered by filing return pursuant to search

IT : Where assessee realizing that expenditure claimed towards travelling was untenable under section 57 and therefore, paid tax on same, there was no concealment of income and, thus, penalty under section 271(1)(c) could not be levied

INCOME TAX : Where assessee sold land but did not file her return of income under section 139(1) but had filed it only in response to notice under section 148 that too by computing capital gains based on value in registered sale deed and not by adopting provisions of section 50C, such act of assessee amounted to concealment of income, therefore, penalty levied upon assessee under section 271(1)(c) was justified

IT : Where assessee claimed depreciation on assets purchased from a subsidiary company and further leased back to parent company, since sale and lease back transaction was found to be bogus and assessee failed to substantiate with evidence its claim of 100 per cent depreciation on leased assets, imposition of penalty for concealment of income under section 271(1)(c) was justified

IT : Where assessee received gifts from NRI's and stated that same was received due to his financial difficulty which was found to be incorrect and further, he could not provide details of said donees, penalty levied under section 271(1)(c) was justified

IT : Where assessee did not explain cash deposits and did not disclose income in response to notice issued under section 153C and did not give details as to how he would fall within explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c), penalty would be levied

INCOME TAX : Where penalty under section 271(1)(c) was levied following reassessment wherein unrecorded cash income was disclosed in return, since assessee voluntarily disclosed income and same was accepted without further investigation, it could not be concluded that there was concealment of income and thus, impugned penalty was to be deleted

IT : Where assessee, engaged filed a revised return pursuant to survey proceedings declaring certain undisclosed income, said return could not be regarded as a voluntary return and, therefore, assessee being guilty of concealment of particulars of income, was liable to pay penalty under section 271(1)(c)

IT: Where though huge cash was confiscated, assessee filed his return without addressing cash detected, and when scrutiny notice was issued, filed revised return and offered cash receipts as undisclosed income, penalty was to be levied under section 271(1)(c)

IT : Where search and seizure was conducted by Central Excise Department, penalty under section 271(1)(c) was not to be levied by Income Tax Officer as concealment was not conducted by Income-tax Department

IT : Where assessee claimed excess depreciation on machinery on basis that machinery was of foreign origin but facts showed that such machinery was of Indian make and excess claim was only withdrawn in view of action initiated by department, penalty under section 271(1)(c) was justified

INCOME TAX : Where assessee understated its net profit in its return of income and had failed to come forth with any plausible explanation for having suppressed/understated net profit, it was liable to be saddled with penalty under section 271(1)(c)

IT : Where assessee himself admitted in presence of his Chartered Accountant that he had undisclosed income which was utilized for renovation of his bunglow, revenue authorities were not required to prove by bringing any positive evidence of existence of undisclosed income with assessee so as to levy penalty under section 271(1)(c)

IT: Where assessee in support of gift received from donor filed a copy of his residential address which was found to be false, and, moreover, he also failed to prove that gift in question was made by executing a valid gift deed, assessee's case fell under Explanation 1(B) to section 271(1)(c) and, therefore, impugned penalty order passed on account of deemed concealment of income was to be upheld

INCOME TAX : Where assessee's claim for deduction under section 54F was partly disallowed due to lack of supporting documents for some expenditure and penalty for concealment was levied solely on basis of such disallowance, making a claim not fully substantiated by bills does not amount to furnishing inaccurate particulars of income, and penalty under section 271(1)(c) was not justified and was to be deleted
Mere compliances with requirements for sec. 80-IA relief isn't enough to grant immunity from concealment penalty
Concealment penalty upheld as claim of depreciation on computer was not genuine: HC
Concealment penalty upheld as assessee surrendered income after reassessment notice and not voluntarily

IT : Where assessee surrendered certain amount only after detection of concealment by Assessing Officer, assessee failed to discharge initial onus laid down upon it in terms of Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c) and, thus, impugned penalty order was to be confirmed

IT: SLP granted against High Court's ruling that where assessee disclosed additional income only after search of premises of another assessee by DIT (Investigations) which unearthed certain evidences indicating that certain expenditure claimed by assessee was disallowable, it would amount to concealment of income liable to penalty under section 271(1)(c)
INCOME TAX : Penalty under section 271(1)(c) may be imposed only on occurrence of concealment of income and not on under-disclosure of income

INCOME TAX : Where show cause notice issued under section 274 read with section 271 did not specify charge against assessee as to whether it was for concealment of income or for furnishing inaccurate particulars of income, penalty notice issued under section 271(1)(c) was invalid in law
Concealment penalty was justified as confiscated cash was disclosed in return after issuance of scrutiny notice

IT : Where assessee had made certain claims which could not be found to be plausible and additions had been made, there being no concealment of income, penalty under section 271(1)(c) could not be sustained

IT: (i) As long as the assessee has not concealed any material facts, or the 'factual' information given by him is shown to be correct, he is not liable for penalty under section 271(1)(c), even if the claim made is not sustainable in law

IT: In case of imposition of penalty under section 271(1)(c), it is incumbent upon Assessing Officer to come to a positive finding as to whether there was concealment of income by assessee or whether any inaccurate particulars of such income had been furnished by assessee

IT : Where difference between loan amount, due and payable by assessee was on account of non inclusion of interest amount in loan amount by bank, no concealment was to be alleged against assessee for imposition of penalty under section 271(1)(c)

IT-I : Where assessee wrongly claimed deduction of payment of advance tax and certain amount debited to profit and loss account which was infact a mere appropriation of profit, it being a case of concealment and furnishing inaccurate particulars of income, penalty order passed by Assessing Officer under section 271(1)(c) was to be confirmed

IT: Where after completion of assessment, consequent upon inquiry assessee surrendered amount of certain loan as bogus loan and interest on said loan, concealment of income was established making a case for levy of penalty under section 271(1)(c)

IT: Wrong deduction of an amount for computation of income could not be equated with concealment and it would not amount to furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income or concealment of income so as to attract penalty under section 271(1)(c)

IT : Where assessee having agreed to surrender certain amount in course of survey proceedings, filed its return subsequently wherein said amount was infact offered to tax, there was no concealment on part of assessee and, thus, impugned penalty order passed under section 271(1)(c) was to be set aside

digest.text:
HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1979-80 - Assessee claimed non-resident status and exemption for salary income on that basis, he also furnished details in respect of leaving India and arriving in India from years 1974 to 1978 which showed that his stay in India during relevant previous year was less than 180 days and did not satisfy requirement of section 6(1)(a) - Later ITO found that assessee’s stay in India during preceding years was such as to satisfy section 6(1)(c) and held that assessee was not non-resident and, hence, not entitled to exemption claimed - Assessee had obtained a certificate under section 80RRA but did not disclose it to ITO - Whether assessee could be held guilty of concealment under section 271(1)(c) - Held, no.

FACT: For the assessment year 1979-80 the assessee claimed his status as non-resident. He also gave details in an annexure showing dates of departure from and arrival in India from the year 1974 to 1978, which showed, inter alia, that for the relevant previous year, the assessee had stayed in India only for 137 days and, hence, did not satisfy the requirement of section 6(1)(a). Later, the ITO, however, noticed that the assessee’s stay in India during the preceding four years was such as to satisfy section 6(1)(c) and held that the assessee was not a non-resident and, hence, not entitled to the exemption claimed. The assessee had also obtained a certificate under section 80RRA which was not disclosed before the ITO. The ITO initiated penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) and held that since the assessee did not disclose the fact of the certificate under section 80RRA and his correct residential status although he knew about it there was a breach of the obligation under section 139(1) and, therefore, he was guilty of concealment of income. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the imposition of penalties.

On second appeal:

HELD: It could not be disputed that the assessee had fully disclosed all the material facts of arrival and departure in India for the past four years in an annexure to the statement of income. Although in that statement the assessee had claimed the status of a non-resident, immediately below that he had mentioned ‘see Annexure A’.

Therefore, his statement regarding non-resident status could not be read in isolation and separately from the annexure. It was for the ITO to come to the conclusion regarding the assessee’s status. The conclusion by the ITO or by the assessee regarding the status of the assessee might be one or the other, but that did not mean that the facts had been concealed by the assessee. Concealment can only be of facts and not of the conclusion. Where the assessee had disclosed all the material facts to enable the ITO to come to a conclusion, it could not be said that the assessee was guilty of concealment. It is the duty of an assessee to disclose all the facts and not to conceal any material fact which would give a false suggestion as to the conclusion to be drawn. This is the extent of the disclosure expected of an assessee. In other words, there should not be any suppressio yeri which would amount to suggestio falsi. In the instant case, the assessee had not done any such thing.

Although the assessee had not disclosed the fact of his having the certificate under section 80RRA, strictly speaking, it was not his duty to do so before the ITO because the ITO had all the materials before him to enable him to come to the conclusion regarding the assessee’s status. Ideally or morally speaking, it might be expected of the assessee to have made this disclosure, but that was not the expectation of law when imposing penalty for which a positively dishonest conduct was necessary. The assessee’s own belief in that regard was also immaterial because the conclusion to be drawn by the ITO was independent of any belief that the assessee might have had. The penalty imposed on the assessee was, therefore, cancelled.

Committee Report. Earlier the concealment penalty was based on the quantum of income concealed and there was an Explanation that in case the returned income is less than 80 per cent of the assessed income, then the burden of proving that concealment was on the assessee. Wanchoo Committee recommended that the penalty should be based on the amount of tax sought to be evaded. What is meant by tax sought to be evaded was mentioned in the Explanation 4. [Para 3.20] From the judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Dharamendra Textile Processors [2008] 306 ITR 277/ 174 Taxman 571, it was clear that the object behind enactment of section 271(1)(c ) was to provide a remedy for loss of revenue. Wilful concealment is not an essential ingredient for imposing penalty, as that is the requirement in case a prosecution is launched. However, in the instant case, the assessee was fully aware of the fact of unaccounted sales. He was fully aware of the income from such sales. He had not given any explanation to say as to why such sales were not disclosed in the original return. The explanation for not disclosing such sales was not forthcoming. Only explanation given was that the income had been surrendered to purchase peace and to avoid litigation. [Para 3.21]

The assessee had not agreed to an item to be included in the income, which was being reflected in the books of account. This was a case where unaccounted sales were found during the course of search and amount outstanding on account of such sales were found. Even in respect of accounted sales, the assessee was preparing the purchase vouchers as actual purchases were made from hawkers and no purchase bills were obtained from them. [Para 3.22]

In the original return, the assessee had not disclosed the entire sales. That fact was material to the computation of the total income. No explanation had been offered as to why such sales were not reflected in the original return. The only explanation submitted was that the assessee agreed to the addition to purchase peace. Such explanation could not be considered as bona fide because the documents relating to such unaccounted sales were found. It was also found that the assessee was having unaccounted debtors to the extent of Rs. 93.54 lakhs as on 31-3-2004. Hence, in the instant case, the Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c) was squarely applicable for imposition of penalty. [Para 3.24]

As per section 271(1B), there is deemed satisfaction in respect of additions made. The Assessing Officer had imposed penalty not only on the addition made to the income returned under section 153A but also on the difference between the original returned income and the income returned in response to the notice under section 153A. The Act does not require any specific form of satisfaction to be recorded. The satisfaction can be inferred from the assessment order. [Para 4.1]

From the observations of the Assessing Officer recorded in the assessment order it was clear that the Assessing Officer was satisfied that the additional income being offered was the concealed income. The narration of the facts in the assessment order and mentioning of incriminating documents found during the course of search showing unaccounted sales clearly indicated that the Assessing Officer was satisfied during the course of proceedings that penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) were required to be initiated. The satisfaction was evident and it could not be held that the proceedings had been initiated without recording satisfaction. [Para 4.2]

Relying on the decision of the Tribunal in Asstt. CIT v. Goutham Public School [2004] 88 ITD 31 (Visakhapatnam) and considering the facts as mentioned above, it was to be held that the Assessing Officer was satisfied before initiating the proceedings under section 271(1)(c). [Para 4.3]

It was true that the show-cause notice did not contain the specific allegation, i.e., whether it was in respect of concealment of income or furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income. The notice was to be read along with the assessment order during the course of which proceedings had been initiated. The proceedings had been initiated for concealment of income. The assessee in his reply had understood the spirit in which notice had been issued. In his reply, it had been mentioned that he had offered additional income to buy peace and to have an end to the proceedings. If the notice in substance and effect is in conformity with or according to the intent and purpose of the Act, then such notice cannot be held as invalid as per section 292B. The purpose of issuing the show-cause notice is to give the assessee an adequate opportunity in respect of default, which is detected and alleged against him. From the nature of the assessment proceedings and the fact mentioned in the assessment order, it was clear that there was a specific charge of concealment of income and the assessee got adequate opportunity in rebutting such charge. Hence, it could not be said that penalty proceedings were invalid because the Assessing Officer had not struck off the column for which the assessee was not required to give reply. Hence, on that ground, penalty proceedings could not be cancelled. [Para 5.1]

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1964-65 - Whether Explanation to section 271(1) inserted with effect from 1-4-1964 would apply to income returned after it came into force irrespective of fact whether income related period prior to 1-4-1964 or thereafter - Held, yes - Whether by Explanation to section 271(1) classifying assessees in two varieties and in allocating burden of proof in one class of cases on assessee and in other on departmental authority, Parliament has adopted an intelligible differentia dictated by experience gathered in administering Act and, therefore, said Explanation does not offend article 14 of Constitution - Held, yes

FACT: For the year 1964-65 the petitioner submitted a return of its income on 21-10-1964, showing its total income at Rs. 28,270. The ITO, however, assessed the income of the petitioner at Rs. 47,273 for that year and a penalty under section 271(1)(c) was imposed.

The assessee filed the writ petition challenging the penalty contending that the penalty having been imposed by the aid of the Explanation appended to sub-section (1) of section 271, which Explanation had come into force with effect 1-4-1964, the Explanation did not apply as the return in question related to the year which had concluded on 31-3-1964. The assessee further contended that the aforesaid Explanation offends article 14 of the Constitution.

HELD: On its plain wording, the Explanation, to section 271(1) applies to the income returned by an assessee after it came into force irrespective of the fact whether the income related to a period prior to 1-4-1964, or thereafter. The penalty clause (c ) can be invoked only if a false return is filed, and if the return is filed after the Explanation had become operative, surely such return, if it offends the Explanation, would attract its applicability. Therefore, the Explanation applied to the instant case since the relevant return was admittedly filed after 1-4-1964. This interpretation does not tantamount to operation of the Explanation retrospectively.

True, it cannot be gainsaid that the Explanation does create two classes; one class of those assessees whose returned income happens to be less than 80 per cent of the assessed income, which may appropriately be described as the actual income, and the assessees whose returned income is not less than 80 per cent of their actual income. Article 14, it has been consistently held by the Supreme Court, does not forbid classification though it prohibits class legislation. Equality before the law means that among equals the law should be identical and that the like should be treated alike. At the same time, put in other words, equality before the law does not mean that things which are different shall be treated as though they were the same. The permissible classification, according to the pronouncements of the Supreme Court, must satisfy two conditions, namely, (1) it must be founded on intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from others who are left out of the group, and (2) the differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the impugned provision. It has also been repeatedly held that the differentia and object are different elements and that the object by itself cannot be the basis of classification. Another principle equally well settled is that article 14 condemns discrimination not by substantive law alone but even by procedural law.

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1968-69 - Whether state has a wide discretion in selecting persons or objects it would tax, and a statute is not open to attack on ground that it taxes some persons and objects and not others - Held, yes - Whether it is only when within range of its selection, law operates unequally, and that can not be justified on basis of any valid classification, that it would be violative of article 14 of Constitution - Held, yes - Whether section 271(1)(c) can not be regarded as violative of article 14 of Constitution as there is nothing in said section pointing out any hostile discrimination against a particular type of taxpayer - Held, yes - Whether moreover, since object of section 271(1)(c) is not to provide for any confiscation but to provide a penalty for concealment of income and that too by providing a deterrent penalty, it can not be said that provisions of section 271(1)(c)(iii) infringe article 19(1)(f) Constitution - Held, yes

FACT: For the assessment year 1968-69, the assessee filed his original return without showing the income from sale of land, but when required to produce the sale deed in respect of the land sold by him, the assessee filed a revised return showing therein capital gains and business income on estimate basis. The ITO passed the assessment order and also issued notice under section 274 read with section 271 for failure to furnish the return within the stipulated time and also for concealment of income. Later, he levied penalty only under section 271(1)(c) of an amount equal to 100 per cent of the concealed income.

On writ, the assessee challenged the constitutional validity of section 271(1)(c) on two grounds: (1) that section 271(1)(c) is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as there is no classification at all even though there is a difference between various types of tax evasions; and (2) that the impugned provisions are a colourable exercise of legislative power inasmuch as in the guise of levying penalty the legislature had enacted for expropriation of the whole of the property of the citizen.

HELD: As regards the challenge on the basis of Article 14 of the Constitution, it is well-settled that while article 14 forbids class legislation, it does not forbid reasonable classification for the purposes of legislation. In order, however, to pass the test of permissible classification, two conditions must be fulfilled, namely : (i) that the classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from others left out of the group ; and (ii ) that that differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the statute in question.

In deciding whether a taxation law is discriminatory or not it is necessary to bear in mind that the State has a wide discretion in selecting the persons or objects it would tax, and that a statute is not open to attack on the ground that it taxes some persons and objects and not others. It is only when within the range of its selection, the law operates unequally, and that cannot be justified on the basis of any valid classification, that it would be violative of article 14. It is for the person who assails a legislation as discriminatory to establish that it is not based on a valid classification and it is well-settled that this burden is all the heavier when the legislation under attack is a taxing statute. In taxation even more than in other fields, legislatures possess the greatest freedom in classification. The burden is on the one attacking the legislative arrangement to negative every conceivable basis which might support it. Thus, unless the petitioner succeeds in establishing that there was a clear and hostile discrimination by virtue of the impugned legislation, the challenge on the ground of article 14 can not be sustained.

Circulars and notifications - CBDT Instruction No. 1979, dated 27-3-2000 and CBDT Instruction No. 1903 dated 1-11-1992

FACT: Two of the partners of the assessee-firm introduced Rs. 19,500 and Rs. 30,000, respectively, as part of their share capital in the firm. It was explained that the amounts had been introduced out of their agricultural income. The assessee could not produce evidence regarding sale of agriculture produce and, therefore, amounts were treated as the assessee’s concealed income. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed some reduction. In penalty order, the Assessing Officer held that the assessee had not produced the correct particulars of its income and, thus, concealed the income of Rs. 34,500. Accordingly, penalty under section 271(1)(c) was imposed. On appeal, the assessee contended that the mere fact that the Assessing Officer had not accepted the explanation furnished was not sufficient ground for levy of penalty. The Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the penalty.

On the revenue’s appeal and cross-objection by the assessee, the assessee besides opposing the penalty order, also took preliminary objection to the maintainability of the appeal in the light of Instruction No. 1979, dated 27-3-2000, issued by the Central Board of Direct Taxes, asking all officers of the Income-tax Department under their control not to file appeals before the Tribunal in cases where the tax effect involved in appeal did not exceed Rs. 1.00 lakh. On the other hand, it was contended on behalf of the Department that the instructions were by way of guidelines and could not override the specific provisions of the Act and that these instructions were not in the nature of ‘benevolent Circulars’ for the benefit of the assessee. Thus, it was urged that the preliminary objection raised was not legally sustainable.

HELD: As regards the preliminary objection, it is only those circulars or instructions which are issued by the Board under section 119 that will have statutory force and will be binding on the income-tax authorities. Delegated legislation can be issued only when the authority concerned has statutory power to do so. But statutory power is not necessary for issuing directions/instructions. The basic distinguishing feature between a direction and delegated legislation is that while delegated legislation is binding on both the administration and the individual and is enforceable through a court of law at the instance of either the individual or the administration, an administrative direction, generally speaking, is not so binding and enforceable. There may be an administrative remedy available to the individual concerned for enforcing such directions.

If the income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment for any assessment year, by reason of omission or failure of the assessee to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for his assessment, reassessment proceeding can be initiated as provided under section 147. This again shows that full and true disclosure of income is a primary obligation of the assessee. If a person obliged to furnish the particulars of his income omits to furnish them, he thereby conceals the particulars. This concealment may take various forms. A glaring illustration of concealment would be where the assessee does not disclose or fully disclose in the return the income derived by him which would fall under a particular head, e.g., ‘Income from other sources’ while disclosing his income falling under other heads of income prescribed by section 14. To the extent he does not disclose that income, he conceals the particulars of income. The obligation is not only to disclose particulars of income but to disclose them correctly and completely. If while disclosing the particulars of income in the return he puts them under a wrong head, he can be said to be furnishing inaccurate particulars of income. The particulars of income can be made inaccurate in a variety of ways, a glaring illustration of which would be where the assessee while stating the income under a particular head, works out the income chargeable to tax after making deductions which are falsely made. Such a process would make the particulars of income inaccurate. In all such cases, whether the income is not disclosed against the constituent item of the return in which it falls or is partly not disclosed, or the particulars of income given in the return are incorrectly stated by any machination, the impact is bound to be on the figure of gross total income to be mentioned under various heads of income and also on the total income chargeable to tax. In fact, reducing the figure of income that would be chargeable to tax would be for the purpose of concealment of particulars of income or giving inaccurate particulars of income. The expression ‘particulars of income’ would have relevance to all the particulars of income which the assessee is required to give in his return fully and truly, including the particulars of income chargeable to tax under various heads and the total income. Therefore, any concealment or inaccuracy in the particulars of income in the return occurring at any stage upto and inclusive of the ultimate stage of working out of total income, would attract the penalty provision of section 271(1)(c). Every figure in the return which is set opposite to the item of income is a particular of income, whether the figure is one which is stated independently of anything else that appears in the return or the documents accompanying it or whether it is something derived from other figures elsewhere stated in such return or documents. False result may be produced by the falsity of one or more of the constituent items in the return. The words ‘inaccurate particulars’ would cover falsity in the final figure as also the constituent elements or items. They simply would mean inaccurate in some specific or definite respect whether in the constituent or subordinate items of income or the end result.

Editor's note

The High Court considered only the question whether the case was covered by the Explanation to section 271(1)(c) without considering the question whether the requirements of section 271(1)(c) were independently satisfied.

271(1)(c) may be issued for concealment of income. During the course of penalty proceedings, apart from issuing a formal show-cause notice under section 271(1)(c ), the Assessing Officer had specifically confronted the assessee with the facts pertaining to diversion of profits through the instrumentality of sham sale transactions with the sister concerns and called upon the assessee to explain why penalty for concealing the particulars of income may not be levied. The assessee furnished its reply. The Assessing Officer after elaborate discussion of the facts and circumstances of case came to the conclusion that the assessee had concealed the income by diverting the profits to its sister concerns. The Assessing Officer had further observed that the assessee had furnished inaccurate particulars of its income. On these facts the charge of concealment had been specifically and unambiguously brought out by the Assessing Officer in the show-cause notice issued to the assessee as well as in the penalty order passed by the Assessing Officer. In the show-cause notice, the Assessing Officer had clearly indicated the default of concealing the particulars of income. The satisfaction recorded in the assessment order using the words ‘concealment of income’ clearly brought out the charge that the penalty was proposed to be levied for concealing the particulars of income. The income could be concealed obviously by concealing the particulars thereof. Looking to the fact that the penalty proceedings before the Assessing Officer do not have formal trappings of a criminal trial and nuances of criminality cannot be imported into such proceedings, strict procedural requirements of a criminal trial like issue of the formal charge-sheet are not necessary in such proceedings. The assessee had been allowed appropriate opportunity of being heard as per the provisions of section 274. The basic requirement had been duly complied with by the Assessing Officer inasmuch as the Assessing Officer had indicated that the penalty under section 271(1)(c) was proposed to be levied for concealing the particulars of income represented by diversion of profits through sham transactions with the sister concerns. No prejudice, therefore, had been caused to the assessee in the matter of rebutting the case against it.

The assessee had taken resort to routing its sales through sham or unreal transactions which were merely paper transactions, with its sister concerns for the sole purpose of diverting its profits. There were tell tale signs in ample measure starting from the record which indicated that these sale transactions with the sister concerns were illusory transactions. The transactions with the sister concerns were admittedly at rates much lower than the prevailing market rates. The assessee had obviously resorted to a make believe arrangement whereunder the sister concerns had been used as conduits for siphoning off of its profits. The Assessing Officer had brought out in the penalty order the close inter-connection of the assessee with the sister concerns. Five partners of the assessee-firm were also partners in the three sister concerns utilised for profit diversion. The substantiated chunk of sham transactions were routed through one of the firms. Thus, 70 per cent of profits in the sister concerns was held by the five partners of the assessee firm who were common. The other partners also were closely related family members. These facts provided irrefutable evidence that the transactions with the sister concerns were merely a ruse to divert the profits; in fact the sale transactions of the assessee with the sister concerns and the subsequent transactions of the sister concerns with the outside parties formed an integral and indivisible part of the composite scheme of tax planning of the assessee. Hence, the assessee-firm had adopted non-genuine and artificial device of showing paper transactions with the sister concerns with the objective of reducing its tax liabilities. These transactions were commercially inert and had been entered into as part of tax saving scheme. The penalty for concealment levied under section 271(1)(c) was, therefore, liable to be upheld.

Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c ) incorporates a rule of evidence and shifts the onus on the shoulders of the assessee in furnishing the explanation before the Assessing Officer. The Explanation does not constitute an ingredient of the offence and it lays down only a rule of evidence. The Explanation does not confer any discretion on the assessing authority to invoke it or not. It automatically applies to cases where penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) for the offence of concealing the particulars of income have been initiated. The consequences from the applicability of Explanation 1 follow as a matter of law. If the assessee fails to offer explanation or the explanation is found to be false or the assessee is not able to substantiate the explanation, the presumption that he concealed the particulars of income is bound to be drawn. In the instant case there was no infirmity in the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) in invoking the Explanation 1 for the purpose of considering the exigibility of the penalty under section 271(1)(c).

HELD: No questions had been raised on behalf of the department on the findings recorded by the Tribunal.

In the decision of the Supreme Court in Karnani Properties Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax [1971] 82 ITR 547 (SC) it was held that when the question referred to the High Court speaks of 'on the facts and circumstances of the case', it means 'on the facts and circumstances found by the Tribunal' and not 'facts and circumstances' that may be found by the High Court on a reappraisal of the evidence. In view of that pronouncement of law, it was held that the findings recorded by the Tribunal could not be gone into.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c) read with section 131, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment years 1996-97 to 1998-99 - During course of assessment proceedings, it was noticed that assessee was making bogus purchases from various concerns belonging to ‘F’ - Assessing Officer asked assessee to produce those parties but assessee failed to do so despite repeated opportunities given - Assessing Officer having treated those purchases as bogus, made addition to assessee’s income - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) as well as Tribunal upheld a part of addition so made - Assessing Officer also imposed penalty upon assessee under section 271(1)(c) - Whether when assessee filed complete details of party, revenue authorities had ample power including issue of summon under section 131 whereas assessee had no such power under Act to bring party personally to produce before Assessing Officer - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, when revenue authorities did not exercise such power under section 131, assessee could not be blamed for concealing particulars and/or furnishing inaccurate particulars of income - Held, yes - Whether in view of aforesaid, it was to be held that it was not a fit case for levy of penalty under section 271(1)(c) - Held, yes
Words and phrases : Words  ‘concealed’, ‘particulars’ and ‘inaccurate’ as occurring in section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

FACT: During the course of assessment proceedings, it was noticed that the assessee was making bogus purchases from various concerns belonging to ‘F’. The Assessing Officer asked the assessee to produce those parties but the assessee failed to do so despite repeated opportunities given. The Assessing Officer treated the said purchases of Rs. 15,99,295 as bogus purchases for the assessment year 1996-97. The assessee filed an appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals), who confirmed the addition to the extent of 25 per cent of the total purchases. The order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was confirmed by the Tribunal. The Assessing Officer levied penalty under section 271(1)(c), which had been confirmed by the Commissioner (Appeals).

On second appeal :

HELD: The crux of the matter to be examined was whether penalty under section 271(1)(c), read with the Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c ) was applicable to the facts of the instant case. The proceedings under section 271(1)(c ) can be initiated only if the Assessing Officer or the first appellate authority is satisfied in the course of any proceedings under the Act that any person has concealed the particulars of his income or has furnished inaccurate particulars of such income and he may direct that such person shall pay by way of penalty the sum mentioned in sub-clause (iii) of clause (c) of section 271(1)(c). The expression used in clause (c) is ‘has concealed the particulars of his income’ or ‘furnished inaccurate particulars of such income’. Therefore, in both cases of concealment and inaccuracy the phrase ‘particulars of income’ is used. The expressions ‘has concealed the particulars of income’ and ‘has furnished inaccurate particulars of income’ have not been defined either in section 271(1)(c) or elsewhere in the Act. [Para 8]

The word ‘conceal’ is derived from the latin word concelare which implies to hide. The offence of concealment is, thus, a direct attempt to hide an item of income or a portion thereof from the knowledge of the income-tax authorities. [Para 10]

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1975-76 - Pursuant to original assessment of income of assessee, a search took place at residence of assessee's father in which a black handwritten diary of assessee was seized wherein an entry relating to Rs. 10,000 in respect of some transaction with one 'L' was found - He surrendered said amount as its income in reassessment proceeding - Penalty under section 271(1)(c) was imposed - Whether since assessee had not disclosed income in original return and disclosed it only after search was conducted and re-assessment proceeding was initiated, it could be said that there had been a conscious effort on part of assessee to conceal income - Held, yes - Whether since assessee had not been able to rebut presumption raised under Explanation to section 271(1)(c), which was upon him to prove that there was no gross or wilful neglect on his part it could be said that order of Tribunal in sustaining penalty, did not suffer from any legal infirmity - Held, yes

HELD: The Explanation inserted to section 271(1)(c) was clearly attracted in the instant case as the returned income was less than 80 per cent of the assessed income. [Para 6]

In the instant case, the assessee had not disclosed the income in the original return and had disclosed it only after the search was conducted and re-assessment proceeding was initiated. Thus, there had been a conscious effort on the part of the assessee to conceal the income. issued only when the authority concerned has statutory power to do so. But statutory power is not necessary for issuing directions/instructions. The basic distinguishing feature between a direction and delegated legislation is that while delegated legislation is binding on both the administration and the individual and is enforceable through a court of law at the instance of either the individual or the administration, an administrative direction, generally speaking, is not so binding and enforceable. There may be an administrative remedy available to the individual concerned for enforcing such directions. Perusal of the said Instruction No. 1979 shows that the said instructions have not been issued by the CBDT in exercise of its powers conferred under section 119. The Board while referring to earlier circulars has mentioned that "in supersession of the above instruction, it has been decided by the Board that the appeals will be filed only in cases where the tax effect has exceeded the revised monetary limits given hereunder". Thus, the forms which are used does not indicate source of power under which it is issued. It merely indicates that the Board is conveying its executive decision to the Chief Commissioners, Directors General. Further, it can seen that Board has been issuing instructions/circulars in exercise of its powers conferred under section 119. Thus, it is clear that the Board while exercising its power under section 119, the practice has been to mention the source of power. However, there is no mention of source of power in the recital of the instruction No. 1979. In the absence of such a recital in the case of the said circular, the inference would be that the same is not issued under section 119. Thus, the same can be said to be administrative instruction having no statutory force behind it. Therefore, the same cannot be enforced through a court of law. Even assuming that these instructions are statutory in nature, the same cannot stand the legal scrutiny as no subordinate legislation can abrogate or override the provisions of the Act under which they have been framed. What section 119 has empowered the Board is to issue orders, instruction, or directions for the ‘proper administration’ of the Act or for such other purposes specified in sub-section (2) of that section. Such an order, instruction or direction cannot override the provisions of the Act. That would be destructive of the known principle of law as that would really amount to giving powers to a delegated authority even to amend the provisions of law enacted by Parliament. It may be seen that under section 253 both the assessee and the Commissioner have been allowed to prefer appeal before the Tribunal if they are aggrieved by the order of first appellate authority. Thus, the law has specifically authorized the Commissioner to direct the Assessing Officer to appeal to the Tribunal against such orders. This is a statutory right conferred by the statute on the Commissioner. Any instruction or direction of the CBDT curtailing the said statutory right would amount to overriding the provisions of the Act. Further, under section 119(2) the Board has been empowered to issue instructions/orders for the purpose of proper and efficient management of the work of the assessment and collection of revenue by way of relaxation of any provision of sections mentioned therein. The filing of appeal by the Commissioner does not fall in any of the categories for which the Board has been authorized to issue instruction under section 119; thus, the instruction in question would be beyond the scope of the provision of section 119. Therefore, it can be said that the instructions in question are not legally sustainable, being in violation of the provisions of Act and also beyond the scope of power conferred on the CBDT.

In view of the above, the Instruction No. 1979 being not issued in exercise of power conferred on the CBDT under section 119 is not statutory instruction but merely administrative instruction for the guidance of the income-tax authorities. Thus, the same cannot be enforced through a court of law. Therefore, there was no force in the preliminary objection raised by the assessee.

As regards imposition of penalty under section 271(1)(c), as per Explanation-1 to section 271(1)(c), penalty for concealment can be imposed only if both the conditions, namely, the assessee has failed to substantiate its explanation and has also failed to prove its bona fide, have been fulfilled. In case any of the two conditions is not fulfilled, no penalty under section 271(1)(c) is imposable. In other words, even if the assessee is not able to substantiate its explanation but if such explanation is bona fide, no penalty under section 271(1)(c) is imposed. In the instant case, the assessee had failed to substantiate its explanation in respect of the deposits made in the name of partners satisfactorily. However, bona fide of his explanation made in that regard had not been doubted by the department. In the circumstances, there was no infirmity in the order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals) cancelling the penalty order of the Assessing Officer.

HEADNOTE: Section 297, read with section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 28(1)(c) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Repeals and savings - Assessment year 1959-60 - Whether for purposes of penalty, there is no doubt classification under section 297(g) between assessees who had filed returns of income before 1-4-1962, and whose assessments were completed before that date and assessees who had filed returns of income before 1-4-1962, but whose assessments were completed on or after 1-4-1962 and, this is an intelligible classification - Held, yes - Whether clauses (f) and (g) of section 297(2) is not to discriminate against those assessees whose assessments for year ending on 31-3-1962, or any earlier year had not been completed before 1-4-1962, but to bring them in line with other assessees whose assessments are completed on or after 1-4-1962, in matter of imposition of penalty - Held, yes - Whether, in view of aforesaid, it could be concluded that section 297 (2)(g) was not violative of Article 14 of Constitution of India - Held, yes

FACT: The petitioner, assessee took forest contracts. It ran a saw-mill and also manufactured and sold furniture. It also did stone quarrying business. For the assessment year 1959-60 the petitioner filed a return of its income under section 22(2) of Act, 1922, on 21-10-1959, showing an income of Rs. 7,896. In the assessment proceedings the ITO noticed some discrepancies in the accounts and registers maintained by the assessee of its business and called upon the assessee to explain the discrepancies and furnish certain particulars. Thereupon, the assessee filed a revised return of its income on 17-1-1964, disclosing its total income as Rs. 50,605. The ITO finalized the assessment on 19-3-1964, after taking into consideration the revised return and issued a notice to the petitioner under section 271(1)(c) for concealment of income. The ITO referred the matter to the AAC as penalty intended to imposed by him exceeded Rs. 1,000.

The Inspecting Assistant Commissioner, finding that the assessee had concealed the particular of its income, made the impugned order imposing a penalty of Rs. 25,000 on the petitioner. The petitioner then preferred an appeal before the Tribunal which was dismissed. In the instant writ petition. It was contended by the petitioner that section 297(2)(g) being violative of article 14 of the Constitution is invalid and, therefore, no penalty could be imposed on the petitioner under section 271 and, that under section 271(1) a penalty can be imposed by the Income-tax Officer or the Appellate Assistant Commissioner only if he, in the course of any proceedings under the Act of 1961, is satisfied that any person has committed any of the acts enumerated in clauses (a), (b) or (c) of section 271(1); that, as the assessment against the petitioner was made under the Act of 1922, and not under the Act of 1961, the Income-tax Officer or the Appellate Assistant Commissioner had no jurisdiction to impose any penalty under section 271(1).

HELD: The effect of clauses (a), (f) and (g) of section 297(2) is that where the assessee files a return of income before the commencement of the Act of 1961, that is before 1-4-1962, for any assessment year, then the assessment of that person for that year is under the 1922 Act; any proceeding for the imposition of a penalty in respect of any assessment completed before 1-4-1962, can be initiated and penalty can be imposed under the 1922 Act; any proceedings for the imposition of a penalty in respect of any assessment for the year ending on 31-3-1962 or any earlier year which is completed on or after 1-4-1962 can be initiated and penalty can be imposed under the 1961 Act. In the present case, the petitioner filed a return of income before 1-4-1962, but the assessment was completed on 19-3-1964, that is after 1-4-1962, therefore, clause (g) of section 297(2) was plainly attracted for the initiation of proceedings for imposition of penalty under the Act of 1961.

to the knowledge of the assessee and it is established, then such disclosure cannot take it out from the purview of the act of concealment of particulars of furnishing inaccurate particulars thereof for the purpose of levy of penalty. The penalty under section 271(1)(c) is leviable if the Assessing Officer is satisfied in the course of any proceedings under this Act that any person has concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars of such income. [Para 11.2] Indisputedly, the assessee, instead of rebutting the statement of 'S' recorded on oath during the remand proceedings, surrendered the amount and sought to withdraw the appeal filed before the Commissioner (Appeals). Even during the penalty proceedings, the assessee did not submit any explanation at all before the Assessing Officer. In these circumstances, it does not lie in the mouth of the assessee that it did not conceal particulars of its income in the return filed originally. In the course of penalty proceedings, the assessee did not bring any material before the Assessing Officer to rebut the inference drawn by the Assessing Officer in the course of reassessment proceedings. In terms of provisions of section 271(1)(c) read with Explanation 1 thereto. It is well established that whenever there is difference between the returned and assessed income, there is inference of concealment. The Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c) raises a presumption that can be rebutted by the assessee with reference to facts of the case. Thus, the onus is on the assessee to rebut the inference of concealment. The absence of explanation itself would attract penalty. The onus laid down upon the assessee to rebut the presumption raised under Explanation 1 would not be discharged by any fantastic or fanciful explanation. It is not the law that any and every explanation has to be accepted. The provisions of clause (A) to Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c), when the assessee did not submit any explanation during penalty proceedings, is clearly attracted and the assessee has miserably failed to discharge the onus laid down in this explanation. The plea of the assessee that copy of the statement of 'S' recorded on oath was not confronted to them for rebuttal, is baseless in view of observations of the Commissioner (Appeals), wherein it is clearly mentioned that copy of the statement was supplied to the assessee and thereafter alone, the assessee surrendered the amount and sought permission to withdraw the appeal. Even otherwise, for the first time an affidavit has been filed by 'S', director of the assessee company before the Tribunal in quantum proceedings wherein it is stated that the said statement of 'S' was not made available to them. However, 'S', who appeared before the Tribunal was specifically informed that the affidavit is not of the appropriate person. Thereafter, the assessee did not file any affidavit of 'S' nor disputed the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) in quantum proceedings before the Tribunal. In penalty proceedings also, the assessee did not submit any reply before the Assessing Officer. Since the facts on record establish that the assessee was supplied a copy of the aforesaid statement recorded on oath and only thereafter, amount was surrendered during the remand proceedings and the assessee sought to withdraw their appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals), the plea made that copy of the said statement was not made available is meaningless and is not tenable. Even otherwise, since the transaction was between the assessee company and 'F' Ltd., a company controlled by 'S', all the facts were within the specific knowledge of the assessee and its Director. In fact, 'S' was confronted with the statement of 'S' recorded during the course of survey, in the reassessment proceedings. In any case, the fact remains that the said surrender was not voluntary and it is only after statement of 'S' was recorded during the remand proceedings, the assessee felt cornered and offered the amount to tax. [Para 11.3]

In this reasoning the Tribunal further held that the burden of establishing that the unexplained cash credits were the income of the assessee, was on the department and as the department had not produced evidence to show that such credits were either false or represented the income of the assessee, or that the payments were fictitious, no penalty was leviable and, therefore, deleted the penalty so imposed.

On reference : HELD: A consideration of the provisions of section 297( 2)(f) and (g) establishes that the completion of the assessment before 1-4-1962 or after 1-4-1962 would be determinative of the applicability of the provisions of the 1922 Act or the 1961 Act, as the case may be. In the instant case, though on the basis of the return originally submitted by the assessee, the assessment was completed on 12-8-1960, there was a reopening of the assessment and the reassessment was completed only on 29-2-1972. The word 'assessment' has been defined in section 2(8) as including reassessment and the definition provision would apply, if there is nothing repugnant in the subject or the context and there is nothing to indicate that the definition under section 2(8) cannot be read into section 297(2)( g). Thus, if reassessment for the year ending on 31-3-1962 or any earlier year, was completed on or after 1-4-1962, proceedings for penalty could be initiated and penalty also imposed or levied under the provisions of the 1961 Act. In the instant case, at the time when the assessment was completed, there was no finding nor even any possibility of a finding that there was any concealment, which would justify the initiation of proceedings for the levy of penalty and also the imposition of penalty and it was only at the stage of reassessment, it came to light that large unexplained hundi credits existed and that formed the basis of the reassessment, which was completed on 29-2-1972. Under those circumstances, there could be no question of any concealment prior to the completion of the original assessment on the basis of the original return filed by the assessee. What was, therefore, relevant for purpose of initiating action for levy of penalty was only the reassessment and not the original assessment and since the reassessment was completed only on 29-2-1972, according to section 297(2)(g ), proceedings for levy of penalty could be initiated under the 1961 Act and penalty could be levied in accordance with the provisions of section 271.

As regards the question of imposition of penalty, in the instant case, there was no dispute that the income returned by the assessee in respect of the relevant assessment year was far less than 80 per cent of the total income assessed. Therefore, the requirement of the first part of the Explanation to section 271(1)(c) was fully satisfied. Further, in the instant case, no explanation at all was offered by the assessee regarding the increase in perk of non-genuine hundi credits. No further evidence was also produced by the assessee despite the opportunities given to the assessee to prove the genuineness of the hundi credits. The Tribunal, while dealing with the appeals against the order of assessment for the assessment year in question, had also categorically found that the assessee did not place any evidence to prove that it had made any effort to obtain the particulars of the credit or had met with practical difficulties in that regxrd. Therefore, the entire facts and materials considered during the reassessment proceedings established clearly and cogently that there had been a concealment. The Explanation to section 271(1)(c) got attracted and the assessee was liable for penalty. The Tribunal was, therefore, not justified in cancelling the penalty.

wilful neglect on the part of the assessee results in discharge of the burden placed on the assessee under the Explanation and once that burden is discharged the position reverts to as it was before the insertion of the Explanation . That is to say that on a finding that return of income which is less than 80 per cent of the assessed income is not the result of fraud or gross or wilful neglect, the penalty cannot be sustained by raising a presumption of concealment of income under the Explanation. If in an appropriate case the Tribunal or fact-finding authority is satisfied that there is no fraud or gross or wilful neglect on the part of assessee in submitting his return, then in such a case the assessee cannot be found within the mischief of the Explanation. At best additions made on account of the provisions of sections 68, 69, 69A, 69B and 69C become relevant at the time of raising the presumption under the Explanation to section 271(1)(c) on account of difference between the assessed income and the returned income. Once the presumption of concealment or concealed income stands rebutted, it is for the department to establish that the income which the assessee is alleged to have concealed is, in fact, his income as distinguished from deemed income of the assessee which he failed to disclose in his returns. The contention that in view of the provisions of section 68 for treating unexplained cash credits in the books of account of the assessee as income of the previous year relevant to the assessment years in question, the further question of proving that the additions were income of the assessee of the relevant previous year for the purpose of penalty proceeding did not arise, could not be accepted.

Sections 68, 69, 69A, 69B and 69C are all part of the same scheme where certain amounts though not proved to be the income of the assessee of the previous year concerned are for the purpose of charging to tax are deemed to be so by creating legal fiction absolving the department from its initial duty to prove that any such is the income of the assessee. But for these provisions, it was for the revenue to prove that any sum, not disclosed by the assessee but which is sought to be taxed as income of the assessee, is the income of the assessee for the previous year relevant to the assessment year.

The Explanation which was inserted in section 271(1)(c) with effect from 1-4-1976 cannot be held to be retrospective in operation to govern the cases coming earlier. That fact went to show that prior to the insertion of this Explanation it was not open to the Assessing Officer to raise any presumption about specific sums added or deductions disallowed, to consider it as income in respect of which particulars of income have been concealed merely on the ground of non-submission of explanation or explanation furnished but not found satisfactory though in such an event the amount could be added or deduction disallowed by resorting to other deeming provisions. It is to be noticed that falsity of explanation was expressly put differently from mere unsatisfactory nature of explanation offered. So also a clear distinction was drawn between an explanation which is not satisfactory and which is not bona fide. The former was sufficient to include the disputed sum in the computation of income of the assessee as falsity of explanation inheres wilful non-disclosure. In the latter case, though explanation offered by the assessee in respect of such additions or disallowance may be not satisfactory in the opinion of the ITO, it may be sufficient to include it in income, but still if the assessee establishes his bona fides about the explanation submitted by him, penalty could not be imposed by invoking the Explanation.

However, as the instant case was governed by the Explanation as it existed prior to the above referred provision, the only presumption that could be raised was that in case returned income was less than 80 per cent of the assessed income, the assessee could be deemed to have concealed particulars of income. On the assessee's showing that the difference was not owing to fraud or gross or wilful neglect on his part the presumption stood rebutted.

The fiction created under sections 68, 69, 69A, 69B and 69C by itself cannot be extended to penalty proceedings to raise the presumption about concealment of such income.

The Tribunal was right in law in cancelling the penalty imposed by the ITO under section 271(1)(c).

Note - The case was decided in favour of the assessee.
