u Section 271(1)(c) of Income-tax Act, 1961
Ram Saran Gupta v. Asstt. Commissioner [1997] 58 TTJ (Jp.) 599
The word ‘conceal’ is derived from the Latin word ‘concelare’ which implies ‘Con + celare = to hide’. Webster’s International Dictionary equates its meaning “to hide or withdraw from observa­tion; to cover or keep from sight; to prevent the discrepancy of; to withhold knowledge.”
The offence of concealment is, thus, a direct attempt to hide an item of income or a portion thereof from the knowledge of the Income-tax authorities. It is implicit in the word ‘concerned’ that there has been a deliberate act on the part of the assessee.
The Apex Court in the case of Sir Shadilal Sugar & General Mills Ltd. v. Commissioner [1987] 168 ITR 705 (SC) held that where the assessee for one reason or the other, agrees or surrenders certain amount for assessment the imposition of penalty solely on the basis of the assessee’s surrender, will not be well-founded.
The additions made solely on the basis of admission do not amount to concealment where the Assessing Officer does not make any enquiry nor gives any reasoning to justify that the additional income amounted to concealment.
Where the assessee, for one reason or the other, agrees or sur­renders certain amount for assessment, the imposition of penalty solely on the basis of the assessee’s surrender, will not be well-founded, where department does not prove factum of conceal­ment by independent enquiry.

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment years 1965-66 To 1970-71 - Where in response to notice under section 148 assessee disclosed income which he did not show in original return penalty was rightly imposed [In favour of revenue]

Section 271(1)(c), Explanation 1(B) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1979-80 - Whether where assessee disclosed all facts relating to and material to computation of income, but was not able to substantiate explanation offered by it in regard to consumption of raw materials, penalty was not imposable in view of proviso to section 271(1)(c) Explanation - Held, yes - Whether where Tribunal based its conclusion of factual aspects, no referable question of law arose from its order - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1996-97 - Whether merely because case of assessee is not covered by any particular Explanation to section 271(1)(c), it does not mean that penalty cannot be imposed when there is no difficulty in determining tax sought to be evaded - Held, yes - Whether where tax sought to be evaded was because of lower rate of tax paid and not because of any addition to income, penalty was imposable under main provision and there was no need to refer to any Explanation to section 271(1)(c) - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment years 1995-96 to 1997-98 - Whether claiming of excess deduction also amounts to concealment of income - Held, yes - Whether falsehood of account can take either of two forms, either an item of receipt may be suppressed fraudulently or any item of expenditure may be falsely claimed and both types of attempt to reduce taxable income amounts to concealment of particulars of income as well as furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income and, therefore, penalty can be imposed under section 271(1)(c) for either attempt - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income
¦ Where penalty proceedings related to assessment year 1979-80 in which Explanation 1 was applicable and Tribunal had failed to consider effect of said Explanation 1, order of Tribunal deleting penalty could not be sustained [Assessment year 1979-80]
Where the penalty proceedings related to the assessment year 1979-80 in which Explanation 1, as inserted with effect from April 1, 1976, was applicable and the Tribunal had failed to consider the effect of the said Explanation 1, the order of the Tribunal deleting the penalty could not be sustained and the Tribunal was to be directed to decide the matter afresh after considering Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c), inserted with effect from 1-4-1976.

facts.text:
For the assessment year 1979-80 the assessee claimed his status as non-resident. He also gave details in an annexure showing dates of departure from and arrival in India from the year 1974 to 1978, which showed, inter alia, that for the relevant previous year, the assessee had stayed in India only for 137 days and, hence, did not satisfy the requirement of section 6(1)(a). Later, the ITO, however, noticed that the assessee’s stay in India during the preceding four years was such as to satisfy section 6(1)(c) and held that the assessee was not a non-resident and, hence, not entitled to the exemption claimed. The assessee had also obtained a certificate under section 80RRA which was not disclosed before the ITO. The ITO initiated penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) and held that since the assessee did not disclose the fact of the certificate under section 80RRA and his correct residential status although he knew about it there was a breach of the obligation under section 139(1) and, therefore, he was guilty of concealment of income. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the imposition of penalties.

On second appeal:

For the assessment year 1968-69, the assessee filed his original return without showing the income from sale of land, but when required to produce the sale deed in respect of the land sold by him, the assessee filed a revised return showing therein capital gains and business income on estimate basis. The ITO passed the assessment order and also issued notice under section 274 read with section 271 for failure to furnish the return within the stipulated time and also for concealment of income. Later, he levied penalty only under section 271(1)(c) of an amount equal to 100 per cent of the concealed income.

On writ, the assessee challenged the constitutional validity of section 271(1)(c) on two grounds: (1) that section 271(1)(c) is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as there is no classification at all even though there is a difference between various types of tax evasions; and (2) that the impugned provisions are a colourable exercise of legislative power inasmuch as in the guise of levying penalty the legislature had enacted for expropriation of the whole of the property of the citizen.

For the assessment year 1970-71, the assessee filed his return showing the income at Rs. 16,339. The ITO found deposits of Rs. 18,000 in the name of the assessee with a firm. The assessee could give no explanation about this amount. Consequently, the ITO made an addition of Rs. 18,000 to the taxable income of the assessee, which was upheld by the AAC. Later on, the ITO imposed penalty under section 271(1)(c). On appeal, the AAC, however, cancelled the penalty holding that the charge of concealment was not established. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the Explanation to section 271(1)(c) (as it stood prior to 1-4-1976) was not attracted. The Tribunal, accordingly, upheld the AAC's order.

On reference:

The assessee was doing business of preparing covers of silver for jail idols. In the year 1976, there was a search by the customs department and duplicate books of account were found in the possession of a friend of the assessee. The assessee admitted during the course of inquiries by the customs department that the duplicate books were kept at the friend’s place for fear of detection by the income-tax authorities in case of raid by that department at his house. After the scrutiny of seized documents, reassessment proceedings were initiated under section 148 for all the assessment years from 1970-71 to 1974-75. The assessing ITO estimated the income of the assessee by adopting higher rates of gross profit disregarding the book results as per the seized books. Penalty was levied for all the years on the basis of concealment as detected on reassessment.

On appeal before the Tribunal, the assessee contended that since the difference between the income returned and that assessed was mainly due to the estimation of income by the ITO, no penalty could be imposed under section 271(1)(c). On the other hand, the revenue contended that since the assessee himself had admitted that he was keeping duplicate sets of books of account at his friend’s place with a view to conceal his true income from the revenue, mens rea was clearly established and, therefore, the penalty imposed was fully justified.

For the assessment year 1968-69, the assessee firm had returned a loss of Rs. 2 lakhs. The ITO directed the assessee to produce its books of account, etc., but on its failure to do so, assessment proceedings were completed under section 144 and the total income was computed at Rs. 50,000 as against the returned loss of Rs. 2 lakhs. Penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) were initiated and the case was referred to the IAC for imposition of penalty. According to the IAC, the income concealed was Rs. 2,50,000 inasmuch as the assessee had shown a loss of Rs. 2 lakhs whereas its income was computed at Rs. 50,000 and the entire sum was the concealed income of the assessee. On appeal the Tribunal held that for the purposes of imposition of penalty under section 271(1)(c) the income concealed was the income actually determined, i.e., Rs. 50,000, and penalty was reduced to Rs. 50,000.

On reference:

While completing the assessment for the assessment year in question, the ITO noticed certain cash credits in the names of different parties. On scrutiny, the ITO did not accept these cash credits as genuine and assessed certain amount being the overall peak credit of the entire transactions as the assessee's income from undisclosed sources. Simultaneously, he disallowed the interest claimed to have been paid to the creditors. These additions were upheld in appeal before the AAC. For such concealment of income, proceedings under section 271(1)(c) were initiated. But, in spite of the service of notice, the assessee did not attend the hearing of the penalty proceedings. The IAC held that the Explanation to section 271(1)(c) as introduced with effect from 1-4-1964, applied as the return was filed after the said date. As the assessee failed to discharge the onus reposed on him, the IAC held the assessee had concealed the income added by the ITO and accordingly imposed penalty. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the Explanation to section 271(1)(c) did not apply to the assessment year in appeal and that the department had failed to prove that the amount in question constituted the assessee's taxable income. In this view of the matter, the Tribunal cancelled the penalty imposed by the IAC. On reference, the High Court held that for imposition of the penalty law applicable would be law operating on the date of filing return and thus, remanded the matter to the Tribunal to determine whether the penalty was imposable bearing in mind the applicability of section 271(1)(c) on the date of filing return. The Tribunal then disposed of the appeal holding that the assessee did not adduce any evidence to show that the concealment was not due to any fraud, gross or wilful neglect on its part and as such, the IAC was justified in drawing the presumption in accordance with the Explanation of section 271(1)(c) that amounts in question represented the concealed income of the assessee.

On reference:

The assessee-firm had two partners ‘M’ and ‘R’ but from 1965 ‘M’ became sole proprietor. On basis of some unadjusted and unclosed books of account seized by police, which were disowned by ‘M’, and certain other papers, proceedings under sections 147 and 148 for the assessment years 1962-63 to 1965-66 were initiated. No returns were filed and ‘M’ became untraceable from 1966. ‘R’, who left the country, filed some returns for the assessment years 1962-63, 1964-65 and 1965-66 with nil income. However, assessments were made and penalty under section 271(1)(c) was imposed. On appeal, the Tribunal found that the Assessing Officer had made no mention of the sales disclosed in the assessee’s books, which were stated to be unclosed and unadjusted, and it was, therefore, abso-lutely clear that the Assessing Officer was not even in a position to charge the assessee of having suppressed its sales to the department-far less was he in a position to establish that the assessee had actually made certain profits and that it had concealed the same from the department. Hence, the Tribunal held that the charge of concealment of income must fail. Further, the assessments for the assessment years 1962-63, 1964-65 and 1965-66 differed from that of the assessment year 1963-64. For the first named year, the Assessing Officer had been able to correlate the entries in the diary seized by the police with those made in the books of account produced before the department. It was clear from the assessment orders for the other three years that there was no such connection. Further, the books of account were unclosed and unadjusted, and the managing partner, who knew everything about the books, had not filed any return and became untraceable. In this position, the other partner ‘R’, who had evidently not been taking active part in the running of the firm’s business, filed some returns estimate and made no secret of how he had arrived at those figures. As ‘M’, the managing partner, had made himself scarce, the IAC could naturally not have made any attempt to give him an opportunity of being heard. So, a probe into his conduct was just not possible. In this context, it would be quite impossible to hold that the failure to return the correct income did arise out of any fraud or gross or wilful neglect, calling for the levy of penalty under section 271(1)(c). Thus, the Tribunal deleted the penalty.

On reference :

The petitioner, assessee took forest contracts. It ran a saw-mill and also manufactured and sold furniture. It also did stone quarrying business. For the assessment year 1959-60 the petitioner filed a return of its income under section 22(2) of Act, 1922, on 21-10-1959, showing an income of Rs. 7,896. In the assessment proceedings the ITO noticed some discrepancies in the accounts and registers maintained by the assessee of its business and called upon the assessee to explain the discrepancies and furnish certain particulars. Thereupon, the assessee filed a revised return of its income on 17-1-1964, disclosing its total income as Rs. 50,605. The ITO finalized the assessment on 19-3-1964, after taking into consideration the revised return and issued a notice to the petitioner under section 271(1)(c) for concealment of income. The ITO referred the matter to the AAC as penalty intended to imposed by him exceeded Rs. 1,000.

The Inspecting Assistant Commissioner, finding that the assessee had concealed the particular of its income, made the impugned order imposing a penalty of Rs. 25,000 on the petitioner. The petitioner then preferred an appeal before the Tribunal which was dismissed. In the instant writ petition. It was contended by the petitioner that section 297(2)(g) being violative of article 14 of the Constitution is invalid and, therefore, no penalty could be imposed on the petitioner under section 271 and, that under section 271(1) a penalty can be imposed by the Income-tax Officer or the Appellate Assistant Commissioner only if he, in the course of any proceedings under the Act of 1961, is satisfied that any person has committed any of the acts enumerated in clauses (a), (b) or (c) of section 271(1); that, as the assessment against the petitioner was made under the Act of 1922, and not under the Act of 1961, the Income-tax Officer or the Appellate Assistant Commissioner had no jurisdiction to impose any penalty under section 271(1).

While completing the assessment for the assessment year 1982-83, the Assessing Officer found that out of total sales, major sales had been made by the assessee-firm to its three sister concerns at prices which were lower than the prices which were charged by the assessee for selling the same goods to outsiders. The sister concerns had in turn sold the goods to third parties on the same date and in the same quantity but at a higher price. The delivery of the goods was made directly by the assessee to third parties whereas the sales to the sister concerns were merely paper transactions. Out of the three sister concerns, H was a manufacturing concern having no separate manufacturing premises and was using the assessee’s factory premises without payment of any rent whatsoever. Second sister concern P had five partners, who were family members and were partners of the assessee-firm also. The Assessing Officer held that the transactions with the sister concerns were sham and bogus and amount of profits had been diverted to the sister concerns. He, therefore, made additions and completed the assessments.

On appeal, the Tribunal, on the basis of its order for the assessment year 1981-82, upheld the addition. The Assessing Officer also initiated penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) and levied penalty for the concealment of income. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the levy of penalty under section 271(1)(c).

On second appeal, the assessee contended that the Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c) had not been specifically invoked and considered by the Commissioner (Appeals) :

The assessee-firm filed a return showing an income. The ITO completed the assessment on the higher income. The penalty proceedings were initiated under section 271(1)(c) in respect of unexplained cash credit and unexplained investment. The case was referred by the ITO to the IAC who issued a show-cause under section 274 in response to the notice the assessee filed a written reply which was not accepted by the IAC and he found that the assessee interpolated the entries in the cash book with regard to the credit of certain amount. He further recorded a finding that the assessee tried to evade taxes by claiming the business as a separate unit and that the explanation given regarding the cash credit was not even probable. The assessee filed an appeal and the Tribunal set aside both these findings and held that in the absence of finding that the assessee made any attempt to conceal the facts, it would be difficult to give a finding that merely because the assessee failed in his device to illegally avoid taxes he could be held guilty within the provisions of section 271(1)(c)

During the period relevant to the assessment year 1969-70, the assessee's wife and minor sons received interest income of Rs. 6,449 from the firm in which the assessee was a partner. This sum was included in assessee's hands, in terms of section 64, in addition to Rs. 3,500 (representing low drawings for meeting his expenditure) and Rs. 4,660 (towards unexplained investment in house construction) under the head "Income from other sources". As the returned income fell short of 80 per cent of the income finally assessed, action under section 271(1)(c) was initiated, and the IAC levied penalty of Rs. 14,609 by invoking Explanation to section 271(1)(c). On appeal, the Tribunal held that (i) mere addition on estimate did not indicate concealment of income; and (ii) since neither section 64 nor section 139 imposed any obligation on the assessee to include the income of his wife and minor sons in his returns of income, section 271(1)(c) was not attracted. The penalty was, accordingly, cancelled.

On reference:

The assessee-firm was carrying on business as transport contractors. The assessee did not own any lorries of its own. It arranged lorries for transport on brokerage, commission or contract basis. For the assessment years 1975-76 to 1979-80, the ITO in view of oral evidence gathered from several lorry owners held that the assessee had inflated hire charges paid to lorry owners. The assesses having come to the Commissioner for settlement on the issue of addition, it was agreed that the inflation on hire charges paid might be taken at a sum of Rs. 50 per lorry per trip. The ITO also levied penalty for concealment of income under section 271(1)(c). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that Explanation to section 271(1)(c) was attracted and the assessee was liable to penalty under section 271(1)(c).

On second appeal:

For the assessment year 1968-69, the assessee, an unregistered firm, deriving income from the business of manufacture and sale of oil, returned a loss of Rs. 2,00,000. On its failure to produce its accounts, the ITO, under section 144, computed its total income at Rs. 50,000 and the IAC imposed a penalty of Rs. 2,50,000, holding (i) that the Explanation to section 271(1)(c) [as it stood before 1-4-1976] was attracted, and (ii) that the income concealed was Rs. 2,50,000, i.e., Rs. 2,00,000 plus Rs. 50,000. On appeal, the Tribunal, by majority, reduced the quantum of penalty to Rs. 50,000 on the ground that the income concealed was the income actually determined by the ITO, i.e., Rs. 50,000.

On reference:

The assessee- company filed a return showing income without adjustment of brought forward losses of earlier years. Its income was finally assessed which was subject to the brought forward losses being adjusted. This resulted in a net loss to be carried forward. The ITO Initiated penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) on the ground that the particulars of income in respect of five items had been concealed to evade tax. These items were expenses relating to furnace oil, fixed deposit and interest thereon, closing stock and bad debts. The assessee contended that no part of the income should be treated as concealed income, and that no penalty was leviable because after adjustment of carry forward losses the assessed income would be in the negative figure. The ITO rejected both the contentions and imposed penalty. The Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the penalty.

On second appeal:

For concealment of income the ITO imposed penalty upon the assessee under section 271(1)(c) read with Explanation thereto. The Tribunal, however, cancelled the penalty imposed upon the assessee. It, inter alia, followed the judgment of the Punjab and Haryana High Court in Addl. CIT v. Karnail Singh V. Kaleran [1974] 94 ITR 505, holding that the Explanation appended to section 271(1)(c) by the Finance Act, 1964, did not supersede the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. Anwar Ali [1970] 76 ITR 696.

On reference:

The assessee derived income from commission earned by booking goods for transportation. A search operation resulted in seizure of incriminating documents on the basis of which the Assessing Officer found (a) variation between the figures shown in a seized paper and those shown in the commission receipt book, and (b) income generated from gitti business, and (c) commission income from transportation of gitti. He accordingly made addition in respect of all the three sources of income even though the assessee disclaimed any such income from gitti business or from the gitti transportation and furnished confirmation letters from the truck owners and purchasers to the effect that no commission was being paid to the assessee. On the same basis, the Assessing Officer levied penalty under section 271(1)(c). The assessee took the plea that as once a truck was going with gitti, on return trip it was getting commission for transportation of goods of others and not from transportation of gitti. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the assessee’s further plea that no penalty was leviable since income determined from various sources was on estimate, and observed that the fact stood proved on record that the assessee had concealed bare facts by which it could be easily inferred that it was concealing the sources of income as well as the real income from commission. He, thus, upheld the penalty.

On second appeal :

For the assessment year 1974-75, the assessee-company returned an income of Rs. 1,39,180. But assessment was made on an income of Rs. 2,80,060. The additions were made on account of (i) certain purchases of raw materials and other items for which payments were not shown or bills not produced, (ii ) low inadequate and unsatisfactory G.P. rate, (iii) cessation of certain liabilities under section 41(1), and (iv) under-statement of profit and short-term capital gains on sale of certain machines, etc. In all these cases, the assessee opted to surrender the respective amounts. The Assessing Officer levied penalty under section 271(1)(c ) on the ground that additions represented a clear case of concealment of particulars of income by the assessee.

On appeal, the first appellate authority cancelled the penalty on the ground that there was no case of conscious concealment and additions were made simply on account of lack of opportunity to the assessee, that addition made on account of low G.P. rate did not make out a case for concealment, that books of account were in possession of the department and assessment was being finalised in March and that the surrenders were made with a view to buy peace and to avoid penalty.

On revenue’s appeal :

During the course of assessment proceedings of the assessee-firm, the ITO noticed certain cash credits in its account books in the names of certain parties. The ITO, being dissatisfied with the explanation of the assessee with regard to nature and source thereof, treated all those credits as income of the assessee from undisclosed sources. The ITO also initiated penalty proceedings with a view to levy penalty under section 274/271(1)(c) on the ground that the assessee had concealed its income represented by the cash credits. The IAC examined the items of cash credits separately and found that in respect of some cash credits the assessee had led no evidence and in respect of others the evidence led by it was not acceptable. He, accordingly held that all the cash credits had rightly been treated as the assessee's income inasmuch as he had not included this income in its return and was guilty of concealment. He, accordingly, levied a penalty of Rs. 35,754. On appeal before the Tribunal, the revenue sought to rely upon the Explanation to section 271(1)(c) which has been added with effect from 1-4-1964, and submitted that as per the Explanation, where the total income returned by any person is less than 80 per cent of the total income as assessed, such person shall, unless he proves that the failure to return the correct income did not arise from any fraud or any gross or wilful neglect on his part, be deemed to have concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars of such income for purposes of clause (c) of section 271(1).

The Tribunal repelled that contention on ground that the authority below had acted upon basis that assessee would come under the main provision of section 271(1)(c) and charge was not under Explanation and as such the penalty could not be justified under Explanation.

On reference :

For the assessment year 1978-79, the assessee-firm had filed a loss return but its accounts were treated as unreliable by the ITO and assessment was made on positive income of a certain amount, under the proviso to section 145(1). The assessee accepted the assessment and did not go in appeal for the reason that the firm had since been dissolved and the amount of tax was small. Subsequently, on the basis of the assessment order and influenced by the factor that no appeal had been filed, the ITO initiated penalty proceedings and imposed penalty on the assessee for concealment of income. The assessee’s appeal was rejected by the Commissioner (Appeals) as its explanation was found unsubstantiated.

On second appeal, the assessee, in addition to contesting the levy of penalty on merit, contended that the lower authorities were wrong in applying the old Explanation to section 271(l)(c) as it stood prior to 1-4-1976, instead of the new Explanation.

section 271AAB before the Commissioner (Appeals) and it was submitted that penalty under this provision was not leviable as the assessment year 2014-15 was not covered under the definition of 'specified year' as due date for filing return of income for assessment year under appeal had already been expired before the date of search. The Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the contention of the assessee and quashed the penalty order passed by the Assessing Officer under section 271AAB. The Commissioner (Appeals), however, proceeded to note that assessee filed return of income in response to notice under section 153A, and, therefore, it was clear that although due date of filing of return under section 139(1) had expired, the assessee had not filed return of income till the date of the search on 16-10-2014. After the search, assessee filed return of income. Therefore, the general provisions of section 271(1)(c), read with Explanation 5A, were attracted. He noted that Commissioner (Appeals) had power to initiate penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c). The Commissioner (Appeals) had recorded satisfaction during proceedings pending under the Act and opined that since no return of income was filed in the regular course and it was filed only after search and seizure operation, it was clear cut case of concealment of income. The Commissioner (Appeals) noted that Explanation 5A to section 271(1)(c) was applicable in this case. As per assessment order incriminating material was seized from the premises of R.K. Kedia which evidenced that unaccounted cash (earned through purchase and sale of gold) of the assessee was utilised for obtaining accommodation entries of bogus long term capital gain in the hands of family members of the assessee and material was confronted to the assessee. Therefore, it was a case of concealment of income under section 271(1)(c). The Commissioner (Appeals), therefore, held that as no return of income under normal course i.e., under section 139 was filed, the entire tax calculated on the assessed income i.e., Rs.7.16 crores was tax sought to be evaded in this case. The Commissioner (Appeals) levied the penalty at 150 per cent of the tax sought to be evaded and worked-out the penalty to Rs. 3.48 crores.

On appeal to the Tribunal:

For the assessment year 1965-66, the assessee-firm, due to change in its constitution, initially filed two returns on 30-9-1965—one for 1-10-1963 to 9-7-1964 and another for 10-7-1964 to 30-9-1964—declaring the incomes at Rs. 3,96,083 and Rs. 1,72,868, respectively. It subsequently filed two revised returns. One on. 2-1-1970 (showing the income for the first period at Rs. 1,72,868) and another on 7-1-1970 (declaring the income for the second period at Rs. 5,70,849). After detection by the ITO of a deficit cash balance of Rs. 19,087, the assessee again submitted another revised return on 31-1-1970 showing the income for the second period at Rs. 5,89,936. The ITO completed the assessment on 30-3-1970 on a total income of Rs. 6,82,028, which was reduced to Rs. 5,92,030 by the AAC. Except the last return filed on 31-1-1970, the assessee had concealed the particulars of income in the preceding four returns. The ITO, accordingly, instituted penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) in respect of all these four returns. Acting under section 274(2), the IAC eventually imposed a penalty of Rs. 20,000 under section 271(1)(c ), as it stood amended by the Finance Act, 1968, with effect from 1-4-1968. On appeal, the Tribunal found, as a fact, that although there was a concealment in all the four returns, the particulars shown in the original returns as well as in the revised returns, were identical. It, therefore, observed that since all the four returns were, based on the self-same facts, it could not hold that there were two offences of concealments. It further held that since the pre-amended provisions of section 271(1)(c) were applicable, a minimum penalty should be computed.

On reference:

The assessee had constructed four shops and he had shown the cost of construction as per books in a sum of Rs. 15,337. The ITO, however, was of the view that the cost of construction he had shown in the books of account was on the lower side. Later on, the assessee submitted a report from the approved valuer who had estimated the cost of construction in a sum of Rs. 35,900. He produced before the ITO another valuation report showing the cost of construction in a sum of Rs. 21,000. In view of the difference, the ITO had valuation through a valuer of the Department, who estimated the cost of construction at Rs. 24,000. The officer was of the view that the difference between the cost of construction shown as per the books of account and the first estimated value given by the assessee should be taken as income concealed from the Department. On that view, penalty was levied under section 271(1)(c). On second appeal the Tribunal while confirming the view of the authorities below that there was concealment of income on the part of the assessee, fixed the penalty by taking the difference between the second valuation report given by the assessee and the actual cost of construction shown in the books of account.

On reference :

After the assessee-firm had filed its return of income for the relevant assessment year, a search was conducted at its business premises. Among the papers seized was a diary in which substantial sales were recorded. These sales were not recorded in the assessee’s books of account. The ITO asked the assessee to explain those documents.

The assessee, without tendering any explanation, surrendered the entire amount of unaccounted sales by way of a revised return. In a forwarding letter accompanying the revised return, the assessee stated that it was doing so to purchase peace and close litigation, as it lacked documentary evidence to establish the nature and source of the investment in the un-accounted sales or the profit therefrom. The ITO completed the assess- ment by including, inter alia, the amounts so surrendered in the assessee’s income. The ITO also initiated penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) for concealment of income and under section 273(c) for failure to furnish an estimate of advance tax payable by the assessee under section 212(3A), and eventually levied penalties under both the sections. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the penalties.

On second appeal, the assessee contended, inter alia (i ) that the revised return filed by it in the circumstances given in the letter accompanying it was a bona fide one and no penalty should have been levied, and (ii) that the department had failed to discharge its burden of proving conceal- ment.

During the assessment year 1968-69, the assessee obtained a licence for import of nickel anodes and made two bills which worked out to be Rs. 30,863. These goods were not received by the assessee during the relevant accounting year. The ITO found that the assessee had paid certain amount towards clearing, shipping and forwarding charges. The assessee then debited to the goods account the entire amount but in drawing up profit and loss account, the assessee failed to include the value of the goods in closing stock. However, when the assessee was asked to explain it, it immediately filed a revised return in which income with reference to the original return was increased by Rs. 30,863 while the amount spent towards shipping/clearing charges was not included even at that stage. The IAC initiated penalty proceedings in regard to the total amount of Rs. 39,363 and levied penalty under section 271(1)(c). held.text:
From the facts which were found during the course of search on the basis of documents maintained by the assessee, it was clear that the assessee was indulged in the unaccounted sales. The sales which were being shown to the Income-tax Department were not fully accounted for. It was not the case of the assessee that the unaccounted sales had not resulted into any profit. Sundry debtors from which amounts were receivable against unaccounted sales as on 31-3-2004 were to the extent of Rs. 93.54 lakhs. Thus, the sales which were material for the purpose of disclosing the income had not been disclosed in the return. During the course of the proceedings under section 153A, the assessee had also filed a chart showing unaccounted income and investment statement for all the assessment years. [Para 3.19]

The Explanations 1 to 4 to section 271(1)(c) were introduced by the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 1975. These Explanations were introduced on the basis of the Wanchoo Committee Report. Earlier the concealment penalty was based on the quantum of income concealed and there was an Explanation that in case the returned income is less than 80 per cent of the assessed income, then the burden of proving that concealment was on the assessee. Wanchoo Committee recommended that the penalty should be based on the amount of tax sought to be evaded. What is meant by tax sought to be evaded was mentioned in the Explanation 4. [Para 3.20]

From the judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Dharamendra Textile Processors [2008] 306 ITR 277/ 174 Taxman 571, it was clear that the object behind enactment of section 271(1)(c ) was to provide a remedy for loss of revenue. Wilful concealment is not an essential ingredient for imposing penalty, as that is the requirement in case a prosecution is launched. However, in the instant case, the assessee was fully aware of the fact of unaccounted sales. He was fully aware of the income from such sales. He had not given any explanation to say as to why such sales were not disclosed in the original return. The explanation for not disclosing such sales was not forthcoming. Only explanation given was that the income had been surrendered to purchase peace and to avoid litigation. [Para 3.21]

The assessee had not agreed to an item to be included in the income, which was being reflected in the books of account. This was a case where unaccounted sales were found during the course of search and amount outstanding on account of such sales were found. Even in respect of accounted sales, the assessee was preparing the purchase vouchers as actual purchases were made from hawkers and no purchase bills were obtained from them. [Para 3.22]

In the original return, the assessee had not disclosed the entire sales. That fact was material to the computation of the total income. No explanation had been offered as to why such sales were not reflected in the original return. The only explanation submitted was that the assessee agreed to the addition to purchase peace. Such explanation could not be considered as bona fide because the documents relating to such unaccounted sales were found. It was also found that the assessee was having unaccounted debtors to the extent of Rs. 93.54 lakhs as on 31-3-2004. Hence, in the instant case, the Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c) was squarely applicable for imposition of penalty. [Para 3.24]

As per section 271(1B), there is deemed satisfaction in respect of additions made. The Assessing Officer had imposed penalty not only on the addition made to the income returned under section 153A but also on the difference between the original returned income and the income returned in response to the notice under section 153A. The Act does not require any specific form of satisfaction to be recorded. The satisfaction can be inferred from the assessment order. [Para 4.1]

From the observations of the Assessing Officer recorded in the assessment order it was clear that the Assessing Officer was satisfied that the additional income being offered was the concealed income. The narration of the facts in the assessment order and mentioning of incriminating documents found during the course of search showing unaccounted sales clearly indicated that the Assessing Officer was satisfied during the course of proceedings that penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) were required to be initiated. The satisfaction was evident and it could not be held that the proceedings had been initiated without recording satisfaction. [Para 4.2]

Section 271(1)(c) imposes penalty for concealment of particulars of the income or furnishing inaccurate particulars thereof. This obviously means that the act o f concealment is an overt act and stems from the return of income filed by the assessee. If an assessee does not file a return at all, action is contemplated under section 277(7)(a). But when a return is filed and particulars of income are conceale d, action is contemplated under section 271(1)(c) . Hence, the very basis for an imposition of the penalty under section 271(1)(c) is not the assessment year in respect of which the return of income has been filed but the return itself. The question is as to when the act of concealment occurred. If an act of concealment is the basis for applying the law, then the date of filing the return will be the crucial date and the law in force on that date will be applicable for deciding the quantum of penalty.

Accordingly, in the instant case, the penalty was leviable in accordance with the amended provisions of section 271(1)( c) which came into force on 1-4-1968.

The Tribunal had ignored the amendment made in Explanation to section 271(1)(c) which came into effect from 1-4-1976. The relevant part of the said Explanation was inserted by the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 1975 and the amendment has prospective effect and not retrospective effect. After this amendment, whether there is a case of penalty or not, that has to be considered in the light of the amended Explanation. After this Explanation if the Assessing Officer or the first appellate authority is satisfied that (a) any person has concealed the particulars of his income, or (b) has furnished inaccurate particulars of such income, the penalty under section 271(1)(c) should be imposed.

The expressions ‘has concealed’ and ‘has furnished inaccurate particulars’ have not been defined anywhere else in the Act but that makes no difference. The word ‘conceal’ is derived from the Latin word ‘concelare’ which implies ‘to hide’. In the Webster’s New International Dictionary, the word has been equated to hide or withdraw from observation, to cover or keep from sight; to prevent discovery of; to withhold knowledge of.

Once the Assessing Officer is satisfied and found that the assessee has offered ‘no explanation’ or offers an explanation which is not substantiated by the assessee, that represents the concealed income and in that case, that income should be deemed to have been concealed by the assessee for the purpose of section 271(1)(c).

In the instant case, the basis of addition of income was some papers found at the time of search. The author of those papers, a son of one of the partners, had admitted in the statement before the ITO that he had prepared those papers, and those papers were related to the business of the assessee-firm. On these facts and circumstances, the addition had been made on account of the concealed income that had been finally sustained by the Tribunal. That addition had not been challenged by the assessee. In these circumstances, this was a fit case for penalty. There was no reason for cancelling the penalty imposed by the Assessing Officer and sustained by the Commissioner (Appeals).

In view of the decisions in Brij Mohan v. CIT [1979 ] 120 ITR 1( SC), Hajee K. Assainar v. CIT [ 1971] 81 ITR 423 (Ker.). and CIT v. Ram Achal Ram Sewak [1977] 106 ITR 144 (All.), it has to be held that the Explanation to section 271(1)( c) shall apply to the penalty proceedings for the assessment years 1974-75 and 1975-76 and that Explanation after its amendment with effect from 1-4-1976 shall apply to the penalty proceedings for the assessment year 1976-77. In the present case, the Commissioner ( Appeals) did not take into consideration the effect of the Explanation ( before and after its amendment on 1-4-1976) in deciding the question whether the assessee was guilty of concealment of income or not. Therefore, the matter was restored to the file of the Commissioner (Appeals ) for decision afresh after considering the effect of that Explanation before and after its amendment on 1-4-1976.

If the income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment for any assessment year, by reason of omission or failure of the assessee to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for his assessment, reassessment proceeding can be initiated as provided under section 147. This again shows that full and true disclosure of income is a primary obligation of the assessee. If a person obliged to furnish the particulars of his income omits to furnish them, he thereby conceals the particulars. This concealment may take various forms. A glaring illustration of concealment would be where the assessee does not disclose or fully disclose in the return the income derived by him which would fall under a particular head, e.g., ‘Income from other sources’ while disclosing his income falling under other heads of income prescribed by section 14. To the extent he does not disclose that income, he conceals the particulars of income. The obligation is not only to disclose particulars of income but to disclose them correctly and completely. If while disclosing the particulars of income in the return he puts them under a wrong head, he can be said to be furnishing inaccurate particulars of income. The particulars of income can be made inaccurate in a variety of ways, a glaring illustration of which would be where the assessee while stating the income under a particular head, works out the income chargeable to tax after making deductions which are falsely made. Such a process would make the particulars of income inaccurate. In all such cases, whether the income is not disclosed against the constituent item of the return in which it falls or is partly not disclosed, or the particulars of income given in the return are incorrectly stated by any machination, the impact is bound to be on the figure of gross total income to be mentioned under various heads of income and also on the total income chargeable to tax. In fact, reducing the figure of income that would be chargeable to tax would be for the purpose of concealment of particulars of income or giving inaccurate particulars of income. The expression ‘particulars of income’ would have relevance to all the particulars of income which the assessee is required to give in his return fully and truly, including the particulars of income chargeable to tax under various heads and the total income. Therefore, any concealment or inaccuracy in the particulars of income in the return occurring at any stage upto and inclusive of the ultimate stage of working out of total income, would attract the penalty provision of section 271(1)(c). Every figure in the return which is set opposite to the item of income is a particular of income, whether the figure is one which is stated independently of anything else that appears in the return or the documents accompanying it or whether it is something derived from other figures elsewhere stated in such return or documents. False result may be produced by the falsity of one or more of the constituent items in the return. The words ‘inaccurate particulars’ would cover falsity in the final figure as also the constituent elements or items. They simply would mean inaccurate in some specific or definite respect whether in the constituent or subordinate items of income or the end result.

Undisputedly, the Explanation to section 271(1)(c) is a part of section 271 and, therefore, it applies notwithstanding that it may not have been separately mentioned. It is, however, clear that the presumption is not irrebutable and from the material on record, the assessee can show that there is no concealment.

The assessee had admitted that he had purchased the car for Rs. 31,000 and, therefore, that was a valid basis on which the Tribunal held that there was concealment of income to the tune of Rs. 31,000. As regards the amount which was in excess of Rs. 31,000, the Tribunal had found that it was a mere estimate by the ITO while fixing the amount that went into the purchase of the car. The finding of the Tribunal that the amount which was in excess of Rs. 31,000 involved in a factor of estimate, could not be said to be a perverse or unreasonable finding. Therefore, the Tribunal was right in law in confirming the penalty only in respect of Rs. 31,000 and cancelling the balance penalty levied under section 271(1)(c). [Para 6]

The revenue's contention that Explanation added to section 271(1)(c) with effect from 1-4-1964, applied, had no substance. In fact the return was filed much earlier to 1-4-1964, and reassessment was completed on 28-8-1958, which again was set aside by the AAC on 6-11-1959. That being the position, the Tribunal was correct in its view that the revenue was required to prove concealment. Accordingly, the penalty under section 271(1)(c) could not be imposed.

The order passed by the Tribunal was based upon two decisions in CIT v. Ravail Singh & Co. [2002] 254 ITR 191 / 122 Taxman 831 and Hari Gopal Singh v. CIT [2002] 258 ITR 85 / 125 Taxman 242. In both these decisions, the Court had held that in order to attract clause (c) of section 271(1), it is necessary that there must be concealment by the assessee of the particulars of his income or furnishing of inaccurate particulars of such income. The provisions of section 271(1)(c) are not attracted to cases where the income of an assessee is assessed on an estimate basis and additions are made therein. It was held that when the addition had been made on the basis of estimate and not on account of any concrete evidence of concealment, then the penalty was not leviable. The similar view was also taken by the Court in CIT v. Dhillon Rice Mills [2002] 256 ITR 447 /[2003] 127 Taxman 529. [Para 7]

In view of the aforesaid factual and legal position, no substantial question of law arose from the order passed by the Tribunal. [Para 8]

In view of the above, the Instruction No. 1979 being not issued in exercise of power conferred on the CBDT under section 119 is not statutory instruction but merely administrative instruction for the guidance of the income-tax authorities. Thus, the same cannot be enforced through a court of law. Therefore, there was no force in the preliminary objection raised by the assessee. As regards imposition of penalty under section 271(1)(c), as per Explanation-1 to section 271(1)(c), penalty for concealment can be imposed only if both the conditions, namely, the assessee has failed to substantiate its explanation and has also failed to prove its bona fide, have been fulfilled. In case any of the two conditions is not fulfilled, no penalty under section 271(1)(c) is imposable. In other words, even if the assessee is not able to substantiate its explanation but if such explanation is bona fide, no penalty under section 271(1)(c) is imposed. In the instant case, the assessee had failed to substantiate its explanation in respect of the deposits made in the name of partners satisfactorily. However, bona fide of his explanation made in that regard had not been doubted by the department. In the circumstances, there was no infirmity in the order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals) cancelling the penalty order of the Assessing Officer.

Section 271(1)(c) may be attracted where in the course of any proceedings under the Act the Assessing Officer or first appellate authority is satisfied that any person has concealed the particulars of his income; or has furnished inaccurate particulars of such income.

The expressions ‘has concealed the particulars of income’ and ‘has furnished inaccurate particulars of income’ have not been defined either in this section or elsewhere in the Act. It is quite obvious that in the former situation the keeping of certain portion of income is direct whereas in the latter situation it may be indirect. In furnishing the return of his income the assessee is required to furnish particulars and accounts on which such returned income has been arrived. These may be particulars as per the books of account. Inaccuracy made in such books of account which resulted in keeping off or concealing a portion of his income would be liable to be penalized as furnishing inaccurate particulars of income. The assessee may in such a situation also be construed as having concealed the particulars of its income inasmuch as a portion of his income has been kept off of the return by him. Both the offences thus in most situations may be overlapping.

In the instant case the Assessing Officer had recorded in the assessment order that the notice for default under section 271(1)(c) may be issued for concealment of income. During the course of penalty proceedings, apart from issuing a formal show-cause notice under section 271(1)(c ), the Assessing Officer had specifically confronted the assessee with the facts pertaining to diversion of profits through the instrumentality of sham sale transactions with the sister concerns and called upon the assessee to explain why penalty for concealing the particulars of income may not be levied. The assessee furnished its reply.

The Assessing Officer after elaborate discussion of the facts and circumstances of case came to the conclusion that the assessee had concealed the income by diverting the profits to its sister concerns. The Assessing Officer had further observed that the assessee had furnished inaccurate particulars of its income. On these facts the charge of concealment had been specifically and unambiguously brought out by the Assessing Officer in the show-cause notice issued to the assessee as well as in the penalty order passed by the Assessing Officer. In the show-cause notice, the Assessing Officer had clearly indicated the default of concealing the particulars of income. The satisfaction recorded in the assessment order using the words ‘concealment of income’ clearly brought out the charge that the penalty was proposed to be levied for concealing the particulars of income. The income could be concealed obviously by concealing the particulars thereof. Looking to the fact that the penalty proceedings before the Assessing Officer do not have formal trappings of a criminal trial and nuances of criminality cannot be imported into such proceedings, strict procedural requirements of a criminal trial like issue of the formal charge-sheet are not necessary in such proceedings. The assessee had been allowed appropriate opportunity of being heard as per the provisions of section 274. The basic requirement had been duly complied with by the Assessing Officer inasmuch as the Assessing Officer had indicated that the penalty under section 271(1)(c) was proposed to be levied for concealing the particulars of income represented by diversion of profits through sham transactions with the sister concerns. No prejudice, therefore, had been caused to the assessee in the matter of rebutting the case against it.

The crux of the matter to be examined was whether penalty under section 271(1)(c), read with the Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c ) was applicable to the facts of the instant case. The proceedings under section 271(1)(c ) can be initiated only if the Assessing Officer or the first appellate authority is satisfied in the course of any proceedings under the Act that any person has concealed the particulars of his income or has furnished inaccurate particulars of such income and he may direct that such person shall pay by way of penalty the sum mentioned in sub-clause (iii) of clause (c) of section 271(1)(c). The expression used in clause (c) is ‘has concealed the particulars of his income’ or ‘furnished inaccurate particulars of such income’. Therefore, in both cases of concealment and inaccuracy the phrase ‘particulars of income’ is used. The expressions ‘has concealed the particulars of income’ and ‘has furnished inaccurate particulars of income’ have not been defined either in section 271(1)(c) or elsewhere in the Act. [Para 8]

The word ‘conceal’ is derived from the latin word concelare which implies to hide. The offence of concealment is, thus, a direct attempt to hide an item of income or a portion thereof from the knowledge of the income-tax authorities. [Para 10]

It may be noted that these words ‘concealed’, ‘particulars’ and ‘inaccurate’ are with regard to income and not with regard to any other thing. In the light of above discussion it can be said that there cannot be a straitjacket formula for detection of default of concealment of particulars or furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income. It depends upon the facts of each case. In the case under consideration, there was no dispute that purchases were made, though the assessee failed to substantiate its claim to the extent that the purchases were made from that particular party. Therefore, in the case under consideration, the word ‘particulars’ used in section 271(1)(c ) would embrace the meaning of the purchases made and not the party from whom these were made. As stated above that words ‘concealed’, ‘particulars’ and ‘inaccurate’ are with regard to income and not with regard to any other thing. From which party the purchases were made is not much important while computing the income. The important aspect in computing income is purchases. In the case under consideration, the purchases were recorded regularly in the books of account on day-to-day basis. The Tribunal while deciding the quantum matter observed that the assessee must have made purchases from the market from unregistered dealers in cash and details could not be obtained from such dealers. The assessee, therefore, obtained hawala bills from ‘F’. The Tribunal further observed that the Commissioner (Appeals) was of the view that in these circumstances the assessee must have inflated the purchase bills and on that account the disallowance to the extent of 25 per cent was found to be reasonable. The case of the Assessing Officer in quantum matter was that the entire purchases were disallowable whereas the appellate authorities found that the assessee must have made the purchases but the same might not be from ‘F’. Actual purchases made by the assessee were not doubted by the appellate authorities while deciding the quantum matter. However, considering the circumstances, they confirmed the addition to the extent of 25 per cent of the relevant purchases on the basis of the facts, figures and particulars provided by the assessee. Thus, the main basis on which the Assessing Officer levied penalty was not sustained by the appellate authorities. [Para 11]

In addition to main provisions of concealment, namely, ‘has concealed the particulars of his income’ or ‘has furnished inaccurate particulars of such income’ there are those which are deemed to represent the income in respect of which particulars have been concealed. The deemed concealment is provided in the Explanations. Often a question arises whether in cases where additions or disallowances are made by the ITO, the penal provisions of section 271(1)(c) would attract. The Explanation 1 takes care of this situation. [Para 12]

In the instant case, there was no evidence to prove that the assessee had purchased the silver on credit. If the assessee had purchased the silver on credit, it could have very easily produced copies of the accounts of the party from whom the silver had been purchased, but no such evidence was produced. If the assessee had received any silver from the customers whom it was allegedly used to hand over silver to the assessee, the assessee could have very well given the names of those customers so that the department could have examined them, but the assessee did not give any such names of the customers. In the case of CIT v. Mussadilal Ram Bharose [1987] 165 ITR 14 (SC) , it was held that under the Explanation to section 271(1)(c) , the presumption raised against the assessee is a rebuttable one and it is for the fact-finding body to judge the relevancy and sufficiency of the materials. Thus, in the instant case, it was for the assessee initially to prove that it was not guilty of gross or fraud or wilful neglect as a result of which it had concealed the income. This presumption could be rebutted but the assessee had not placed any convincing evidence to rebut the presumption against it. Thus, the assessee had not discharged the onus under the Explanation to section 271(1)(c) . This was a clear case where the assessee had deliberately suppressed the transactions in respect of 23 post parcels received and the investment made in the purchase of silver in respect of these 23 post parcels had not been entered into the books of account. The assessee had deliberately concealed the particulars of income and, thus, it was a clear case which fell within the mischief of section 271(1)(c) read with Explanation thereto. Thus, the penalty was rightly levied in respect of the sum of Rs. 95,442 which represented unexplained investment by the assessee.

violate article 14 of the Constitution. As regards the challenge on the grounds of article 19(1)(f ), it could not be said that the provisions are expropriatory. After all, all kinds of punishment and penalties can be said to be ex-proprietary in the sense that some part of the property of the delinquent concerned goes to the State. But, the power to impose punishment and penalties is incidental to the power for vindicating the main purpose of that power. The power to levy tax on income is vested in Parliament and, as incidental thereto, the power to impose penalties to vindicate that particular power of imposition of tax must also be given to the legislature.

The object of the legislature in the impugned provision is not to provide for any confiscation but to provide a penalty for concealment of income and that too by providing a deterrent penalty. Deterrence is the main theme or object behind the imposition of penalty and the whole object as shown by the history to this scheme of provisions is to provide gradually more and more deterrent penalties with a view to see that tax evasion does not take place and result in detriment to society as a whole. Therefore, it was not possible to say that the provisions of section 271(1)(c)( iii) infringe article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. Therefore, each of the special civil applications was dismissed.

Note: The case was decided in favour of revenue.

Section 271(1)(c ) may be attracted where in the course of any proceedings under the Act, the Assessing Officer or the first appellate authority is satisfied that any person has concealed the particulars of his income or has furnished inaccurate particulars of such income.

The word ‘deliberately’ appearing before the expression ‘furnished inaccurate particulars of income, was deleted by the Finance Act, 1964 (5 of 1964) with effect from 1-4-1964. The expressions ‘has concealed the particulars of income’ and ‘has furnished inaccurate particulars of income’ have not been defined either in section 271 or elsewhere in the Act. One thing is certain that these two circumstances are not identical in detail, although they may lead to the same effect : keeping off a certain portion of income. The former is direct and the latter may be indirect in its execution. The word ‘conceal’ is derived from the latin expression ‘concelare’ which implies con + celare meaning ‘to hide’. In Webster’s New International Dictionary its meaning is equated ‘to hide or withdraw from observation; to cover or keep from sight; to prevent the discovery of; to withhold knowledge of’. The offence of concealment is, thus, a direct attempt to hide an item of income or a portion thereof from the knowledge of the income-tax authorities. ‘Concealment’ can be said to be in law the intentional suppression of truth or fact known to the injury or prejudice of another.

Where, in order to make good an omission in the originally filed return, the assessee voluntarily furnishes a revised return inclusive of the so omitted income, a question arises whether the filing of a revised return will not expatiate the contumacious conduct, if any, on the part of the assessee in not having disclosed a true income in the originally filed return. Blameworthiness attached to the assessee with reference to the original return cannot be avoided by filing a fresh return after concealment was detected by the assessing authority. Where the surrender of income made in the revised return was not voluntary, but was as a result of detection by the assessing authority, the filing of the revise return is of no consequence. The very word ‘omission’ connotes an international act. The factual position was that revised return was a veiled attempt to present a mitigating circumstance. Further, a return in response to notice under section 148 is not to be treated at par or compared to a revised return. That being the position, filing of the return including the agreed concealed income did not constitute a mitigating circumstance and penalty has been rightly levied.

It is well-settled that mere non-production of the creditors is not sufficient and only on that basis the penalty under section 271(1)(c ) cannot be levied. There are two opinions regarding the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Anwar Ali (supra ). One opinion is that even after insertion of the Explanation, the Supreme Court’s decision in Anwar Ali’s case (supra) laid down that before a person can be visited with a penalty for concealment, etc., the Department must prove that the amount in question was the income of the assessee and that he had concealed it with a motive. The other opinion is that the penalty could not be imposed because the explanation given by the assessee in regard to the items in question was not believed to be true. It is pertinent to note that the new Explanation added to section 271(1)(c) has been intelligently designed to get over the Supreme Court’s verdict in the above case.

The provisions of section 271(1)(c ) may be attracted where in the course of proceedings under the IT Act the Assessing Officer or the appellate authority is satisfied that any person—

(i)has concealed the particulars of his income, or

(ii)has furnished inaccurate particulars of such income.

The expressions "has concealed the particulars of his income" and "has furnished inaccurate particulars of his income" have not been defined either in that section or elsewhere in the Act. These two expressions are not at all identical in details but they may lead to the same effect, that is, keeping off a certain portion of income. The former expression relates to direct concealment and the latter leads to indirect concealment.

The word ‘conceal’ which is the main gist of that section, is derived from the Latin word concelare which implies con + celare - to hide. Webster, in his new International Dictionary equates its meaning "to hide; or withdraw from observation; to cover or keep from sight; to prevent discovery of; to withhold knowledge of". The concealment is, thus, a direct attempt to hide an item of income or a portion thereof from the knowledge of the IT authorities.

In Shorter Oxford Dictionary III Edn. Vol. I, the meaning of the word ‘concealment’, is given as "in law, the intentional suppression of truth or fact known to the injury or prejudice of another". In both these phrases, the words "the particulars of income" are common. There cannot be a straight-jacket formula for deduction of these defaults of concealment or of furnishing inaccurate particulars of income and indeed concealment of particulars of income and inaccurate particulars of income may, at times, overlap, as, for example, when 1/2 of the income particulars is not at all disclosed, that would amount to concealed income while the remaining 1/2, which is, in fact, disclosed, would not be complete disclosure and it would amount to inaccurate particulars of income as regards that constituent item. However, in case the returned loss is further reduced in a loss or any additions are made on the positive side by increasing the taxable income, these do not, ipso facto give a connotation that a penalty is to be levied under section 271(1)(c). Had that been the position, the Legislature, in its wisdom, could have clearly used the words "that in any and every case where the returned income is enhanced after computation of income, penalty should be levied," but the Legislature, in its wisdom, has definitely made out some room for excuse or exoneration in bona fide cases, particularly keeping in mind the ignorance of majority of taxpayers in the country, unawareness of the assessee and the particular set-up of the Indian society and their mind-set have been considered by the law-makers who are well aware of all the real facts prevailing in the Indian society. The Legislature would never repeat two expressions, that too, with the conjunction "or", so the conclusion by anybody that the two expressions, namely, "concealment of income" and "furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income" are one and not different is a wrong conclusion. Both these terminologies for the sake of expression and/or phrases have got their own meaning although with a very minute nuance which has to be deciphered by applying judicious mind to the given facts and circumstances of a particular case.

Under section 68, there can be no proceedings for the imposition of penalty because it cannot make the sole basis for the imposition of the penalty in the absence of any other material which goes to prove concealment unmistakably.

In cases of assessment on the basis of an estimate applicability of section 27I(1)(c) cannot be ruled out. It was not in dispute that the facts of the present case would fall within the above Explanation to section 271(1)(c), and, therefore, the onus would stand shifted to the assessee to show that there was no concealment of income. The assessee had not established that the gap between the income returned and the income assessed was not due to any fraud or wilful neglect on its part, for it did not produce the requisite material even when called for, for proving the correctness of the income returned. The only explanation given by the assessee was that it was not able to produce the records because of lapse of time. To find out whether the assessee had returned the income by sale of licences truly and correctly, the nature of the goods sold, the time at which it was sold and the parties to whom they were sold were all material, and so long as the assessee had not furnished the requisite particulars, the assessee should be taken to have concealed the particulars of its income. Therefore, the Tribunal was not justified in cancelling the penalties for the relevant assessment years.

As is evident from clause (c ) of section 271(1), the words used are 'has concealed the particulars of his income' or furnished 'inaccurate particulars of such income'. Thus, both in case of concealment and inaccuracy, the phrase 'particulars of income' has been used. The Legislature has not used the words 'concealed his income'. From this it would be apparent that penal provision would operate when there is a failure to disclose fully or truly all the particulars. The words 'particulars of income' refer to the facts which lead to the correct computation of income in accordance with the provisions of the Act. So, when any fact material to the determination of an item as income or material to the correct computation is not filed or that which is filed is not accurate, then the assessee would be liable to penalty under section 271(1)(c ). If the income has to be assessed under section 145, then the presumption would be that the income was not properly returned. In the instant case also , the assessee was not maintaining the accounts during the course of the business year after year and, in fact, the assessee was writing the accounts after the close of the year and inflating the expenses so as to show the income at his will. In these circumstances, it did not lie in the mouth of the assessee that he was not concealing his income by furnishing inaccurate particulars thereof, as concluded by the Assessing Officer and the Commissioner (Appeals). [Para 8]

In the case under consideration, during the course of survey, statements of various employees of the assessee were recorded. It was found that books of account for the year under consideration were to be written only after completion of March and even the books of the assessee for the preceding years were written after completion of the financial year by way of regular practice. It was also noticed that inflated expenses were debited to accounts under the instructions of the assessee even when payment for such expenses was not being made. In the light of facts found during the course of survey and on the basis of statements of various employees, ITP and the assessee, the Assessing Officer concluded that the assessee had suppressed his profit by claiming huge expenses under various heads. As a result books of account were rejected and net profit was estimated at the rate of 10 per cent in the year under consideration. The Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld the rejection of books and rate applied by the Assessing Officer while the Tribunal reduced the rate to 7 per cent on the basis of rate adopted by the Settlement Commission in the period relevant to the assessment years 1999-2000 to 2001-02. Had there been no survey operations in the premises of the assessee, the particulars which were made the basis of addition in the assessment would not have come to the notice of the Assessing Officer. In fact, the material particulars were not disclosed. The expression "conceal" as defined in Dilip N. Shroff v. Jt. CIT [2007] 291 ITR 519 / 161 Taxman 218 (SC)means to hide or keep secret. The word conceal has been derived from con plus celare, which implies to hide. There is apparently no distinction for the purpose of levy of penalty under section 158BFA(2) as to whether new item of concealment is discovered by the Commissioner (Appeals) or enhancement is proposed by him in the item already discovered by the Assessing Officer.

A comparison of these two sections, i.e., section 158BFA(2) and section 271(1)(c) clearly indicates that they are not pari materia in all respects. Following are some of the differences as apparent from the bare reading of these two sections:—

(1)

At the time of initiating penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c), the Assessing Officer is required to arrive at a satisfaction during the course of the assessment proceedings or any other proceeding during the course of which he intends to initiate penalty proceedings. There is no such requirement of satisfaction in section 158BFA(2).

(2)

Section 271(1)(c) refers to levy of penalty on income which is concealed or in respect of which inaccurate particulars have been furnished when compared with regular return of income. Thus, there is a comparison of income declared in return filed under section 139 which is treated as disclosed income with the finally assessed income which includes concealed income. In the finally assessed income, there are two types of income - one which is declared income in the regular return and which is treated as disclosed and the second is discovered by the Assessing Officer during the course of the assessment proceedings which is treated as undisclosed and which becomes the basis for levy of penalty under section 271(1)(c ). In section 158BFA(2), all the income is concealed income whether declared in the return filed under Chapter XIV-B or added by the Assessing Officer during the course of block assessment proceedings. Thus, there is no two types of income under section 158BFA(2) as compared to section 271(1)(c).

(3)

In section 271(1)(c ), explanation furnished by the assessee in respect of addition made by the Assessing Officer is considered within the meaning of Explanation (1), but recourse of this Explanation (1 ) to section 271(1)(c) cannot be taken in section 158BFA(2). The explanation furnished by the assessee for the addition made under section 158BFA(2) has to be considered only on the basis of equity and fair play and reasonableness of the explanation furnished by the assessee for not being able to work out correct undisclosed income for declaring in the return filed under section 158BC. Thus, what is to be considered is only reasonableness, bona fide, fair play and cumulative effect of surrounding circumstances under the influence of which the assessee was not able to declare complete undisclosed income. The explanation furnished by the assessee cannot be judged or evaluated on the standards set by Explanation (1) to section 271(1)(c ) or the main provisions thereof.
