(v)

Section 273B of the Act – Shelter of "reasonable cause" not available for penalties under Section 270A of the Act

As we are aware, section 273B of the Act provides for non-levy of penalty, levied under the specific provisions mentioned therein, if the taxpayer proves that there was a reasonable cause for the failure.

Interestingly and to an extent even surprisingly, the said shelter of "reasonable cause" has not been made available for penalty levied under section 270A of the Act.

(vi)

Immunity under Section 270AA of the Act not available for misreporting of income

To reduce instances of levy of penalty inter-alia in cases where the addition(s) made in the assessment /re-assessment proceedings (leading to the levy of penalty) has(ve) been accepted, section 270AA of the Act has been introduced by the Finance Act, 2017 to provide the taxpayer an opportunity to seek, from the Assessing Officer, immunity from imposition of penalty under section 270A of the Act.

This is subject to fulfillment of the following conditions:

(a)

Payment of tax and interest within the specified time.

(b)

Non filing of any appeal against the order of assessment/reassessment.

An important point to note here is that the aforesaid immunity provisions are applicable for penalty levied/sought to be levied under section 270A only vis-à-vis cases related to "underreporting of income". In other words, no immunity can be sought in cases of "misreporting of income".

In addition to above, the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT), vide Circular No. 05/2018 dated 16 August 2018, has clarified that an application made by an assessee under section 270AA of the Act seeking immunity, will not bar the assessee from contesting the same issue in any earlier assessment year. This circular also clarifies that the tax authority shall not take an adverse view in penalty proceedings for earlier assessment year(s) under the old penalty regime merely because the taxpayer has applied for immunity under the new penalty regime.

(vii)

Interplay between Section 271G of the Act and Section 270A of the Act – Double blow?

Section 270A of the Act inter-alia provides for the levy of penalty for underreporting of the income, if information prescribed under Section 92D of the Act is not maintained.

Section 271G of the Act seeks to levy a penalty of 2 percent of the value of international transaction for failure to furnish any information as required under section 92D (3) of the Act. The said section is an independent section.

Accordingly, a literal interpretation of the above sections may seemingly lead to a double blow to taxpayer by levy of the penalty in both the sections. However, one point of difference could be that penalty under section 270A of the Act may only be sustained if the transfer pricing adjustment is upheld before the higher authorities whereas the penalty under section 271G of the Act is usually independent of the fate of transfer pricing adjustments; though there are contradicting decisions on the subject.

(viii)

Thin line of difference exists between the term 'suppression of fact' (misreporting of income) and 'disclosure of material facts' (underreporting of income)

There is a thin line of difference between the term 'suppression of fact' as mentioned under misreporting of income and 'disclosure of material facts' as contemplated under underreporting of income. Given that either of the terms are not defined under the Act, it may open up the doors for prolonged litigation as penalty under the head 'underreporting' is lower than what is contemplated under 'misreporting of income'.

D. To sum up

Taxpayers and professionals, need to gear up for the new penalty regime which will have its own set of propositions to be laid out and tested at the appellate fora. It will be interesting to see how they shape up specifically in the transfer pricing world which is more a fact driven exercise. Indeed, there are exciting times ahead!

Another instance can be one where 'misrepresentation' and/or 'suppression' of facts was made by the assessee in as much as it had received amount in violation of section 269ST but gave a different shape, colour or texture to the said transaction so that it could not be caught on the parameters of section 269ST. Even if this transaction is discovered in assessment, it may not lead or result into any addition of income due to the fact of such transaction otherwise proved to be genuine. Such brazen 'misrepresentation' and/or 'suppression' of facts may be saddled with other adverse consequences, for instance, penalty under section 271DA but certainly since it is not giving rise to increase in the assessed income, this would not result into 'under reported income' and hence, there would be no penalty under section 270A.

(h)

Interestingly, clause (b) of subsection (9) of section 270A speaks of a case where there is 'failure to record investment in the books of account'. But, such 'failure to record any investment in the books of account' may result into addition under section 69 which would though result into 'under reported income' but since income under section 69 is subject to higher tax rate under section 115BBE, penalty provision as prescribed under section 271AAC would come into being not penalty provision under section 270A. Section 271AAC specifically mentions that penalty under section 270A shall not be imposed where penalty under section 271AAC is imposed. Therefore, there may be a case of 'misreporting' of such income resulting into 'under reported income' yet it is outside the scope of penalty under section 270A.

This situation would in fact emerge in all such cases where addition to the income is made in the assessment order under section 68,69, 69A to 69D, as in all such cases, penalty can be levied under section 271AAC and not under section 270A. Question arises as to when in such cases penalty under section 270A cannot be imposed, where was the necessity of enacting clause (b) to sub section (9) of section 270A.

In fact, this anomaly seems to have crept in the statute due to the reason that penalty provision of section 270A was brought into effect by the Finance Act, 2016 whereas section 271AAC was brought subsequently by the Taxation Laws (Second Amendment) Act, 2016 and legislature seems to have glossed over this 'lapse' creptor resulted subsequently in section 270A(9)(b). Therefore, when there is no such penalty that can be levied for such a situation as mentioned in clause (b) of sub section (9) under section 270A, there is no justification for continuing to retain clause (b) under subsection (9) of section 270A.

Also, it may be noted that though there is clause (b) in subsection (9) to cover the 'failure to record investment in the books of account' but there is no clause enacted as to the 'failure to record expenditure in the books of account' on similar lines. Though even if, had such clause been there under sub section (9), then also that would have led to addition under section 69C, on which penalty under section 271AAC alone could have been imposed not the one prescribed under section 270A for the reason explained in preceding paragraph. But, absence of such clause i.e. 'failure to record expenditure in the books of account' in sub section (9) on the lines of clause (b) is astonishing.

(i)

Clause (c) of subsection (9) covers claim of such 'expenditure which are not substantiated by any evidence' but despite existence of such unsubstantiated expenditure, there may not be a case of penalty under section 270A qua such expenditure.

As explained by us in the preceding paragraphs that if disallowance of an expenditure does not lead to the 'under reported income', it would not result into penalty. It may so happen in certain situations in case of unsubstantiated expenditure also.

For instance, any disallowance of expense on account of non-substantiation in case of 100% tax-exempt units would go on to swell the business profits of that unit, thus resulting into no addition to the returned income. Since there would not be 'under reported income' in such a situation, there would be no case of penalty under section 270A.

This too may have been done by 'misrepresenting the facts' and it is very well possible that it was on account of rather 'suppressing the correct facts'.

(e) 'Misrepresentation of facts' as per its natural meaning would cover within its ambit the cases where facts were something else but have been presented differently, thus leading to 'misreporting of income'. For example, income of a minor child which was to be included in the total income of the parent under section 64 was not so included and shown to have been earned by the child as if the child was major.

'Suppression of facts' would cover such cases where facts itself have been withheld, thus leading to 'misreporting of income'. For example, factum of some income though earned but was withheld from offering to tax.

If we closely examine 'Misrepresentation' and 'Suppression', we would end up in reaching traversing through the old concepts of 'furnishing inaccurately' 'concealment' of particulars of income. 'Suppression' is concealment whereas 'misrepresentation' is something, may not be concealing but 'furnishing inaccurately'. In fact, if we examine further, we would find that all the clauses covered by (b) to (f) may be covered under the clause (a) as every other clause would be a case of either misrepresentation of facts or of suppression of facts.

(f)

All cases viz. clause (a) to (f) of sub section (9) ought to lead to addition to income or disallowance of a claim resulting into the difference between assessed income and processed income. This is so because if there is no such difference, that would mean that there is no 'under reported income' and when there is no 'under reported income', there would not be 'under reported income in consequence to 'misreporting of income'. In other words, this can be put like this that even if 'charge' is there but if quantification or machinery fails, no pecuniary consequence in the form of penalty under section 270A would follow.

For instance, even if there was 'failure to report international transaction' or 'specified domestic transaction' but during the course of assessment, there may not result any addition/adjustment on this account as assessee may have proved that such transaction was entered into at arm's length price. In that situation, 'failure to report' such transaction was though ostensibly a case of 'misreporting of income' under clause (f) of subsection (9), yet in so far as the penalty under section 270A is concerned, no penalty can be imposed under that section since there was no addition/adjustment made in the assessment order and thus there was no difference on that account resulting between the assessed income and processed income and accordingly, there was thus no 'under reported income'. Since, there was no 'under reported income' resulting, there was no question of penalty under section 270A.This may be an altogether different matter that there may be other consequence for such non-disclosure, for instance, levy of penalty u/s 271AA for failure to report the international transaction or specified domestic transaction under section 92B/92BA. But, there is certainly no case of penalty under section/s 270A.

(g)

Similarly, not all the 'misrepresentation' or 'suppression' of facts as mentioned in clause (a) of sub section (9) may lead to the addition of income or disallowance of a claim, which means that in the absence of such addition or disallowance made in the assessment order to the returned income, there would not be 'under reported income' and since there would be no 'under reported income' in such a case, there would be no question of penalty under section 270A.

For instance, if a closely-held company having accumulated profits had given a loan to a shareholder who was holding more than 10% shareholding. But in order to camouflage real character of this transaction so that it can avoid the glare of applicability of section 2(22)(e), such company misrepresented this fact by terming and showing this transaction as not in the nature of loan but in the nature of advance in the course of business. Such transaction its real nature when exposed in the assessment of the company would obviously not lead to the addition of income in the hands of the company as the deemed dividend can be taxed in the hands of the shareholder. The fact of the matter is that there would be no addition in the hands of the company on this score. There would thus be no difference between the assessed income and processed income on this account in the hands of the company and thus, there would be no 'under reported income' and accordingly, there would be no penalty on the company under section 270A. Therefore, this is a classic case where despite such rank 'misrepresentation of facts', there may not be 'under reported income' in the hands of the company with no penal consequence under section 270A.

Section 158BC mandates that a person subjected to a search on or after 01-09-2024 must file a return of income in response to a notice issued by the Assessing Officer. The notice requires a person to furnish the return within the prescribed period but not exceeding 60/90 days2. Rule 12AE, which prescribes Form ITR-B for filing such returns, has been made applicable retrospectively from 01-09-2024. However, this Rule was notified only on 7th April 2025, and until this date, Form ITR-B did not exist in Income-tax Rules, 1962. Even after its notification, the form is not yet functional on the e-filing portal, creating a procedural gap in compliance with the requirement of Section 158BC.

This raises a critical issue if a notice under Section 158BC is issued on or after 01-09-2024 but before the notification of Rule 12AE, i.e., 07-04-2025, the assessee was legally required to file a return, but no prescribed form was available to comply with this obligation. This effectively places the assessee in a compliance dilemma, where a statutory obligation exists, but no practical mechanism to fulfill it has been provided.

The Rule fails to address how relief will be extended to taxpayers when a search is conducted after 01-09-2024 and a notice under Section 158BC is issued. Further, Rule 12AE does not provide any solution where an assessee is considered a defaulter because the due date for filing a return under Section 158BC had lapsed before the availability of an online mechanism to file Form ITR-B.

Introductory Remarks

1. The procedure for assessment is streamlined in Chapter XIV of the Income-tax Act (the Act). The provisions of sections 147 to 153 of the Income-tax Act (the Act) deal with assessments covering escapement of income, time limit for issuance of notice etc. The corresponding provision in the Indian Income-tax Act 1922 (the 1922 Act) was covered in section 34 of the 1922 Act. Virtually section 147 of the Act corresponds to section 34(1) and Explanation of the 1922 Act.

However, with regard to service of notice, the Supreme Court in the case of R.K. Upadhyaya v. Shanabhai P. Patel [1987] 33 Taxman 229/166 ITR 163 succinctly explained the difference between the Act and the 1922 Act.

"The scheme of the Act so far as notice for reassessment is concerned, is quite different. What used to be contained in section 34 of the 1922 Act has been spread out into three sections, being sections 147, 148 and 149 in the 1961 Act (as the Act stood then). A clear distinction has been made out between 'issue of notice' and 'service of notice' under the 1961 Act. Section 34 of the 1922 Act conferred jurisdiction on the Assessing Officer to reopen an assessment subject to service of notice within the prescribed period. Section 149 prescribes the period of limitation. It categorically prescribes that no notice under section 148 shall be issued after the prescribed limitation has lapsed. Section 148(1) provides for service of notice as a condition precedent to making the order of assessment. Once a notice is issued within the period of limitation, jurisdiction becomes vested in the Assessing Officer to proceed to reassess. The mandate of section 148(1) is that reassessment shall not be made until there has been service. The requirement of issue of notice is satisfied when a notice is actually issued. In the present case, admittedly, the notice was issued within the prescribed period of limitation, as 31-3-1970 was the last day of that period. Service under the 1961 Act is not a condition precedent to conferment of jurisdiction in the Assessing Officer to deal with the matter but it is a condition precedent to making of the order of assessment. As the Assessing Officer in the instant case had issued notice within limitations, the appeal was to be allowed and the order of the High Court was vacated."

The Finance Bill, 2021 proposes to insert a new section 148A which contains provisions for conducting an inquiry and providing an opportunity before issuance of notice under new section 148 of the Act. However, this procedure of enquiry, providing opportunity and passing an order, before issuing notice under new section 148 of the Act, shall not be applicable in search or requisition cases.

Section 149 of the Act is proposed to be amended with regard to time limit for issuance of notice.

False entry is an inclusive explanation - It includes, use or intention to use forged or falsified documents such as a false invoice, false piece of documentary evidence (challan, Dispatch proof, vouchers, confirmation, debit and credit notes, etc.), false invoice without actual supply or receipt of such goods or services or to or from a person who does not exist (hawala). As the false entry is inclusively explained, let us understand from judicial view: - When the word used is "includes" such definition is to be given a wider meaning and not exhaustive or restricted to the items contained in the definition - Krishi Utpadan Mandi Samiti v. Shankar Industries AIR 1993 SCW 762 *Tamil Nadu Kalyana Mandapam Association v. UOI [2004] 267 ITR 9/136 Taxman 596/4 STT 308 (SC)* CCT v. TTK Health Care Ltd. [2007] 11 SCC 796 (SC).

Since it is an inclusive explanation, it means the explanation is not exhaustive and will also cover its ordinary, popular and natural meaning - Lucknow Development Authority v. M. K. Gupta [1994] 1 SCC 243 & Black Diamond Beverages v. CTO [1998] 1 SCC 458.

So, as per the above judicial view scope of false entry is not restricted to the situations given in explanation to section 271AAD(2), but it can be extended by assessing officer to give natural and ordinary meaning during any proceedings.

9. 'Bitumen' is not a 'valuable article'; No Section 69A addition if transporter does not deliver it to Govt.: SC

[D. N. Singh v. CIT, [2023] 150 taxmann.com 301 (SC)]

The assessee carried on business as a carriage contractor for bitumen. It was involved in a scam of misappropriating the bitumen and not delivering the quantity lifted to the various divisions of the Road Construction Department of the Government of Bihar. Finding out that the actual quantity was not delivered, the AO invoked Section 69A and made additions due to the short supply of bitumen.

The matter reached the Supreme Court of India.

The Supreme Court held that the assessee at any point did not claim ownership over the bitumen not delivered to the authorities. It was also not a case where the assessee exercised rights available in law, entitling it to possess goods as of right or pass on the title to another under law as permitted. At best, the assessee's possession was a shade better than that of a thief as the possession had its origin under a contract of bailment.

It would be straining the law beyond justification if the Court recognised a thief as the property owner within the meaning of Section 69A. Recognising a thief as the property owner would also mean that the owner would cease to be recognised as the owner, which would indeed be the most startling result.

When the facts are clear that the assessee is not the owner and somebody else is the owner, then treating the assessee as the owner may produce the most illegal results apart from being unjust.

The intention behind introducing Section 69A was to get at income not reflected in the books of account but found to belong to the assessee. Not only must it belong to the assessee, but it must be other valuable articles.

Applying the Principle of Ejusdem Generis, bitumen would stand out as a strange bedfellow in the company of its immediate predecessor words, viz., money, bullion, and jewellery. Bitumen is a clear misfit and could not have been the legislative intention to treat it as another valuable article.

Bitumen is a residual product in petroleum refineries and is usually used in road construction. It may be found in small quantities or large quantities. If the 'article' is to be found 'valuable', then in small quantity, it must not just have some value, but it must be 'worth a good price' or 'worth a great deal of money'. If this is so, Section 69A would then stand attracted.

But if treating it as a 'valuable article' requires ownership in large quantity and multiplying the value in large quantity, a 'good price' or a 'great deal of money' is arrived at, then it would not be valuable.

Thus, the AO acted illegally in holding that the assessee was the 'owner' and made the addition under Section 69A on the said basis.

This is quite surprising that section 270A does not envisage any penalty on account of additions/disallowances/adjustments made to the returned income under section 143(1)(a). It may be recalled that section 143(1)(a) contains 6 different types of adjustments which can be made while processing the return. Such additions/disallowances/adjustments may be on account of any arithmetical error in the return, any incorrect claim if such incorrectness is apparent from any information in the return, disallowance of loss brought forward from earlier year and set off in this year which was not allowed to be carried forward as the return for that year was filed beyond the due date prescribed under section 139(1), disallowance of expenditures indicated in the audit report but not disallowed in the return, disallowance of deduction under section 10AA, 80IA, 80IAB, 80IB, 80IC, 80ID, 80IE if the return is furnished beyond the due date as prescribed under section 139(1). Legislature has not created any disincentive in the form of any additional tax on the lines of erstwhile section 143(1A), or any penalty under section 270A on account of the difference between the returned income and the processed income. Under section 271(1)(c), there was 'Explanation 6' which provided that no penalty under section 271(1)(c) would be levied in respect of prima facie adjustments made if as per the then existing provision under section 143(1A), additional tax had been charged which was equal to 20% of the tax payable on such adjustments. Under the existing provisions, there is no concept of additional tax on such adjustments except the normal tax levied on such difference. Introduction

1. It is common in enforcement provisions in a statute like levy of penalties to prescribe the minimum and maximum amount, setting forth the limits within which penalties can be imposed at the discretion of the officers authorized for the same taking into account the facts and circumstances of the cases where penalties are called for. In fiscal enactments like those relating to levy of taxes such as income-tax, wealth tax, service tax, etc., penalties are attracted for various defaults such as for delays in furnishing the returns, non-compliance of notices, failure to pay tax in time or for concealments, frauds, misrepresentations, etc. The legal provisions prescribing penalties mention the minimum and maximum amounts of penalties that can be imposed. For example, in the I.T. Act, 1961, section 271(1)(c) provides that for concealment of particulars of income or for furnishing inaccurate particulars thereof, penalties that can be imposed shall not be less than, but which shall not exceed three times the amount of tax sought to be evaded for such defaults. In other words, the penalty to be imposed cannot be less than 100% of the tax sought to be evaded, but shall not exceed 300% of such tax. Similarly, u/s 76 of the Finance Act, 1994 (Act) relating to levy of service tax from 8-4-2011, the amount of penalty leviable u/s 76 is not less than Rs.100 per day during which the failure continues or 1% of such tax per month, whichever is higher. The total amount of penalty leviable u/s 76, however, cannot exceed 50% of the service tax payable.

2. Whether in exercise of discretion, penalty can be imposed even below the minimum amount prescribed?

This issue came up for consideration of the Gujarat High Court in the case of CCE&C v. Port Officer [Tax Appeal No. 1367 of 2009, dated 8-7-2010]. The year for which the proceedings came up before the High Court section 76 of the Act provided for levy of penalty at Rs.200 for every day of default or equal to 2% of such tax a month, whichever was higher, not exceeding the amount of tax due. Similarly, penalties were imposable in respect of defaults mentioned in sections 77 to 79 also. Section 80 stipulated that despite sections 76 to 79, no penalty might be levied if the taxpayer proved that there was reasonable cause for failure.

2.1 Facts of the case - In the case that came up before the High Court, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the penalty imposed as per section 76 of the Act and the matter was taken to Tribunal - CESTAT - by the Central Excise Department. The Tribunal decided the issue by saying that penalty could be reduced below the minimum prescribed in view of section 80 of the Act. The issue was then taken to the High Court contending that the penalty could not be reduced below the minimum prescribed.

2.2 Arguments before the High Court - It was claimed before the Court that when the Act gives discretion to the authority of levying the penalty, the penalty amount could as well be below the minimum prescribed by the statute. It was argued that when section 80 of the Act (supra) gives discretion to the authority not to levy the penalty at all in cases of reasonable cause, the provision (section 80) could as well be construed to give power even to levy the penalty below the minimum prescribed, if the facts and circumstances of the case warrant such a decision on 'reasonable cause' ground.

2.3 Court's decision - The High Court observed that a plain reading of section 76 of the Act indicates that a person, who is liable to pay service tax and who has failed to pay such tax, is under an obligation to pay, in addition to the tax so payable and interest on such tax, a penalty for such failure. The quantum of penalty has been specified in the provision by laying down the minimum and the maximum limits, with a further rider for the maximum limit. The discretion vested in the authority is to levy minimum penalty as laid down in the section.

From the discretion it is not possible to read a further discretion being vested so as to entitle the authority to levy a penalty below the stipulated limit. The moment one reads such further discretion in the provision, it would amount to re-writing the provision, which is not permissible. It is not as if the provision is couched in a manner so as to lead to absurdity if it is read in a plain manner.

Exceptions to or Exclusions from the 'Under reported Income' Proceeding further from the stage that there was difference between the assessed income and processed income and thus there was 'under reported income', it would be open for the assessee to explain on the parameters of clauses (a) to (e) of sub section (6) that despite such difference and ostensible 'under reported income', there is in fact no or lower' under reported income' in the sense that the addition/disallowance made in the assessment order is covered under one or more of such clauses of sub section (6).

(a)

As to the exception or exclusion carved under clause (a) of sub section (6), if an assessee offers an explanation about any addition or disallowance made in the assessment order, which is found bona fide by the assessing officer and assessee has disclosed all the material facts to substantiate the explanation offered, such amount of addition or disallowance in that situation would not be treated as 'under-reported income'. Burden envisaged under this clause is akin identical to the burden placed under Explanation 1(B) of section 271(1)(c) on the shoulders of the assessee.

Therefore, for instance, a disallowance was made under section 40A(2) in the assessment order on the ground that the expenditure paid to the related person was excessive having regard to the fair market value of goods or services. If the assessee gives explanation in respect of payment made to the related person, which is found bona fide by the assessing officer and all the material facts in this regard were disclosed substantiated by the assessee by producing evidence, say, comparative rates to prove fair market value their evidences, such disallowance though made in the assessment would nonetheless be excluded from the purview of 'under reported income'.

(b)

Further, under clause (b) of sub section (6), if such amount of addition or disallowance made in the assessment order has been determined on the basis of an estimate on the ground that method employed by the assessee is such that the income cannot be properly deduced in spite of the books of account of the assessee having been found correct and complete, such addition/disallowance made in the assessment order would nonetheless be excluded from the purview of 'under-reported income'.

For instance, in case a builder-assessee was following Completed Contract Method whereas Percentage Completion Method ought to have been followed and no defect in the books of account is found in the assessment, addition made on estimate by the assessing officer in the assessment would fall under clause (b) of sub section (6) such addition would therefore not partake the character of 'under reported income'.

(c)

'Under-reported income' under clause (c) of sub section (6) would not include such income if addition/disallowance was made on the basis of estimate as against the lower estimated addition/disallowance made by the assessee on the same issue in the return of income and assessee has disclosed all the facts material to such addition/disallowance.

Example of this case may be taken where disallowance on account of personal user of the car etc. is estimated if some disallowance was already made by the assessee in the return of income under this head by disclosing all material facts. Such enhanced estimated disallowance would not be treated as part of 'under reported income.'

(d)

Going further and dealing with clause (d) of sub section (6), addition made in the assessment order on the basis of arms' length price determined by Transfer Pricing Officer whereas assessee had maintained information and documents as prescribed under section 92D, declared international transaction and disclosed all material facts relating to the transaction, would not be part of 'under reported income'.

For instance, where addition/adjustment has been made by the Transfer Pricing Officer/assessing officer due to the application of different method of transfer pricing analysis, or due to application of additional filters or rejection of filters applied by the assessee for making comparative analysis, or acceptance or rejection of comparable(s) so on and so forth, such addition/adjustment made in the assessment order in such circumstance would not be 'under reported income'. In fact, earlier there was Explanation 7 to section 271(1)(c) in respect of addition/disallowance made as a result of the order of the Transfer Pricing Officer which in the opinion of the authors was somewhat more onerous for the assessee.

(e)

Lastly, any amount of 'undisclosed income' as referred to in explained through the Explanation (c) to section 271AAB would also not become 'under-reported income' as there is separate penalty provision under that section to deal with the penalty on the amount of such 'undisclosed income'.

Is Initiation of penalty under section 270A 'Satisfaction' as to the default in the assessment/appeal/revision order still necessary?

(a)

Legislature's Unpleasant Encounters with Penalty Under Section 271(1)(c)

Matters of penalty levied in the past under section 271(1)(c) had been the subject matter of intense litigation on various technical super technical grounds which may, inter alia, be listed briefly hereunder:

(a)

That penalty was not initiated during the course of assessment.

(b)

That 'satisfaction' as to the initiation of penalty has not been recorded in the assessment order and penalty notice has straightway been issued.

(c)

That 'satisfaction' as to the charge of 'concealment of particulars of income' or 'furnishing inaccurate particulars of income' has not been recorded or is not discernible from the assessment order.

(d)

That there was no definiteness in the 'charge' or 'satisfaction' recorded in the assessment order.

(e)

That penalty notice issued is vague and does not strike off the inapplicable clause of 'concealment of particulars of income' or 'furnishing inaccurate particulars of income'

(f)

That in the penalty order, conclusion is also vague and penalty has been imposed on both the above mentioned charges.

(g)

That penalty was initiated for one charge in the assessment order whereas while passing penalty order, penalty has come to be levied for other charge.

(b)

Legislature's Attempt to be Wiser while Drafting new Penalty Section 270A

Under the new penalty regime, legislature has sought to draft the law in section 270A in such a manner so as to do away with all the possibilities of the above grounds available with the tax payers while contesting the levy of penalty under section 270A.Phraseology used in sub section (1) of section 271(1)(c) and the present penalty provision of sub section (1), (8) other sub sections of section 270A are materially different in this regard which is evident from the plain reading of the referred sub sections of the both the penalty provisions.

Anxiety of the legislature to do away with such pre-requisite of 'recording satisfaction' etc. can be well understood. 'Not recording the satisfaction' or 'recording the satisfaction inappropriately' or the above mentioned variety of technical super-technical grounds raised by the tax payers in the appeals against the penalty levied, had cost the Revenue very dearly in the past, had been the source of the severe body blow profuse bleeding to the exchequer. At the same time, such penalties lost the deterrence effect too due to such penalties having been deleted on these short legal grounds, even when there was enough justification for their levy sustenance on merit. Language of section 270A has thus been so drafted by the legislature as not to admit any such interpretation requiring the initiation of penalty proceeding recording of the 'satisfaction' in the assessment order or meeting the other technical aspects as discussed above, on the lines of the language of section 271(1)(c) its judicial interpretations placed by the Courts.

On the first blush on bare reading of section 270A, there appears to be no legal necessity of initiation or 'satisfaction' and that too for 'recording' of such 'satisfaction' by the assessing officer in the assessment order as to the existence of the 'charge' of penalty under section 270A which used to be there in section 271(1)(c). New dispensation of penalty regime as is evident from the plain literal reading of sub section (1) of section 270A requires assessing officer merely to 'direct' to pay penalty on the 'under reported income'. 6. Instances of Misreporting of Income

7. Difference between Underreporting and Misreporting

Underreporting of income entails ignoring or just partially declaring the real income obtained, and misreporting of income refers to knowingly submitting inaccurate or misleading information regarding income.

| Particulars | Under reporting of Income | Misreporting of Income |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nature | While underreporting of income entails ignoring or just partially declaring the real income obtained | Misreporting of income refers to knowingly submitting inaccurate or misleading information regarding income |
| Intent | While underreporting may result from ignorance, negligence, or a failure to understand the reporting requirements, | Misreporting suggests an intentional act of submitting inaccurate data to deceive or manipulate. |
| Scope of Inaccuracy | underreporting entails an inadequate or partial income statement with/without any manipulation. | Misreporting sometimes entails falsifying income projections or inflating deductions to reduce tax payments significantly. |
| Penalties | While underreporting can result in penalties that are usually 50% of the tax due | Penalties for misreporting are typically more severe., income reporting errors can result in larger fines of up to 200% of the tax due. |
| Legal Treatment | Tax authorities usually handle underreporting as a civil tax concern and levy penalties and fines. | Misreporting is often considered a more severe offense and may occasionally be subject to criminal prosecution. |
| Detection | underreporting can make it difficult for tax officials to spot differences between reported and real income. | Misreporting might be harder to spot since it includes deliberate manipulation and the fabrication of misleading records. |

Legislature has not made any provision in the new penalty section 270A on the lines of sub section (1A) of section 271 which also shows the legislative intent of not providing for the initiation of the penalty in the way it used to be understood in section 271(1)(c). It may be recalled that in section 271(1)(c), if penalty was to be initiated for the earlier year(s) in respect of intangible additions made in terms of Explanation 2 to section 27(1)(c), sub section (1A) of section 271 provided for the initiation of penalty even when the assessment proceeding of earlier year(s) during the course of which such penalty proceeding could have been initiated had already been completed. Therefore, when penalty under section 270A would be imposed in a case of intangible addition of earlier year(s) in terms of sub section (4) (5) of section 270A, such penalty proceeding need not be initiated which is evident from the absence of the parity provisions of the nature contained in sub section (1A) of section 271 from the language of section 270A.

(c)

Whether Legislature's Objective achieved? Or Are we back to square ONE?

Therefore in the backdrop of above raised points, a question arises as to whether assessing officer need not to initiate penalty or record 'satisfaction' under section 270A in the assessment order merely has to issue notice for the levy of penalty under section 270A in case of 'under reported income' during the assessment proceedings which may ultimately culminate into lead to the 'direction' to pay penalty on the 'under reported income' in the penalty order to be passed in writing. Does this also mean that assessing officer need not to initiate the penalty under section 270A in the assessment order record 'satisfaction' even where he finds that 'under reported income is in consequence to misreporting of income'?

Answers to these questions may be traced after making discussion at some length to follow hereinafter:

(a)

Penalty under section 270A is on 'under reported income' and even if such 'under reported income is in consequence to misreporting of income', yet the penalty would be levied quantified on income which is termed as 'under reported income' under the law. Sub section (1), (3), (7), (8), (10) of section 270A may be read and referred for this purpose. Thus, the levy of penalty has got direct, proximate inextricable link or relation with the existence and quantification of 'under reported income'. Such 'under reported income' would obviously be assessed in the assessment order and thus penalty under section 270A being closely linked with such 'under reported income' must have to be initiated in the assessment order only, followed by the issue of notice of such penalty before the penalty, if any, is ultimately imposed.

THE ARM’S LENGTH PRINCIPLE

5. As a result of such illegitimate transfers depriving countries of huge amounts, which they would have otherwise received as taxes, the international community brought the ‘Arm’s Length Principle’ into being. The underlying concept of this principle is that the pricing of goods, services or costs that are transferred or shared, as the case may be, should be equivalent or at ‘Arm’s length’ to the price prevailing in an open, competitive market rather than at a price which is determined solely by tax considerations. In other words, the pricing of intra-group transactions within a Multinational Enterprise, operating from two or more countries, should be the same that would have been applied to unrelated parties in similar transactions, under similar circumstances in the open market. Transfer pricing rules in tax laws, therefore, are intended to counter the underpayment of tax.

The ‘Arm’s length principle’ was first incorporated in the tax treaties concluded by the USA, the UK and France in 1920s and 1930s. This principle was later formulated in Article VI of the League of Nations Draft Convention on the Allocation of Profits and Property of International Enterprises in 1936. This article is similar to article 9 of the 1963 OECD Draft Convention as also article 9 of the Present OECD and UN Models of Tax Convention.

The unit should be informed about the break-up of realised exchange difference and unrealised exchange difference. The unit should add back to its profits only the unrealised exchange differences and correspondingly remove the same amount from increase/decrease in the amount due to/from the head office. The head office should similarly reduce the unrealised exchange difference from both the increase/decrease in foreign currency liability and increase/decrease in the amount due to/from the unit. If there is so much complication, why should, then, each unit prepare its own cash flow statement, instead of the head office itself preparing it on the basis of consolidated accounts ? There are two reasons. First, officials of head office may be too busy (or appear to be so!) to find time to prepare the statement. The other, more convincing reason is that each unit is responsible for its own cash management and can review its cash flow against budget and take necessary corrective action. Also, only the units know about the details of provisoins and unrealised exchanges differences to be adjusted in the cash flow statement. [Of course, the details can be obtained by the head office and adjusted in the consolidated cash flow statement, if the head office itself prepares the statement. Introduction

The Finance (No. 2) Act 2024 reintroduced the block assessment scheme by substituting Chapter XIV-B (Sections 158B to 158BI) in cases where a search under Section 132 or a requisition under Section 132A has been made on or after 01-09-2024. The scheme was reintroduced because the absence of a legal requirement for consolidated assessments in search cases has created a situation where only the time-barring year could be reopened annually for the searched assessee. This led to staggered search assessments, extending the search assessment process for up to ten years. A block assessment scheme was reintroduced to make the assessment in search cases more cost-effective, efficient, and meaningful. Under this scheme, the Assessing Officer (AO) shall proceed to assess or reassess the total undisclosed income of the concerned person for the block period in accordance with the provisions of this Chapter.

Despite introducing the chapter with effect from 01-09-2024, it did not come into force meritoriously due to three main factors:

(1)

No ITR Form was notified.

(2)

Though the objective of this chapter is to assess the undisclosed income, the extant provision used the term "total income" instead of "total undisclosed income".

(3)

Section 158BB provided a circuitous approach to compute the total income and undisclosed income of the block period. It deduced undisclosed income by excluding disclosed income from total income.

ITR-B has been notified now vide Income-tax (Tenth Amendment) Rules, 20251 and the other two issues have been fixed by the Finance Act 2025 with retrospective effect from 01-09-2024.

What is ITR-B?

A new Rule 12AE has been notified, prescribing the procedure and form ITR-B for filing the income tax return under Section 158BC.

Who can file a return in ITR B?

A person who is required to furnish the return of income under Section 158BC(1)(a) relating to any search initiated under Section 132 or requisition made under Section 132A on or after 01-09-2024 shall file it in Form ITR-B and be verified in the manner indicated therein.

How to file the ITR-B?

The ITR-B shall be filed electronically. A person whose accounts are required to be audited under Section 44AB, companies, and political parties must file it using the DSC. Other taxpayers can file it either with the DSC or under an electronic verification code. However, the functionality to file it has not been provided yet on the e-filing portal.

How to fill ITR-B?

ITR-B contains 9 Parts as follows:

(a)

Part A: It seeks general information about the assessee, date of search, block period, details of return filing and the assessment status for each year falling within the block period, etc.

(b)

Part B: It seeks the details of the disclosed income computed based on entries recorded in the books of account and other documents maintained in the normal course.

(c)

Part C: It seeks the details of undisclosed income assessment year-wise.

(d)

Part D: It seeks the details of undisclosed income head-wise and source-wise.

(e)

Part E: It seeks the details of tax payable on undisclosed income.

(f)

Part F: It seeks the details of tax paid on undisclosed income.

(g)

Part G: It seeks the details of tax paid earlier, for which a credit is sought against undisclosed income.

(h)

Part H: It seeks the details of tax paid earlier, for which a credit is sought against undisclosed income that has not been claimed earlier.

(i)

Verification: It seeks the details of the authorised person verifying the ITR-B.

How to fill Part A of ITR-B?

Part A of ITR-B seeks general information about the assessee, details of search operations, the status of the return filed of the block period and the year of search. The overview of the key information sought in this part is as follows:

(a)

The date on which the first and the last of the search authorisation or requisition is made.

(b)

The relevant block period* in the DD/MM/YYYY format.

(c)

DIN and date of notice issued under Section 158BC

(d)

Details of returns previously filed for the block period.

(e)

Limited information is sought for Assessment Years Y6 to Y2*, which are the date of filing of the ITR, the section under which the ITR was filed, the acknowledgement number and the status of the assessment on the date of initiation of the search.

Other Expectations and Recommendations

54. Non-residents should be excluded from mandatory ITR filing where they incur on foreign travel

Section 139 lays down the provisions relating to furnishing the return of income. It prescribes that every person other than a company or firm shall furnish the return of income if his total revenue during the previous year exceeds the maximum amount not chargeable to income tax. The proviso to Section 139(1) prescribes various conditions under which the assessee is required to furnish the return of income even if the total income during the previous year does not exceed the maximum amount not chargeable to tax. The following conditions are prescribed:

(a)

He has deposited an amount or aggregate of the amounts exceeding one crore rupees in one or more current accounts maintained with a banking company or a cooperative bank,

(b)

He has incurred expenditure of an amount or aggregate of the amounts exceeding two lakh rupees for himself or any other person for travel to a foreign country,

(c)

He has incurred expenditure of an amount or aggregate of the amounts exceeding one lakh rupees towards consumption of electricity,

(d)

He fulfils such other conditions as may be prescribed.

Since these conditions apply to everyone except a company or firm, such conditions will also apply to non-residents. Consequently, where the non-residents do not have income exceeding Rs. 2.5 lakh but has foreign travel exceeding Rs. 2 lakhs could be held liable to furnish the return of income even if their income during the previous year is below the maximum amount, which is not chargeable to tax.

Therefore, an amendment to Section 139 is recommended to exclude non-residents from the applicability of these provisions.

55. Section 90/90A does not empower AO to issue TRC to a resident person

Though sub-rules (3) and (4) of Rule 21AB prescribe the process of obtaining a tax residency certificate (TRC) by a person resident in India, but no provision under Section 90 or Section 90A empowers either the CBDT or the Government to issue rules concerning the issuance of TRC to a resident person. Therefore, it is recommended that the Government amend these sections to include provisions that empower the requirement and issuance of TRCs to residents.

56. Delay in handing over seized material beyond 60 days should not invalidate search

Section 132(9A) provides that if the authorised officer lacks jurisdiction, seized assets are required to be handed over to the relevant Assessing Officer within 60 days, who will then exercise the powers under subsections (8) or (9) to section 132.

There is no clarity under the statute regarding the consequences in case seized material is not handed over by the authorised officer to the Assessing Officer within 60 days.

The Gujarat High Court ruled that8 the limitation period prescribed by section 132(9A) should be interpreted to be an administrative direction and not a judicial one, and non-compliance cannot make the search vitiated.

Thus, a suitable amendment should be made to clarify that the search shall not be invalidated even if the seized assets are not handed over to the relevant Assessing Officer within 60 days.

57. Time limit should be provided within which the seized documents should be provided to the assessee

Section 132(10) provides that if a person entitled to seized documents objects to the approval given by the authorities under Section 132(8), he can apply to the Board with reasons for the objection and request the return of the documents. After hearing the applicant, the Board may pass suitable orders.

Though the Act specifically provides for supplying copies of books of account or other documents seized during the search, no time limit has been prescribed.

In the absence of a prescribed time limit, it has been observed that the authorised officer seldom gives the assessee copies of the books of account and documents seized during the search. Therefore, to achieve the desired objective, the provisions regarding the time limit for supplying copies of documents and papers seized need to be rationalised.

1225. P.C. Joseph & Bros. v. CIT [2000] 108 Taxman 253/243 ITR 818 (Ker.)

The word 'concealed' is derived from the latin expression 'concelare' which implies contcelare meaning 'to hide'. In Webster's New International Dictionary its meaning is equated 'to hide or withdraw from observation; to cover or keep from sight; to prevent the discovery of; to withhold knowledge of'.

♦♦

India Cine Agencies v. Dy. CIT [2005] 275 ITR 430 (Mad.)

The word 'conceal' as defined in the Concise Oxford Dictionary means—not allowed to be seen; hide; keep secret; prevent from doing known. Concealment implies the existence of a deliberate intent to prevent relevant facts from becoming known.

♦♦

ITO v. R.B.G.M. Modi & Ors. (P.) Ltd. [1988] 31 TTJ (Delhi - Trib.) 550

The expressions 'conceal' has been judicially noticed in several cases by the High Courts and the Supreme Court. In its plain meaning, the word 'conceal' means to hide, to keep secret. The phrase 'concealed the particulars of his income' would, therefore, involve a knowledge on the part of the assessee of income which, though real, is not shown.

♦♦

Ram Saran Gupta v. Asstt. CIT [1997] 58 TTJ (Jp. - Trib.) 599

The word 'conceal' is derived from the Latin word 'concelare' which implies 'con+celare = to hide'. Webster's New International Dictionary equates its meaning 'to hide or withdraw from observation; to cover or keep from sight; to prevent the discrepancy of; to withhold knowledge'. The offence of concealment is thus a direct attempt to hide an item of income or a portion thereof from the knowledge of the income-tax authorities. It is implicit in the word 'concealed' that there has been a deliberate act on the part of the assessee.

♦♦

Yeshwant B. Chigteri v. Asstt. CIT [2000] 75 ITD 377 (Pune - Trib.)

The word 'concealment' or 'conceal' have not been defined in the Income-tax Act, 1961. The words 'conceal' and 'concealment', according to their dictionary meaning, can be used by the Legislature in the widest possible sense. It may include the act of commission as well as the act of omission. But it is a well settled legal position that words in a given statute are to be construed in the context in which they are used. The word 'concealment' is qualified by the words 'of particulars of income'. So one can be said to have concealed the particulars of income if he is under an obligation to disclose the same. The reason is obvious. Penal provisions are to be construed very strictly. No person can be penalised unless he is found guilty on account of his failure to perform his statutory obligation.

♦♦

Sanjay D. Gupta v. Asstt. CIT [2004] 90 ITD 776 (Mum. - Trib.)

Notwithstanding the difference in the expressions 'has concealed the particulars of income' and 'has furnished inaccurate particulars of income', it is well-established that they lead to the same effect, namely, keeping off a portion of the income from the return. The word 'concealment' inherently carries with it the element of mens rea.

♦♦

Mohd. Ibrahim Azimulla v. CIT [1981] 131 ITR 680 (All.)

The dictionary meaning of 'concealment' is to hide, to keep secret. The Explanation does not alter or extend this meaning. It only assumes it to exist if the assessee fails to prove that disclosure was not due to fraud or wilful conduct. Between fraud and innocence, carefulness and gross or wilful conduct, there may be numerous stages. One may not be innocent, yet he may not be a fraud. An action may not be careful but for that reason only it cannot be considered gross or wilful. The assessee may lead evidence in penalty proceedings or may rely on circumstances on records to show that the disclosure was not due to fraud or wilful conduct.

LAW APPLICABLE - Where a return is filed under section 148 which involves an element of concealment, the law applicable for imposition of penalty would be the law as in force at the time when the original return was filed for the assessment year in question, and not the law as it stands on the dates on which returns in response to notice under section 148 was filed - CIT v. Onkar Saran & Sons [1992] 195 ITR 1 (SC). The law applicable is the law as it stood on the date of filing of the return and not on the date of passing the penalty order. The decision in Jain Bros. v. Union of India [1970] 77 ITR 107 (SC) (which related to failure to file return under the 1922 Act) is not an authority for the purpose of interpretation of the provisions contained in section 271(1)(a) vis-a-vis section 271(1)(c) of the 1961 Act - CIT v. Smt. Kamla Devi Rathi [1995] 213 ITR 177 (Pat.)(FB).

SATISFACTION OF ASSESSING OFFICER - Power to impose penalty under section 271(1) depends upon satisfaction of Assessing Officer in course of assessment proceedings and it cannot be exercised if he is not satisfied and has not recorded his satisfaction about existence of conditions specified in clauses (a), (b) and (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 before proceedings are concluded; though mere absence of words 'I am satisfied' in assessment order may not be fatal, yet such a satisfaction must be spelt out from order of Assessing Officer as to concealment of income or deliberately furnishing of inaccurate particulars and in absence of a clear finding as to concealment of income or deliberately furnishing of inaccurate particulars, initiation of penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) would be without jurisdiction - CIT v. Rampur Engg. Co. Ltd. [2009] 176 Taxman 211 (Delhi) (FB).

SUB-SECTION (1B) - Section 271(1B), inserted with retrospective effect from 1-4-1989, is not violative of article 14 of the Constitution; position of law both pre and post amendment is similar inasmuch as Assessing Officer will have to arrive at a prima facie satisfaction during course of proceedings with regard to assessee having concealed particulars of income or furnished inaccurate particulars, before he initiates penalty proceedings - Ms. Madhushree Gupta v. Union of India [2009] 183 Taxman 100 (Delhi).

'INCOME' INCLUDES 'LOSSES' - When word 'income' is read to include losses it becomes crystal clear that even in a case where on account of addition of concealed income returned loss stands reduced and even if final assessed income is a loss, penalty was leviable even during period 1-4-1976 to 1-4-2003; thus amendment made in Explanation 4 to section 271(1)(c)(iii) with effect from 1-4-2003 is clarificatory and, therefore, will have retrospective effect - CIT v. Gold Coin Health Food (P.) Ltd. [2008] 172 Taxman 386 (SC)/CIT v. R.M.P. Plasto (P.) Ltd.[2009] 184 Taxman 372 (SC).

Penalty under section 271(1)(c) can be levied even when assessed income is a loss - CIT v. Unipol Chemicals Intermediates Ltd. [2012] 27 taxmann.com 87/211 Taxman 45 (SC).

Clause (a) of Explanation 4 to section 271(1)(c) replaced with effect from 1-4-2003, was clarificatory - Jt. CIT v. Saheli Leasing & Industries Ltd. [2010] 191 Taxman 165 (SC).

MEANING OF 'CONCEALMENT' - The dictionary meaning of 'concealment' is to hide, to keep secret. The Explanation (as it stood prior to 1-4-1976) does not alter or extend this meaning - Mohd. Ibrahim Azimulla v. CIT [1981] 131 ITR 680 (All.).

FURNISHING OF INACCURATE PARTICULARS, CONNOTATION OF - A duty may be enjoined on assessee to make correct disclosure of income but if such disclosure is based on opinion of an expert, who is otherwise also a registered valuer having been appointed in terms of a statutory scheme, only because his opinion is not accepted or some other expert gives another opinion, the same by itself may not be sufficient for arriving at a conclusion that assessee has furnished inaccurate particulars; primary burden of proof regarding concealment of income or furnishing of accurate particulars of income, is on revenue - Dilip N. Shroff v. Jt. CIT [2007] 161 Taxman 218 (SC).

CONSCIOUS CONCEALMENT - Penalty under section 271(1)(c) is civil liability and for attracting such civil liability, wilful concealment is not an essential ingredient as is case in matter of prosecution under section 276C - Union of India v. Dharamendra Textile Processors [2008] 166 Taxman 65 (SC).

An order imposing penalty for failure to carry out a statutory obligation is the result of a quasi-criminal proceeding, and penalty will not ordinarily be imposed unless the party obliged either acted deliberately in defiance of law or was guilty of conduct contumacious or dishonest, or acted in conscious disregard to its obligation. Penalty will not also be imposed merely because it is lawful to do so. Whether penalty should be imposed for failure to perform a statutory obligation is a matter of discretion of the authority to be exercised judicially and on a consideration of all the relevant circumstances. Even if a minimum penalty is prescribed, the authority competent to impose the penalty will be justified in refusing to impose penalty when there is a technical or venial breach of the provision of the Act or where the breach flows from a bona fide belief that the offender is not liable to act in the manner prescribed by the statute - Hindustan Steel Ltd. v. State of Orissa [1972] 83 ITR 26 (SC).

Mere omission from the return of an item of receipt does neither amount to concealment nor deliberate furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income unless and until there is some evidence to show or some circumstances found from which it can be gathered that the omission was attributable to an intention or desire on the part of the assessee to hide or conceal the income so as to avoid the imposition of tax thereon. In order that a penalty under section 271(1)(iii) may be imposed, it has to be proved that the assessee has consciously made the concealment or furnished inaccurate particulars of his income - K.C. Builders v. Asstt. CIT [2004] 135 Taxman 461 (SC).

'Concealment' refers to a deliberate act on part of assessee; if explanation given by assessee with regard to mistake committed by him has been treated to be bona fide and it has been found as a fact that he has acted on basis of wrong legal advice, question of his failure to discharge his burden in terms of Explanation appended to section 271(1)(c) would not arise - T. Ashok Pai v. CIT [2007] 161 Taxman 340 (SC).

Primary burden of proof is on revenue; even when burden is required to be discharged by an assessee, it would not be as heavy as in prosecution cases; before a penalty can be imposed, the entirety of circumstances must reasonably point to conclusion that disputed amount represented income and that assessee had consciously concealed the particulars of his income or had furnished inaccurate particulars thereof - Dilip N. Shroff v. Jt. CIT [2007] 161 Taxman 218 (SC).

Penalty under section 271(1)(c) is civil liability and for attracting such civil liability, wilful concealment is not an essential ingredient as is case in matter of prosecution under section 276C - Union of India v. Dharamendra Textile Processors [2008] 166 Taxman 65 (SC).

Supreme Court judgment in case of Dilip N.Shroff v. Jt. CIT [2007] 291 ITR 519 requires reconsideration; Explanations added to section 271(1)(c) in their entirety also indicate element of strict liability on assessee for concealment or for giving inaccurate particulars while filing returns - Union of India v. 24.1 Penalty provisions

24.1-1 Penalty for concealment of income [Section 271(1)(c)]

Under the existing provision contained in clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 of the Act penalty for concealment of income or furnishing inaccurate particulars of income is levied on the "amount of tax sought to be evaded", which has been defined, inter alia, as the difference between the tax due on the income assessed and the tax which would have been chargeable had such total income been reduced by the amount of concealed income. Courts have held that penalty under clause (c) of sub- section (1) of section 271 cannot be levied in cases where the concealment of income occurs under the income computed under general provisions and the tax is paid under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC of the Act.

In CIT v. Nalwa Sons Investment Ltd. [2012] 21 taxmann.com 184 (SC), it was held that when assessment was made on income computed under section 115JB and tax had been paid on income so computed, penalty under section 271(1)(c) would not be imposed with reference to additions that would have been made taking into account concealment made by assessee while making assessment under normal procedure.

In CIT v. Jindal Polyester & Steel Ltd. [2014] 52 taxmann.com 259 (All.) the High Court held that book profit disclosed by assessee for purpose of tax liability under MAT provision was relevant and not income determined under provisions of the Income-tax Act. When concealment of income did not lead to tax evasion under MAT provisions, no penalty would be levied.

In Unison Hotels Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2013] 40 taxmann.com 237 (Delhi) it was held that when taxable income is computed on book profits under section 115JB, there cannot be imposition of penalty under section 271(1)(c) for additions made under normal provisions.

Tax paid under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC over and above the tax liability arising under general provisions is available as credit for set off against future tax liability. Understatement of income and the tax liability thereon under general provisions results in larger amount of such credit becoming available to the assessee for set off in future years. Therefore, where concealment of income, as computed under the general provisions, has taken place, penalty under clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 should be leviable even if the tax liability of the assessee for the year has been determined under provisions of section 115JB or 115JC of the Act.

Section 271 of the Act has been amended so as to provide that the amount of tax sought to be evaded shall be the summation of tax sought to be evaded under the general provisions and the tax sought to be evaded under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC. However, if an amount of concealment of income on any issue is considered both under the general provisions and provisions of section 115JB or 115JC then such amount shall not be considered in computing tax sought to be evaded under provisions of section 115JB or 115JC. Further, in a case where the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC are not applicable, the computation of tax sought to be evaded under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC shall be ignored. This amendment will take effect from 1-4-2016 and will accordingly apply, in relation to the assessment year 2016-17 and subsequent assessment years.

To give effect to the above, Explanation 4 to section 271(1)(c) has been substituted Explanation 4 provides that the amount of tax sought to be evaded shall be determined in accordance with the following formula—

(A-B) + (C-D)

where,

A = amount of tax on the total income assessed as per the provisions other than the provisions contained in section 115JB or section 115JC (herein called general provisions);

B = amount of tax that would have been chargeable had the total income assessed as per the general provisions been reduced by the amount of income in respect of which particulars have been concealed or inaccurate particulars have been furnished;

The sub-section requires the Assessing Officer to record satisfaction about initiation of the penalty proceedings. It reads as follows :

10.3-1 Amendment and reasons therefor - Sub-section (1B) is inserted in section 271, with retrospective effect from 1-4-1989 providing for deemed satisfaction of the Assessing Officer, if a direction is contained in the Assessment Order about initiation of penalty proceedings with respect to any disallowance. The Memorandum explains the reasons thereof as follows:

"It is a requirement that the Assessing Officer is required to be satisfied before such a penalty is levied.

There is a considerable variance in the judicial opinion on the issue as to whether the Assessing Officer is required to record his satisfaction before issue of penalty notice under this sub-section. Some judicial authorities have held that such a satisfaction need not be recorded. However, Hon'ble Delhi High Court in the case of CIT v. Ram Commercial Enterprises Ltd. [2000] 246 ITR 568 has held that such a satisfaction must be recorded by the Assessing Officer."

"Given the conflicting judgments on the issue and the legislative intent, it is imperative to amend the Income-tax Act to unambiguously provide that where any amount is added or disallowed in computing the total income or loss of an assessee in any order of assessment or reassessment; and such order contains a direction for initiation of penalty proceedings under sub-section (1), such an order of assessment or reassessment shall be deemed to constitute satisfaction of the Assessing Officer for initiation of penalty proceedings under sub-section (1)."

For the purpose of its decision, Delhi High Court (in the above referred case) had applied earlier Supreme Court decision in CIT v. D.M. Manasvi [1972] 86 ITR 557 and had relied on the following observations of the Supreme Court in CIT v. S.V. Angidi Chettiar [1962] 44 ITR 739, 745 :

"... the power to impose penalty under section 28 depends upon the satisfaction of the Income-tax Officer in the course of proceedings under the Act; it cannot be exercised if he is not satisfied about the existence of conditions specified in clauses (a), (b) or (c) before the proceedings are concluded. The proceeding to levy penalty has, however, not to be commenced by the Income-tax Officer before the completion of the assessment proceeding by the Income-tax Officer. Satisfaction before conclusion of the proceeding under the Act, and not the issue of the notice for initiation of any step for imposing penalty is a condition for the exercise of the jurisdiction ...". (p. 745)

A question that arises is, what is the exact responsibility of the payer in this connection? On a literal reading, the payer has to deduct tax on a sum chargeable under the provisions of the Act which would include the provisions of GAAR and hence a payer is required to deduct tax on the sum that could be taxable after considering the provisions of GAAR. The expression 'chargeable under provision of the Act' in section 195 should mean chargeable after following the procedure laid down under the Act for charging a particular sum to tax. Now, GAAR is not merely a computational provision which would result in taxation of a particular sum. GAAR involves a detailed process and steps before an amount can be taxed as income. (a) assessment proceedings and penalty proceedings are two separate and distinct proceedings and the fact that certain additions are made in assessment proceedings would not automatically justify the Revenue to impose penalty under section 271(1)(c) [CIT v. (c)

The plain meaning of the expression 'furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income' implies furnishing of details or information about income which are not in conformity with the facts or truth. The details or information about income deal with the factual details of income and this cannot be extended to areas which are subjective such as the status of taxability of an income, admissibility of a deduction and interpretation of law. The furnishing of inaccurate information hence relates to furnishing of factually incorrect details and information about income [Kanbay Software India (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2009] 31 SOT 153 (Pune - Trib.)].

(d)

The meaning of the word 'particulars' used in section 271(1)(c) would embrace the details of the claim made. Where no information given in the return is found to be incorrect or inaccurate, the assessee cannot be held guilty of furnishing inaccurate 'particulars'. By no stretch of imagination can making an incorrect claim tantamount to furnishing inaccurate 'particulars' [CIT v. Reliance Petroproducts Pvt. Ltd. [2010] 189 Taxman 322/322 ITR 158 (SC)].

Hence merely because an arrangement is declared as an IAA, it would not necessarily be subject to concealment penalty under section 271(1)(c).

1.23.14 TDS

Chapter XVII-B requires a payer to deduct tax in respect of specified payments/credits. Does he have to consider the GAAR for making a deduction? This is explained below separately for section 195 and other sections. 1.23.14.1 Section 195 - Section 195 provides that any person responsible for paying to a non-resident any sum chargeable under the provisions of the Act shall at the time of credit or payment deduct income-tax. The provision applies to a sum chargeable under the provisions of the Act and hence, if a sum is not chargeable the payer is not required to deduct tax. It may happen that on application of general principles of the Act and the relevant Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement, the income is not chargeable to tax, but upon application of GAAR it becomes chargeable to tax. A question that arises is, what is the exact responsibility of the payer in this connection? On a literal reading, the payer has to deduct tax on a sum chargeable under the provisions of the Act which would include the provisions of GAAR and hence a payer is required to deduct tax on the sum that could be taxable after considering the provisions of GAAR.

The other view is that a payer is not required to take cognizance of GAAR at the time of payment. The expression 'chargeable under provision of the Act' in section 195 should mean chargeable after following the procedure laid down under the Act for charging a particular sum to tax. Now, GAAR is not merely a computational provision which would result in taxation of a particular sum. GAAR involves a detailed process and steps before an amount can be taxed as income. To illustrate, as explained in para 1.20 :

♦ the AO should consider it necessary to invoke provision of Chapter XA.

♦ the AO should refer the matter to the Commissioner.

♦ the Commissioner should be of the opinion that the provisions of the Chapter XA are required to be invoked.

♦ the Commissioner should issue notice to the assessee.

♦ the Commissioner should provide an opportunity have been heard.

♦ where the Commissioner is not satisfied with the reply, he should refer the matter to an Approving Panel

♦ the Approving Panel should give an opportunity of being heard.

♦ the Approving Panel should issues directions and make a declaration that an arrangement is an IAA.

♦ the AO should determine the consequences of the IAA.

♦ the AO obtains prior approval of the Commissioner before passing the assessment order.

Thus, there is an elaborate procedure to be followed before tax consequences are determined under GAAR. If the payer has to determine the chargeability it would mean that the payer occupies the position of the AO, Commissioner and the Approving Panel and decides whether GAAR is applicable or not. Such an interpretation is not warranted.

Again, GAAR can be invoked only during assessment or reassessment proceedings [see section 144BA(1)]; hence, it cannot be invoked in TDS proceedings which are neither assessment nor reassessment proceedings.

A further question that arises is that whether GAAR has to be considered by the officer while issuing certificate under section 195(2)/(7) or 197(1). In view of the reasons given above, it appears that the officer cannot consider GAAR while issuing the certificate.

24.1 Penalty provisions

24.1-1 Penalty for concealment of income [Section 271(1)(c)]

Under the existing provision contained in clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 of the Act penalty for concealment of income or furnishing inaccurate particulars of income is levied on the "amount of tax sought to be evaded", which has been defined, inter alia, as the difference between the tax due on the income assessed and the tax which would have been chargeable had such total income been reduced by the amount of concealed income. Courts have held that penalty under clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 cannot be levied in cases where the concealment of income occurs under the income computed under general provisions and the tax is paid under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC of the Act.

In CIT v. Nalwa Sons Investment Ltd. [2012] 21 taxmann.com 184 (SC), it was held that when assessment was made on income computed under section 115JB and tax had been paid on income so computed, penalty under section 271(1)(c) would not be imposed with reference to additions that would have been made taking into account concealment made by assessee while making assessment under normal procedure.

In CIT v. Jindal Polyester & Steel Ltd. [2014] 52 taxmann.com 259 (All.) the High Court held that book profit disclosed by assessee for purpose of tax liability under MAT provision was relevant and not income determined under provisions of the Income-tax Act. When concealment of income did not lead to tax evasion under MAT provisions, no penalty would be levied.

In Unison Hotels Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2013] 40 taxmann.com 237 (Delhi) it was held that when taxable income is computed on book profits under section 115JB, there cannot be imposition of penalty under section 271(1)(c) for additions made under normal provisions.

Tax paid under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC over and above the tax liability arising under general provisions is available as credit for set off against future tax liability. Understatement of income and the tax liability thereon under general provisions results in larger amount of such credit becoming available to the assessee for set off in future years. Therefore, where concealment of income, as computed under the general provisions, has taken place, penalty under clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 should be leviable even if the tax liability of the assessee for the year has been determined under provisions of section 115JB or 115JC of the Act.

Section 271 of the Act has been amended so as to provide that the amount of tax sought to be evaded shall be the summation of tax sought to be evaded under the general provisions and the tax sought to be evaded under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC. However, if an amount of concealment of income on any issue is considered both under the general provisions and provisions of section 115JB or 115JC then such amount shall not be considered in computing tax sought to be evaded under provisions of section 115JB or 115JC. Further, in a case where the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC are not applicable, the computation of tax sought to be evaded under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC shall be ignored. This amendment will take effect from 1-4-2016 and will accordingly apply, in relation to the assessment year 2016-17 and subsequent assessment years.

To give effect to the above, Explanation 4 to section 271(1)(c) has been substituted Explanation 4 provides that the amount of tax sought to be evaded shall be determined in accordance with the following formula—

(A-B) + (C-D)

where,

A = amount of tax on the total income assessed as per the provisions other than the provisions contained in section 115JB or section 115JC (herein called general provisions);

B = amount of tax that would have been chargeable had the total income assessed as per the general provisions been reduced by the amount of income in respect of which particulars have been concealed or inaccurate particulars have been furnished;

D = amount of tax that would have been chargeable had the total income assessed as per the provisions contained in section 115JB or section 115JC been reduced by the amount of income in respect of which particulars have been concealed or inaccurate particulars have been furnished:
