In Fakir Mohmed Haji Hasan v. CIT [2002] 120 Taxman 11 (Guj.), the Gujarat High Court laid down the following propositions:

The scheme of sections 69, 69A, 69B and 69C of the Act would show that in cases where the nature and source of investments made by the assessee or the nature and source of acquisition of money, bullion, etc., owned by the assessee or the source of expenditure incurred by the assessee are not explained at all, or not satisfactorily explained, then the value of such investments and money, or value of articles not recorded in the books of account or the unexplained expenditure may be deemed to be the income of such assessee.

It follows that the moment a satisfactory explanation is given about such nature and source by the assessee, then the source would stand disclosed and will, therefore, be known and the income would be treated under the appropriate head of income for assessment as per the provisions of the Act.

However, when these provisions apply because no source is disclosed at all on the basis of which the income can be classified under one of the heads of income under section 14 of the Act, it would not be possible to classify such deemed income under any of these heads including 'Income from other sources' which have to be sources known or explained.

When the income cannot be so classified under any one of the heads of income under section 14, it follows that the question of giving any deductions under the provisions which correspond to such heads of income will not arise.

If it is possible to peg the income under any one of those heads by virtue of a satisfactory explanation being given, then these provisions of sections 69, 69A, 69B and 69C will not apply, in which event the provisions regarding deductions, etc., applicable to the relevant head of income under which such income falls will automatically be attracted.

The opening words of section 14 'Save as otherwise provided by this Act' clearly leave scope for 'deemed income' of the nature covered under the scheme of sections 69, 69A, 69B and 69C being treated separately, because such deemed income is not income from salary, house property, profits and gains of business or profession, or capital gains, nor is it income from 'other sources' because the provisions of sections 69, 69A, 69B, and 69C treat unexplained investments, unexplained money, bullion, etc., and unexplained expenditure as deemed income where the nature and source of investment, acquisition or expenditure, as the case may be, have not been explained or satisfactorily explained. Therefore, in these cases, the source not being known, such deemed income will not fall even under the head 'Income from other sources'.

Therefore, the corresponding deductions, which are applicable to the incomes under any of these various heads, will not be attracted in case of deemed incomes which are covered under the provisions of sections 69, 69A, 69B and 69C in view of the scheme of those provisions.

In the case of ACT Central Circle-13 Mumbai v. Rahil Agencies, order dated 23 November, 2016 the Tribunal held that section 115BBE does not apply to business receipts/business turnover. The Tribunal observed as under:

"19. We have considered rival contentions and found that by applying provisions of section 115BBE the AO has declined set off of business loss against income declared during the course of survey/search. The provisions of section 115BE are applicable on the income taxable under section 68, 69, 69A, 69B, 69C or 69D of the Act. The income declared by the assessee is unrecorded stock of diamond found during the course of search. The assessee is in the business of diamond trade and such stock was part of the business affair of the company. Therefore, since income declared is in the nature of business income, the same is not taxable under any of the section referred above and accordingly section 115BBE has no application in case."

New sections 273B, 278AA and 278E, were inserted, shifting the burden on the assessee to prove that the failure or omission or commission is with ‘reasonable cause’ or ‘excuse’ or the absence of the existence of culpable mental state. Explaining reasons for these amendments and insertion of new sections, the Explanatory Memorandum1 states that one of the reasons for the unsatisfactory performance of Income-tax Department in the matter of successfully levying penalty and of prosecuting the defaulters is that invariably appellate authorities and the courts have cast upon the Department the near impossible burden of proving the existence of a culpable state of mind on the part of the defaulters. On a consideration of the relevant factors in this regard, it was announced by the Long Term Fiscal Policy that in order to effectively tackle the problem of tax evasion, the Income-tax Department will implement a strategy consisting, inter alia, of removing weaknesses in the law which hinder effective prosecution of tax evaders and that it was intended to incorporate certain provisions in the direct tax laws similar to those which already exist in the Customs Act and the Gold (Control) Act. For example, under section 123(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, when any gold, diamonds or any other class of specified goods are seized in the reasonable belief that they are smuggled goods, the burden of proving that they are not smuggled goods shall be on the person from whose possession, the goods were seized and any person claiming to be the owner of such seized goods. Similarly, under section 98B of the Gold (Control) Act, 1968 in any prosecution for an offence under that Act which requires a culpable mental state on the part of the accused, the court shall presume the existence of such mental state but it shall be open to the accused to prove the fact that he had no such mental state with respect to the offence. Accordingly, the intention of the Government was announced by the Long Term Fiscal Policy to amend the direct tax laws also to provide similar provisions so that once evasion is proved, the intention to evade need not be proved by the Department.

Apart from the above, in the context of the existing scheme of accepting returns without scrutiny, which is based on trust, it is only logical that the burden should be cast on the assessee to prove his innocence if he has concealed the particulars of his income or to prove the existence of reasonable cause if he has committed any other default under the tax laws.

By this amendment, the onus of proving the existence of reasonable cause for the defaults referred to in these provisions has been cast on the taxpayer. In this context, reference may be made to section 123(1) of the Customs Act, 1962.

13.1.1 Background

Section 271(1)(c) of the Act provides for penalty in case of concealment of income or furnishing inaccurate particulars of income.

It also provides for the circumstances in which it could be said that there is a case of concealment of income or furnishing inaccurate particulars of income. In that, Explanation 71 provides that, in the following circumstances it shall be deemed that in respect of international transactions, the assessee has concealed particulars of income or furnished inaccurate particulars of income:

An assessee has entered into an 'international transaction' as defined in section 92B;

Any amount is added or disallowed in computing the total income under section 92C(4); and

The assessee fails to prove to the satisfaction of AO or Commissioner (Appeals) that the price charged or paid in the 'international transaction' was computed in accordance with and in the manner pres-cribed under section 92C, in good faith and with due diligence.

13.1-7 Intangible additions of past and related penalty

Sub-sections (4) & (5) [as Explanation 2 below section 271] provides for penalty in respect of intangible additions made in past, in certain circumstances, as explained hereafter. Similar provision was made through Explanation 2 in section 271 of the Act and in relation to the provision. CBDT Circular No. 204, dated 24-7-1976 explained the matter as follows: "61.9 New Explanation 2 makes a provision in respect of 'intangible additions'. Additions are sometimes made by the Income-tax Officers for purely technical reasons, for example, application of a presumptive rate of gross profit or of yield, or on account of estimated disallowance of certain expenses, shortfalls, wastage, etc., but no penalty for concealment is levied in respect of these additions for want of adequate evidence to establish that these additions represent the assessee's concealed income. In later assessments, when called upon to explain certain deposits, etc., the assessees urge at times that such deposits, etc., have come out of the income represented by the aforesaid additions made earlier. Despite this virtual confession of concealment on the part of the assessee, no penalty was hitherto leviable in such cases as the time limit for initiating concealment penalty proceedings in respect of the earlier year in which the addition was made would have expired. The penalty could also not be imposed in respect of the year in which the deposit was made, as there was no concealment in that year, the deposit having been explained as out of an earlier year's income. New Explanation 2 provides that in such cases, the assessee would become liable to penalty for concealment in respect of additions made in the earlier year in which the additions were made."

In Chaturvedi and Pithisaria's Income-tax Law, (Sixth Edition, Vol. 9, page 14229), the said Explanation is discussed with decided case laws and illustrations as under:

'Earlier intangible additions made also liable to penalty - Explanation 2 - In S. Kuppuswami Mudaliar v. CIT [1964] 51 ITR 757, the Madras High Court held that where the income-tax authorities make an addition to the income of the assessee over and above the income disclosed by him, on an estimate basis, the amount so added must be treated as the real income of the assessee. It is not open to the authorities to take the view that the addition was only for purposes of taxation and that it should not be regarded as the true income of the assessee. Later, the same High Court in B. Abdul Qadir v . CIT [1964] 52 ITR 364 (Mad.) and the Allahabad High Court in CIT v. Ram Achal Ram Sewak [1969] 73 ITR 501 held that such intangible addition may be employed by the assessee to explain cash credits, etc. found in the assessee's book in that, or a later, year or years [see, "Intangible addition to be treated as real income", under section 68, ante.].

Thus, if an intangible addition of Rs. 30,000 was made in assessment year 1972- 73, and a cash credit of an amount Rs. 20,000 is found in the assessee's books in, say, 1973-74, the assessee could well say that Rs. 20,000 came out of Rs. 30,000 so added to the income of 1972-73.

It may be that when the amount of Rs. 30,000 was added in 1972-73, no penalty proceeding was initiated against the assessee and no penalty was imposed.

The New Explanation 2 has been introduced, with effect from April 1, 1976, in order to deem the utilised amount Rs. 20,000 as the assessee's income, particulars of which had been concealed or inaccurate particulars of which has been furnished for the assessment year 1972-73. Thereafter section 271(1A) provides that penalty proceedings in respect of the assessment year 1972-73 may be initiated during the course of assessment proceedings for 1973-74.

Thereafter section 271(1A) provides that penalty proceedings in respect of the assessment year 1972-73 may be initiated during the course of assessment proceedings for 1973-74.

1-6aAGGREGATION OF PENALTY IN CASE OF THE TOTAL INCOME [115JB/115JC] - To provide for aggregation, in section 271(1), Explanation 4 was inserted by the Finance Act, 2015 and the reasons for the introduction of the same were explained as follows:

'Amount of tax sought to be evaded for the purposes of penalty for concealment of income under clause (iii) of sub-section (1) of section 271 Under the existing provision contained in clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 of the Act penalty for concealment of income or furnishing inaccurate particulars of income is levied on the "amount of tax sought to be evaded", which has been defined, inter alia, as the difference between the tax due on the income assessed and the tax which would have been chargeable had such total income been reduced by the amount of concealed income. Problems have arisen in the computation of amount of tax sought to be evaded where the concealment of income or furnishing inaccurate particulars of income occurs in the computation of income under provisions of section 115JB or 115JC of the Act and also under the provisions other than the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC of the Act (hereafter referred as general provisions). Further, courts have held that penalty under section clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 cannot be levied in cases where the concealment of income occurs under the income computed under general provisions and the tax is paid under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC of the Act. Tax paid under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC over and above the tax liability arising under general provisions is available as credit for set off against future tax liability. Under-statement of income and the tax liability thereon under general provisions results in larger amount of such credit becoming available to the assessee for set off in future years. Therefore, where concealment of income, as computed under the general provisions, has taken place, penalty under clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 should be leviable even if the tax liability of the assessee for the year has been determined under provisions of section 115JB or 115JC of the Act. Accordingly, it is proposed to amend section 271 of the Act so as to provide that the amount of tax sought to be evaded shall be the summation of tax sought to be evaded under the general provisions and the tax sought to be evaded under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC. However, if an amount of concealment of income on any issue is considered both under the general provisions and provisions of section 115JB or 115JC then such amount shall not be considered in computing tax sought to be evaded under provisions of section 115JB or 115JC. Further, in a case where the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC are not applicable, the computation of tax sought to be evaded under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC shall be ignored. This amendment will take effect from 1st April, 2016 and will accordingly apply, in relation to the assessment year 2016-17 and subsequent assessment years. [Clause 68]'.

It appears, as per the Memorandum, the intention was to identify separately tax sought to be evaded in respect of income as per the general provisions and deemed total income and aggregate the same. However, prima facie, it appears that the section, as such, does not aggregate the under-reported income as per the general provisions and under-reported income as per deemed total income.

In the course of the search, an assessee is found to be the owner of:

Undisclosed assets (money, bullion, jewellery or other valuable article or thing); and

Income represented by any entry in books of account or other documents or transactions

(hereafter collectively referred as 'undisclosed income')

The assessee claims that the undisclosed income represents income of any previous year(s) ended before the date of search, the due date for filing the return of income in respect of which has expired.

The assessee has not filed the return of income in respect of such previous year or years.

The assessee may disclose such undisclosed income in the return, which may be filed after the date of search.

In respect of such undisclosed income, it shall be deemed that the assessee has concealed the particulars of income or furnished inaccurate particulars of income.

It does not cover a case where an assessee has filed return of income for any previous year and income found during search related thereto was not disclosed in such return.

FURNISHING INACCURATE PARTICULARS OF INCOME - CLAUSE (c) OF SUB-SECTION (1)

1221. CIT v. Raj Trading Co. [1996] 217 ITR 208/86 Taxman 282 (Raj.)

Furnishing incorrect particulars and concealing the particulars of income are different things.

The words 'furnishing inaccurate particulars of income' refer to the particulars which have been furnished by an assessee of his income and the requirement of concealment of income is that income has not been declared at all or is not even recorded in the books of account or in a particular case the concealment of the particulars of income may be from the books of account as well as from the return furnished.

♦♦

Van Oord Dredging and Marine Contractors BV v. Asstt. DIT [2020] 117 taxmann.com 194 (Mum. - Trib.)

The expression 'inaccurate' refers to 'not in conformity with the fact of truth' and i.e. the meaning which in our humble opinion, is relevant to the context of 'furnishing of inaccurate particulars'. The expression 'particulars' refers to 'facts, detail, specifies, or information about someone or something'. Thus, the plain meaning of expression 'inaccurate particulars of income' implies furnishing of details or information about income which are not in conformity with the facts of truth. The details or information about income deal with the factual detail of income and this cannot be extended to areas which are subjective such as the status of taxability of an income, admissibility of a deduction and interpretation of law. The furnishing of inaccurate information thus relates to furnishing of factually correct details and information about income. What is correct claim and what is an incorrect claim is a matter of perspective. Raising a legal claim, even if it is ultimately found to be legally unacceptable, cannot amount to furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income just because the AO did not accept the interpretation, such an interpretation is not rendered incorrect.

◆ The search is initiated in case of any assessee on or after 1-6-2007.

◆ Undisclosed income is found pursuant to the search (for the purpose, undisclosed income means undisclosed assets, income represented by book entry and expenditure recorded in the books, etc., found to be false).

◆ Such undisclosed income is assessed in respect of specified previous years.

◆ Specified previous years mean:

■ Previous year in which search is conducted; and

■ Previous year ended before the date of search but the due date for filing return has not expired and the assessee has not filed return of such previous year before the date of search.

In the above circumstances, the assessee may be liable to pay penalty at 10% of the undisclosed income, in addition to the tax, if any, payable by him.

It is further provided that :

◆ In the above circumstances, the provisions of section 271(1)(c) of the Act would not apply; and

◆ For the purposes of levy of penalty, the provisions of sections 274 and 275 of the Act, respectively, providing for the procedure to be followed for levying penalty (like, opportunity to the assessee of being heard, jurisdiction, etc.) and limitation period would apply.

It is also provided that the above penalty may not be levied, where the assessee:

◆ In the course of search and in the statement recorded under section 132(4) of the Act admits the undisclosed income;

◆ Specifies the manner in which the undisclosed income has been derived in such statement;

◆ Substantiates the manner in which the undisclosed income has been derived; and

◆ Pays the tax, with interest, if any in respect of such undisclosed income.

Thus, in case of any assessee, where search is initiated on or after 1-6-2007, in respect of the undisclosed income of the previous year in which the search was conducted as well as the previous year ended before the date of search but the due date for filing return has not expired and the return has not been furnished, he may be liable to penalty of 10% of the undisclosed income of such previous years. In that case, he would not be liable to pay any penalty in respect of the undisclosed income under section 271(1)(c) of the Act.

Further, if the assessee, in the course of search admits the undisclosed income and specifies the manner in which it was derived as well as substantiates the manner of deriving the same and pays the tax with interest, he may not be liable to penalty in respect of the undisclosed income of the specified previous years.

It may be noted that for saving the penalty the section imposes an additional condition (when compared with Explanation 5 applicable upto 1-6-2007), namely, substantiation of the manner of deriving income.

‘Manner’, as explained in the Law Lexicon by P Ramnath Aiyar means : ‘mode of action, way of performing or effecting anything, method, style the way of managing; the way of doing thing, the method of procedure; … method or mode or style... ’.

‘Substantiates’, Webster’s New Collegiate Dictionary means: ‘1 : to impart substance to 2 : to put into concrete form … 3: to establish by proof or competent evidence’.

Accordingly, in the context of ‘deriving income’, for claiming exemption from the penalty, it would be necessary for an assessee to:

◆ Explain the way, mode and method of deriving such income; and

◆ Prove his explanation by proof or competent evidence.

◆ State the manner of deriving the income (that is, the way, mode and method adopted); and

◆ Support the above by leading concrete and competent evidence in the form of relevant documents, etc.

The assessee may lead evidence in penalty proceedings or may rely on circumstances on records to show that the disclosure was not due to fraud or wilful conduct.

♦♦

T. Ashok Pai v. CIT [2007] 161 Taxman 340/292 ITR 11 (SC) The expression 'conceal' signifies a deliberate act of omission on the part of the assessee. Such deliberate act must be either for the purpose of concealment of income or furnishing of inaccurate particulars. Concealment refers to deliberate act on the part of the assessee. A mere omission or negligence would not constitute a deliberate act of suppressio veri or suggestio falsi.

♦♦

Kartik Mehra v. Dy. CIT [2015] 59 taxmann.com 392 (Kol. - Trib.)

The word 'conceal' as per Webster's Dictionary means 'to hide, withdraw, or remove from observation; cover or keep from sight; to keep secret; to avoid disclosing or divulging'. That means non-disclosure of particulars of income. On the other hand, where particulars are disclosed but such disclosure is not correct, true or accurate, it would amount to furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income. For example, in case of businessman, if a particular transaction of sale is not shown in the books, it would amount to concealment of particulars of income while sale is shown but at a lesser value, it would amount to furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income.

♦♦

IT: (i) As long as the assessee has not concealed any material facts, or the 'factual' information given by him is shown to be correct, he is not liable for penalty under section 271(1)(c), even if the claim made is not sustainable in law

IT: In case of imposition of penalty under section 271(1)(c), it is incumbent upon Assessing Officer to come to a positive finding as to whether there was concealment of income by assessee or whether any inaccurate particulars of such income had been furnished by assessee

IT : Where difference between loan amount, due and payable by assessee was on account of non inclusion of interest amount in loan amount by bank, no concealment was to be alleged against assessee for imposition of penalty under section 271(1)(c)

IT-I : Where assessee wrongly claimed deduction of payment of advance tax and certain amount debited to profit and loss account which was infact a mere appropriation of profit, it being a case of concealment and furnishing inaccurate particulars of income, penalty order passed by Assessing Officer under section 271(1)(c) was to be confirmed

IT: Where after completion of assessment, consequent upon inquiry assessee surrendered amount of certain loan as bogus loan and interest on said loan, concealment of income was established making a case for levy of penalty under section 271(1)(c)

IT: Wrong deduction of an amount for computation of income could not be equated with concealment and it would not amount to furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income or concealment of income so as to attract penalty under section 271(1)(c)

IT : Where assessee having agreed to surrender certain amount in course of survey proceedings, filed its return subsequently wherein said amount was infact offered to tax, there was no concealment on part of assessee and, thus, impugned penalty order passed under section 271(1)(c) was to be set aside

digest.text:
HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1979-80 - Assessee claimed non-resident status and exemption for salary income on that basis, he also furnished details in respect of leaving India and arriving in India from years 1974 to 1978 which showed that his stay in India during relevant previous year was less than 180 days and did not satisfy requirement of section 6(1)(a) - Later ITO found that assessee’s stay in India during preceding years was such as to satisfy section 6(1)(c) and held that assessee was not non-resident and, hence, not entitled to exemption claimed - Assessee had obtained a certificate under section 80RRA but did not disclose it to ITO - Whether assessee could be held guilty of concealment under section 271(1)(c) - Held, no.

FACT: For the assessment year 1979-80 the assessee claimed his status as non-resident. He also gave details in an annexure showing dates of departure from and arrival in India from the year 1974 to 1978, which showed, inter alia, that for the relevant previous year, the assessee had stayed in India only for 137 days and, hence, did not satisfy the requirement of section 6(1)(a). Later, the ITO, however, noticed that the assessee’s stay in India during the preceding four years was such as to satisfy section 6(1)(c) and held that the assessee was not a non-resident and, hence, not entitled to the exemption claimed. The assessee had also obtained a certificate under section 80RRA which was not disclosed before the ITO. The ITO initiated penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) and held that since the assessee did not disclose the fact of the certificate under section 80RRA and his correct residential status although he knew about it there was a breach of the obligation under section 139(1) and, therefore, he was guilty of concealment of income. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the imposition of penalties.

On second appeal:

HELD: It could not be disputed that the assessee had fully disclosed all the material facts of arrival and departure in India for the past four years in an annexure to the statement of income. Although in that statement the assessee had claimed the status of a non-resident, immediately below that he had mentioned ‘see Annexure A’.

Therefore, his statement regarding non-resident status could not be read in isolation and separately from the annexure. It was for the ITO to come to the conclusion regarding the assessee’s status. The conclusion by the ITO or by the assessee regarding the status of the assessee might be one or the other, but that did not mean that the facts had been concealed by the assessee. Concealment can only be of facts and not of the conclusion. Where the assessee had disclosed all the material facts to enable the ITO to come to a conclusion, it could not be said that the assessee was guilty of concealment. It is the duty of an assessee to disclose all the facts and not to conceal any material fact which would give a false suggestion as to the conclusion to be drawn. This is the extent of the disclosure expected of an assessee. In other words, there should not be any suppressio yeri which would amount to suggestio falsi. In the instant case, the assessee had not done any such thing.

Although the assessee had not disclosed the fact of his having the certificate under section 80RRA, strictly speaking, it was not his duty to do so before the ITO because the ITO had all the materials before him to enable him to come to the conclusion regarding the assessee’s status. Ideally or morally speaking, it might be expected of the assessee to have made this disclosure, but that was not the expectation of law when imposing penalty for which a positively dishonest conduct was necessary. The assessee’s own belief in that regard was also immaterial because the conclusion to be drawn by the ITO was independent of any belief that the assessee might have had. The penalty imposed on the assessee was, therefore, cancelled.

Committee Report. Earlier the concealment penalty was based on the quantum of income concealed and there was an Explanation that in case the returned income is less than 80 per cent of the assessed income, then the burden of proving that concealment was on the assessee. Wanchoo Committee recommended that the penalty should be based on the amount of tax sought to be evaded. What is meant by tax sought to be evaded was mentioned in the Explanation 4. [Para 3.20] From the judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Dharamendra Textile Processors [2008] 306 ITR 277/ 174 Taxman 571, it was clear that the object behind enactment of section 271(1)(c ) was to provide a remedy for loss of revenue. Wilful concealment is not an essential ingredient for imposing penalty, as that is the requirement in case a prosecution is launched. However, in the instant case, the assessee was fully aware of the fact of unaccounted sales. He was fully aware of the income from such sales. He had not given any explanation to say as to why such sales were not disclosed in the original return. The explanation for not disclosing such sales was not forthcoming. Only explanation given was that the income had been surrendered to purchase peace and to avoid litigation. [Para 3.21]

The assessee had not agreed to an item to be included in the income, which was being reflected in the books of account. This was a case where unaccounted sales were found during the course of search and amount outstanding on account of such sales were found. Even in respect of accounted sales, the assessee was preparing the purchase vouchers as actual purchases were made from hawkers and no purchase bills were obtained from them. [Para 3.22]

In the original return, the assessee had not disclosed the entire sales. That fact was material to the computation of the total income. No explanation had been offered as to why such sales were not reflected in the original return. The only explanation submitted was that the assessee agreed to the addition to purchase peace. Such explanation could not be considered as bona fide because the documents relating to such unaccounted sales were found. It was also found that the assessee was having unaccounted debtors to the extent of Rs. 93.54 lakhs as on 31-3-2004. Hence, in the instant case, the Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c) was squarely applicable for imposition of penalty. [Para 3.24]

As per section 271(1B), there is deemed satisfaction in respect of additions made. The Assessing Officer had imposed penalty not only on the addition made to the income returned under section 153A but also on the difference between the original returned income and the income returned in response to the notice under section 153A. The Act does not require any specific form of satisfaction to be recorded. The satisfaction can be inferred from the assessment order. [Para 4.1]

From the observations of the Assessing Officer recorded in the assessment order it was clear that the Assessing Officer was satisfied that the additional income being offered was the concealed income. The narration of the facts in the assessment order and mentioning of incriminating documents found during the course of search showing unaccounted sales clearly indicated that the Assessing Officer was satisfied during the course of proceedings that penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) were required to be initiated. The satisfaction was evident and it could not be held that the proceedings had been initiated without recording satisfaction. [Para 4.2]

Relying on the decision of the Tribunal in Asstt. CIT v. Goutham Public School [2004] 88 ITD 31 (Visakhapatnam) and considering the facts as mentioned above, it was to be held that the Assessing Officer was satisfied before initiating the proceedings under section 271(1)(c). [Para 4.3]

It was true that the show-cause notice did not contain the specific allegation, i.e., whether it was in respect of concealment of income or furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income. The notice was to be read along with the assessment order during the course of which proceedings had been initiated. The proceedings had been initiated for concealment of income. The assessee in his reply had understood the spirit in which notice had been issued. In his reply, it had been mentioned that he had offered additional income to buy peace and to have an end to the proceedings. If the notice in substance and effect is in conformity with or according to the intent and purpose of the Act, then such notice cannot be held as invalid as per section 292B. The purpose of issuing the show-cause notice is to give the assessee an adequate opportunity in respect of default, which is detected and alleged against him. From the nature of the assessment proceedings and the fact mentioned in the assessment order, it was clear that there was a specific charge of concealment of income and the assessee got adequate opportunity in rebutting such charge. Hence, it could not be said that penalty proceedings were invalid because the Assessing Officer had not struck off the column for which the assessee was not required to give reply. Hence, on that ground, penalty proceedings could not be cancelled. [Para 5.1]

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1964-65 - Whether Explanation to section 271(1) inserted with effect from 1-4-1964 would apply to income returned after it came into force irrespective of fact whether income related period prior to 1-4-1964 or thereafter - Held, yes - Whether by Explanation to section 271(1) classifying assessees in two varieties and in allocating burden of proof in one class of cases on assessee and in other on departmental authority, Parliament has adopted an intelligible differentia dictated by experience gathered in administering Act and, therefore, said Explanation does not offend article 14 of Constitution - Held, yes

FACT: For the year 1964-65 the petitioner submitted a return of its income on 21-10-1964, showing its total income at Rs. 28,270. The ITO, however, assessed the income of the petitioner at Rs. 47,273 for that year and a penalty under section 271(1)(c) was imposed.

The assessee filed the writ petition challenging the penalty contending that the penalty having been imposed by the aid of the Explanation appended to sub-section (1) of section 271, which Explanation had come into force with effect 1-4-1964, the Explanation did not apply as the return in question related to the year which had concluded on 31-3-1964. The assessee further contended that the aforesaid Explanation offends article 14 of the Constitution.

HELD: On its plain wording, the Explanation, to section 271(1) applies to the income returned by an assessee after it came into force irrespective of the fact whether the income related to a period prior to 1-4-1964, or thereafter. The penalty clause (c ) can be invoked only if a false return is filed, and if the return is filed after the Explanation had become operative, surely such return, if it offends the Explanation, would attract its applicability. Therefore, the Explanation applied to the instant case since the relevant return was admittedly filed after 1-4-1964. This interpretation does not tantamount to operation of the Explanation retrospectively.

True, it cannot be gainsaid that the Explanation does create two classes; one class of those assessees whose returned income happens to be less than 80 per cent of the assessed income, which may appropriately be described as the actual income, and the assessees whose returned income is not less than 80 per cent of their actual income. Article 14, it has been consistently held by the Supreme Court, does not forbid classification though it prohibits class legislation. Equality before the law means that among equals the law should be identical and that the like should be treated alike. At the same time, put in other words, equality before the law does not mean that things which are different shall be treated as though they were the same. The permissible classification, according to the pronouncements of the Supreme Court, must satisfy two conditions, namely, (1) it must be founded on intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from others who are left out of the group, and (2) the differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the impugned provision. It has also been repeatedly held that the differentia and object are different elements and that the object by itself cannot be the basis of classification. Another principle equally well settled is that article 14 condemns discrimination not by substantive law alone but even by procedural law.

HEADNOTE: Section 154 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Rectification of mistake - Apparent from record - Assessment years 1974-75 and 1975-76 - During relevant  accounting years customs authorities seized certain foreign watches from assessee’s premises - Customs authorities held that seized watches belonged to assessee and accordingly imposed penalties - Imposition of penalties was confirmed by Magistrate - On basis of aforesaid findings, ITO initiated reassessment proceedings under section 147 and held that investment in aforesaid seized watches came from undisclosed sources. He, therefore, added investment amount in total income of assessee under section 69A - On appeal, AAC upheld reassessment made by ITO - Assessee did not claim loss arising from confiscation of watches either before ITO or before AAC against whose order no appeal was filed - Whether fact of loss arising on account of confiscation of watches by customs authorities not having been allowed to assessee was a mistake apparent form record which could be rectified under section 154 - Held, no

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment years 1974-75 and 1975-76 - Whether in view of facts stated under head ‘Rectification of mistake- apparent from records’ assessee was not liable to penalty under section 271(1)(c)- Held, no

FACT: During the accounting years relevant to the assessment years 1974-75 and 1975- 76, the customs authorities seized certain foreign watches from the assessee’s premises. The customs authorities held that the aforesaid foreign watches seized belonged to the assessee only and accordingly levied penalty with regard to smuggled wrist watches and this penalty was confirmed by the magistrate. On the basis of the aforesaid material the ITO initiated reassessment proceedings for the assessment years in question. The ITO held that the assessee was the real owner of the foreign smuggled watches which were subsequently seized by the customs authorities and also held that the amount invested in the above watches came from sources undisclosed to the department. Therefore, he treated the investment in the watches seized by the customs department as income form undisclosed sources and assessed it as income from other sources. On appeal, the AAC upheld the aforesaid additions made in the reassessment which became final as there were no further appeals against it. However, the assessee filed application under section 154 stating that the loss arising on account of confiscation of watches by the customs authorities should have been allowed following the decision of the Supreme Court in CIT v. Piara Singh [1980] 124 ITR 40. The ITO rejected the assessee’s application on the ground that he reassessment was upheld by the AAC and that as the assessee could not explain the sources for acquisition of watches which were found in his possession, the assessment of their value under the provisions of section 69A was correct. On appeal, the AAC upheld the order of the ITO rejecting the application under section 154. While making the reassessments for the years in question, penalty proceedings were also initiated under section 271(1)(c) against the assessee. The ITO finally imposed penalty for the concealment of income. On appeal, the AAC upheld the imposition of penalties.

On further appeal:

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1968-69 - Whether state has a wide discretion in selecting persons or objects it would tax, and a statute is not open to attack on ground that it taxes some persons and objects and not others - Held, yes - Whether it is only when within range of its selection, law operates unequally, and that can not be justified on basis of any valid classification, that it would be violative of article 14 of Constitution - Held, yes - Whether section 271(1)(c) can not be regarded as violative of article 14 of Constitution as there is nothing in said section pointing out any hostile discrimination against a particular type of taxpayer - Held, yes - Whether moreover, since object of section 271(1)(c) is not to provide for any confiscation but to provide a penalty for concealment of income and that too by providing a deterrent penalty, it can not be said that provisions of section 271(1)(c)(iii) infringe article 19(1)(f) Constitution - Held, yes

FACT: For the assessment year 1968-69, the assessee filed his original return without showing the income from sale of land, but when required to produce the sale deed in respect of the land sold by him, the assessee filed a revised return showing therein capital gains and business income on estimate basis. The ITO passed the assessment order and also issued notice under section 274 read with section 271 for failure to furnish the return within the stipulated time and also for concealment of income. Later, he levied penalty only under section 271(1)(c) of an amount equal to 100 per cent of the concealed income.

On writ, the assessee challenged the constitutional validity of section 271(1)(c) on two grounds: (1) that section 271(1)(c) is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as there is no classification at all even though there is a difference between various types of tax evasions; and (2) that the impugned provisions are a colourable exercise of legislative power inasmuch as in the guise of levying penalty the legislature had enacted for expropriation of the whole of the property of the citizen.

HELD: As regards the challenge on the basis of Article 14 of the Constitution, it is well-settled that while article 14 forbids class legislation, it does not forbid reasonable classification for the purposes of legislation. In order, however, to pass the test of permissible classification, two conditions must be fulfilled, namely : (i) that the classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from others left out of the group ; and (ii ) that that differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the statute in question.

In deciding whether a taxation law is discriminatory or not it is necessary to bear in mind that the State has a wide discretion in selecting the persons or objects it would tax, and that a statute is not open to attack on the ground that it taxes some persons and objects and not others. It is only when within the range of its selection, the law operates unequally, and that cannot be justified on the basis of any valid classification, that it would be violative of article 14. It is for the person who assails a legislation as discriminatory to establish that it is not based on a valid classification and it is well-settled that this burden is all the heavier when the legislation under attack is a taxing statute. In taxation even more than in other fields, legislatures possess the greatest freedom in classification. The burden is on the one attacking the legislative arrangement to negative every conceivable basis which might support it. Thus, unless the petitioner succeeds in establishing that there was a clear and hostile discrimination by virtue of the impugned legislation, the challenge on the ground of article 14 can not be sustained.

HEADNOTE: Section 119 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Central Board of Direct taxes - Instructions to subordinate authorities - Assessment year 1991-92 - Whether instruction No. 1979, dated 27-3-2000 asking all officers of Income-tax Department under their control not to file appeals before Tribunal in cases where tax effect involved in appeal does not exceed Rs. 1.00 lakh, being not issued in exercise of power conferred on CBDT under section 119, are not statutory instructions but merely administrative instructions for guidance of income-tax authorities and cannot be enforced through court of law - Held, yes

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1991-92 - Whether, where assessee was unable to substantiate its explanation in respect of deposits made in name of partners satisfactorily but such explanation was bona fide, no penalty under section 271(1)(c) could be imposed - Held, yes
Circulars and notifications - CBDT Instruction No. 1979, dated 27-3-2000 and CBDT Instruction No. 1903 dated 1-11-1992

FACT: Two of the partners of the assessee-firm introduced Rs. 19,500 and Rs. 30,000, respectively, as part of their share capital in the firm. It was explained that the amounts had been introduced out of their agricultural income. The assessee could not produce evidence regarding sale of agriculture produce and, therefore, amounts were treated as the assessee’s concealed income. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed some reduction. In penalty order, the Assessing Officer held that the assessee had not produced the correct particulars of its income and, thus, concealed the income of Rs. 34,500. Accordingly, penalty under section 271(1)(c) was imposed. On appeal, the assessee contended that the mere fact that the Assessing Officer had not accepted the explanation furnished was not sufficient ground for levy of penalty. The Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the penalty.

On the revenue’s appeal and cross-objection by the assessee, the assessee besides opposing the penalty order, also took preliminary objection to the maintainability of the appeal in the light of Instruction No. 1979, dated 27-3-2000, issued by the Central Board of Direct Taxes, asking all officers of the Income-tax Department under their control not to file appeals before the Tribunal in cases where the tax effect involved in appeal did not exceed Rs. 1.00 lakh. On the other hand, it was contended on behalf of the Department that the instructions were by way of guidelines and could not override the specific provisions of the Act and that these instructions were not in the nature of ‘benevolent Circulars’ for the benefit of the assessee. Thus, it was urged that the preliminary objection raised was not legally sustainable.

HELD: As regards the preliminary objection, it is only those circulars or instructions which are issued by the Board under section 119 that will have statutory force and will be binding on the income-tax authorities. Delegated legislation can be issued only when the authority concerned has statutory power to do so. But statutory power is not necessary for issuing directions/instructions. The basic distinguishing feature between a direction and delegated legislation is that while delegated legislation is binding on both the administration and the individual and is enforceable through a court of law at the instance of either the individual or the administration, an administrative direction, generally speaking, is not so binding and enforceable. There may be an administrative remedy available to the individual concerned for enforcing such directions.

return, he will reach the correct figure of total income and determine the sum payable by the assessee or refundable on the basis of such assessment. If the income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment for any assessment year, by reason of omission or failure of the assessee to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for his assessment, reassessment proceeding can be initiated as provided under section 147. This again shows that full and true disclosure of income is a primary obligation of the assessee. If a person obliged to furnish the particulars of his income omits to furnish them, he thereby conceals the particulars. This concealment may take various forms. A glaring illustration of concealment would be where the assessee does not disclose or fully disclose in the return the income derived by him which would fall under a particular head, e.g., ‘Income from other sources’ while disclosing his income falling under other heads of income prescribed by section 14. To the extent he does not disclose that income, he conceals the particulars of income. The obligation is not only to disclose particulars of income but to disclose them correctly and completely. If while disclosing the particulars of income in the return he puts them under a wrong head, he can be said to be furnishing inaccurate particulars of income. The particulars of income can be made inaccurate in a variety of ways, a glaring illustration of which would be where the assessee while stating the income under a particular head, works out the income chargeable to tax after making deductions which are falsely made. Such a process would make the particulars of income inaccurate. In all such cases, whether the income is not disclosed against the constituent item of the return in which it falls or is partly not disclosed, or the particulars of income given in the return are incorrectly stated by any machination, the impact is bound to be on the figure of gross total income to be mentioned under various heads of income and also on the total income chargeable to tax. In fact, reducing the figure of income that would be chargeable to tax would be for the purpose of concealment of particulars of income or giving inaccurate particulars of income. The expression ‘particulars of income’ would have relevance to all the particulars of income which the assessee is required to give in his return fully and truly, including the particulars of income chargeable to tax under various heads and the total income. Therefore, any concealment or inaccuracy in the particulars of income in the return occurring at any stage upto and inclusive of the ultimate stage of working out of total income, would attract the penalty provision of section 271(1)(c). Every figure in the return which is set opposite to the item of income is a particular of income, whether the figure is one which is stated independently of anything else that appears in the return or the documents accompanying it or whether it is something derived from other figures elsewhere stated in such return or documents. False result may be produced by the falsity of one or more of the constituent items in the return. The words ‘inaccurate particulars’ would cover falsity in the final figure as also the constituent elements or items. They simply would mean inaccurate in some specific or definite respect whether in the constituent or subordinate items of income or the end result.

Merely because of the Explanation has not been referred to in the show cause notice, there is no legal bar against invoking the Explanation during the course of the penalty proceedings. As, in the instant case, income returned was admittedly less than 80 per cent of the income assessed, the essential precondition for applicability of the Explanation was satisfied. 3. The difference between income returned and assessed arose in this case because of undisclosed income of Rs. 3,500, introduced in the books and subsequently withdrawn, and the assessee failed to prove by a preponderance of probabilities that there was no fraud or wilful neglect on its part.

4. Hence, penalty was validly imposed under Explanation to section 271(1)(c).

Editor's note

The High Court considered only the question whether the case was covered by the Explanation to section 271(1)(c) without considering the question whether the requirements of section 271(1)(c) were independently satisfied.

271(1)(c) may be issued for concealment of income. During the course of penalty proceedings, apart from issuing a formal show-cause notice under section 271(1)(c ), the Assessing Officer had specifically confronted the assessee with the facts pertaining to diversion of profits through the instrumentality of sham sale transactions with the sister concerns and called upon the assessee to explain why penalty for concealing the particulars of income may not be levied. The assessee furnished its reply. The Assessing Officer after elaborate discussion of the facts and circumstances of case came to the conclusion that the assessee had concealed the income by diverting the profits to its sister concerns. The Assessing Officer had further observed that the assessee had furnished inaccurate particulars of its income. On these facts the charge of concealment had been specifically and unambiguously brought out by the Assessing Officer in the show-cause notice issued to the assessee as well as in the penalty order passed by the Assessing Officer. In the show-cause notice, the Assessing Officer had clearly indicated the default of concealing the particulars of income. The satisfaction recorded in the assessment order using the words ‘concealment of income’ clearly brought out the charge that the penalty was proposed to be levied for concealing the particulars of income. The income could be concealed obviously by concealing the particulars thereof. Looking to the fact that the penalty proceedings before the Assessing Officer do not have formal trappings of a criminal trial and nuances of criminality cannot be imported into such proceedings, strict procedural requirements of a criminal trial like issue of the formal charge-sheet are not necessary in such proceedings. The assessee had been allowed appropriate opportunity of being heard as per the provisions of section 274. The basic requirement had been duly complied with by the Assessing Officer inasmuch as the Assessing Officer had indicated that the penalty under section 271(1)(c) was proposed to be levied for concealing the particulars of income represented by diversion of profits through sham transactions with the sister concerns. No prejudice, therefore, had been caused to the assessee in the matter of rebutting the case against it.

The assessee had taken resort to routing its sales through sham or unreal transactions which were merely paper transactions, with its sister concerns for the sole purpose of diverting its profits. There were tell tale signs in ample measure starting from the record which indicated that these sale transactions with the sister concerns were illusory transactions. The transactions with the sister concerns were admittedly at rates much lower than the prevailing market rates. The assessee had obviously resorted to a make believe arrangement whereunder the sister concerns had been used as conduits for siphoning off of its profits. The Assessing Officer had brought out in the penalty order the close inter-connection of the assessee with the sister concerns. Five partners of the assessee-firm were also partners in the three sister concerns utilised for profit diversion. The substantiated chunk of sham transactions were routed through one of the firms. Thus, 70 per cent of profits in the sister concerns was held by the five partners of the assessee firm who were common. The other partners also were closely related family members. These facts provided irrefutable evidence that the transactions with the sister concerns were merely a ruse to divert the profits; in fact the sale transactions of the assessee with the sister concerns and the subsequent transactions of the sister concerns with the outside parties formed an integral and indivisible part of the composite scheme of tax planning of the assessee. Hence, the assessee-firm had adopted non-genuine and artificial device of showing paper transactions with the sister concerns with the objective of reducing its tax liabilities. These transactions were commercially inert and had been entered into as part of tax saving scheme. The penalty for concealment levied under section 271(1)(c) was, therefore, liable to be upheld.

Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c ) incorporates a rule of evidence and shifts the onus on the shoulders of the assessee in furnishing the explanation before the Assessing Officer. The Explanation does not constitute an ingredient of the offence and it lays down only a rule of evidence. The Explanation does not confer any discretion on the assessing authority to invoke it or not. It automatically applies to cases where penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) for the offence of concealing the particulars of income have been initiated. The consequences from the applicability of Explanation 1 follow as a matter of law. If the assessee fails to offer explanation or the explanation is found to be false or the assessee is not able to substantiate the explanation, the presumption that he concealed the particulars of income is bound to be drawn. In the instant case there was no infirmity in the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) in invoking the Explanation 1 for the purpose of considering the exigibility of the penalty under section 271(1)(c).

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c) read with  section 256, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1965-66 - Penalty was imposed on assessee firm on ground that assessee tried to evade taxes that explanation given regarding cash credit was not even probable - On appeal, Tribunal held that in absence of a finding that assessee made any attempt to conceal facts, it would be difficult to give a finding that merely because assessee failed in his device to illegally avoid taxes he could be held guilty within provisions of section 271(1)(c) - Whether in view of the decision of Supreme Court in case Karnani Properties v. CIT [1971] 82 ITR 547 (SC), findings recorded by Tribunal could not be gone into in reference application and therefore, no penalty could be levied on assessee under section 271(1)(c) - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-firm filed a return showing an income. The ITO completed the assessment on the higher income. The penalty proceedings were initiated under section 271(1)(c) in respect of unexplained cash credit and unexplained investment. The case was referred by the ITO to the IAC who issued a show-cause under section 274 in response to the notice the assessee filed a written reply which was not accepted by the IAC and he found that the assessee interpolated the entries in the cash book with regard to the credit of certain amount. He further recorded a finding that the assessee tried to evade taxes by claiming the business as a separate unit and that the explanation given regarding the cash credit was not even probable. The assessee filed an appeal and the Tribunal set aside both these findings and held that in the absence of finding that the assessee made any attempt to conceal the facts, it would be difficult to give a finding that merely because the assessee failed in his device to illegally avoid taxes he could be held guilty within the provisions of section 271(1)(c)

HELD: No questions had been raised on behalf of the department on the findings recorded by the Tribunal.

In the decision of the Supreme Court in Karnani Properties Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax [1971] 82 ITR 547 (SC) it was held that when the question referred to the High Court speaks of 'on the facts and circumstances of the case', it means 'on the facts and circumstances found by the Tribunal' and not 'facts and circumstances' that may be found by the High Court on a reappraisal of the evidence. In view of that pronouncement of law, it was held that the findings recorded by the Tribunal could not be gone into.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c) read with section 131, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment years 1996-97 to 1998-99 - During course of assessment proceedings, it was noticed that assessee was making bogus purchases from various concerns belonging to ‘F’ - Assessing Officer asked assessee to produce those parties but assessee failed to do so despite repeated opportunities given - Assessing Officer having treated those purchases as bogus, made addition to assessee’s income - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) as well as Tribunal upheld a part of addition so made - Assessing Officer also imposed penalty upon assessee under section 271(1)(c) - Whether when assessee filed complete details of party, revenue authorities had ample power including issue of summon under section 131 whereas assessee had no such power under Act to bring party personally to produce before Assessing Officer - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, when revenue authorities did not exercise such power under section 131, assessee could not be blamed for concealing particulars and/or furnishing inaccurate particulars of income - Held, yes - Whether in view of aforesaid, it was to be held that it was not a fit case for levy of penalty under section 271(1)(c) - Held, yes
Words and phrases : Words  ‘concealed’, ‘particulars’ and ‘inaccurate’ as occurring in section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

FACT: During the course of assessment proceedings, it was noticed that the assessee was making bogus purchases from various concerns belonging to ‘F’. The Assessing Officer asked the assessee to produce those parties but the assessee failed to do so despite repeated opportunities given. The Assessing Officer treated the said purchases of Rs. 15,99,295 as bogus purchases for the assessment year 1996-97. The assessee filed an appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals), who confirmed the addition to the extent of 25 per cent of the total purchases. The order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was confirmed by the Tribunal. The Assessing Officer levied penalty under section 271(1)(c), which had been confirmed by the Commissioner (Appeals).

On second appeal :

HELD: The crux of the matter to be examined was whether penalty under section 271(1)(c), read with the Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c ) was applicable to the facts of the instant case. The proceedings under section 271(1)(c ) can be initiated only if the Assessing Officer or the first appellate authority is satisfied in the course of any proceedings under the Act that any person has concealed the particulars of his income or has furnished inaccurate particulars of such income and he may direct that such person shall pay by way of penalty the sum mentioned in sub-clause (iii) of clause (c) of section 271(1)(c). The expression used in clause (c) is ‘has concealed the particulars of his income’ or ‘furnished inaccurate particulars of such income’. Therefore, in both cases of concealment and inaccuracy the phrase ‘particulars of income’ is used. The expressions ‘has concealed the particulars of income’ and ‘has furnished inaccurate particulars of income’ have not been defined either in section 271(1)(c) or elsewhere in the Act. [Para 8]

The word ‘conceal’ is derived from the latin word concelare which implies to hide. The offence of concealment is, thus, a direct attempt to hide an item of income or a portion thereof from the knowledge of the income-tax authorities. [Para 10]

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1975-76 - Pursuant to original assessment of income of assessee, a search took place at residence of assessee's father in which a black handwritten diary of assessee was seized wherein an entry relating to Rs. 10,000 in respect of some transaction with one 'L' was found - He surrendered said amount as its income in reassessment proceeding - Penalty under section 271(1)(c) was imposed - Whether since assessee had not disclosed income in original return and disclosed it only after search was conducted and re-assessment proceeding was initiated, it could be said that there had been a conscious effort on part of assessee to conceal income - Held, yes - Whether since assessee had not been able to rebut presumption raised under Explanation to section 271(1)(c), which was upon him to prove that there was no gross or wilful neglect on his part it could be said that order of Tribunal in sustaining penalty, did not suffer from any legal infirmity - Held, yes

FACT: Pursuant to the original assessment of the income of the assessee, a search took place at the residence of the assessee’s father in which a black handwritten diary of the assessee was seized wherein an entry relating to Rs. 10,000 in respect of some transaction with one ‘L’ was found. Pursuant to notice under section 148, the assessee himself surrendered the said sum on the ground that he was not in a position to produce the said person. The ITO reopened the assessment under section 147 and made addition and also imposed penalty under section 271(1)(c). On appeal, the order was set aside by the AAC. However, the Tribunal restored the penalty order.

On reference :

HELD: The Explanation inserted to section 271(1)(c) was clearly attracted in the instant case as the returned income was less than 80 per cent of the assessed income. [Para 6]

It might be mentioned that by section 40 of the Finance Act, 1964, the word ‘deliberately’ occurring in clause (c) of section 271(1) had been omitted. [Para 7]

With the incorporation of Explanation to section 271(1), the Apex Court has held in several cases that it is for the assessee to discharge the onus as contemplated in the said Explanation. [Para 9]

In the instant case, the assessee had not disclosed the income in the original return and had disclosed it only after the search was conducted and re-assessment proceeding was initiated. Thus, there had been a conscious effort on the part of the assessee to conceal the income. The assessee had not been able to rebut the presumption raised under the Explanation to section 271(1)(c), which was upon the applicant to prove that there was no gross or wilful neglect on his part. The question of shifting the burden/onus on the department, in the circumstances, did not arise. The findings recorded by the Tribunal were, therefore, based on the material and evidence on record and did not suffer from any legal infirmity. [Para 15]

issued only when the authority concerned has statutory power to do so. But statutory power is not necessary for issuing directions/instructions. The basic distinguishing feature between a direction and delegated legislation is that while delegated legislation is binding on both the administration and the individual and is enforceable through a court of law at the instance of either the individual or the administration, an administrative direction, generally speaking, is not so binding and enforceable. There may be an administrative remedy available to the individual concerned for enforcing such directions. Perusal of the said Instruction No. 1979 shows that the said instructions have not been issued by the CBDT in exercise of its powers conferred under section 119. The Board while referring to earlier circulars has mentioned that "in supersession of the above instruction, it has been decided by the Board that the appeals will be filed only in cases where the tax effect has exceeded the revised monetary limits given hereunder". Thus, the forms which are used does not indicate source of power under which it is issued. It merely indicates that the Board is conveying its executive decision to the Chief Commissioners, Directors General. Further, it can seen that Board has been issuing instructions/circulars in exercise of its powers conferred under section 119. Thus, it is clear that the Board while exercising its power under section 119, the practice has been to mention the source of power. However, there is no mention of source of power in the recital of the instruction No. 1979. In the absence of such a recital in the case of the said circular, the inference would be that the same is not issued under section 119. Thus, the same can be said to be administrative instruction having no statutory force behind it. Therefore, the same cannot be enforced through a court of law. Even assuming that these instructions are statutory in nature, the same cannot stand the legal scrutiny as no subordinate legislation can abrogate or override the provisions of the Act under which they have been framed. What section 119 has empowered the Board is to issue orders, instruction, or directions for the ‘proper administration’ of the Act or for such other purposes specified in sub-section (2) of that section. Such an order, instruction or direction cannot override the provisions of the Act. That would be destructive of the known principle of law as that would really amount to giving powers to a delegated authority even to amend the provisions of law enacted by Parliament. It may be seen that under section 253 both the assessee and the Commissioner have been allowed to prefer appeal before the Tribunal if they are aggrieved by the order of first appellate authority. Thus, the law has specifically authorized the Commissioner to direct the Assessing Officer to appeal to the Tribunal against such orders. This is a statutory right conferred by the statute on the Commissioner. Any instruction or direction of the CBDT curtailing the said statutory right would amount to overriding the provisions of the Act. Further, under section 119(2) the Board has been empowered to issue instructions/orders for the purpose of proper and efficient management of the work of the assessment and collection of revenue by way of relaxation of any provision of sections mentioned therein. The filing of appeal by the Commissioner does not fall in any of the categories for which the Board has been authorized to issue instruction under section 119; thus, the instruction in question would be beyond the scope of the provision of section 119. Therefore, it can be said that the instructions in question are not legally sustainable, being in violation of the provisions of Act and also beyond the scope of power conferred on the CBDT.

In view of the above, the Instruction No. 1979 being not issued in exercise of power conferred on the CBDT under section 119 is not statutory instruction but merely administrative instruction for the guidance of the income-tax authorities. Thus, the same cannot be enforced through a court of law. Therefore, there was no force in the preliminary objection raised by the assessee.

As regards imposition of penalty under section 271(1)(c), as per Explanation-1 to section 271(1)(c), penalty for concealment can be imposed only if both the conditions, namely, the assessee has failed to substantiate its explanation and has also failed to prove its bona fide, have been fulfilled. In case any of the two conditions is not fulfilled, no penalty under section 271(1)(c) is imposable. In other words, even if the assessee is not able to substantiate its explanation but if such explanation is bona fide, no penalty under section 271(1)(c) is imposed. In the instant case, the assessee had failed to substantiate its explanation in respect of the deposits made in the name of partners satisfactorily. However, bona fide of his explanation made in that regard had not been doubted by the department. In the circumstances, there was no infirmity in the order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals) cancelling the penalty order of the Assessing Officer.

HEADNOTE: Section 297, read with section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 28(1)(c) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Repeals and savings - Assessment year 1959-60 - Whether for purposes of penalty, there is no doubt classification under section 297(g) between assessees who had filed returns of income before 1-4-1962, and whose assessments were completed before that date and assessees who had filed returns of income before 1-4-1962, but whose assessments were completed on or after 1-4-1962 and, this is an intelligible classification - Held, yes - Whether clauses (f) and (g) of section 297(2) is not to discriminate against those assessees whose assessments for year ending on 31-3-1962, or any earlier year had not been completed before 1-4-1962, but to bring them in line with other assessees whose assessments are completed on or after 1-4-1962, in matter of imposition of penalty - Held, yes - Whether, in view of aforesaid, it could be concluded that section 297 (2)(g) was not violative of Article 14 of Constitution of India - Held, yes

FACT: The petitioner, assessee took forest contracts. It ran a saw-mill and also manufactured and sold furniture. It also did stone quarrying business. For the assessment year 1959-60 the petitioner filed a return of its income under section 22(2) of Act, 1922, on 21-10-1959, showing an income of Rs. 7,896. In the assessment proceedings the ITO noticed some discrepancies in the accounts and registers maintained by the assessee of its business and called upon the assessee to explain the discrepancies and furnish certain particulars. Thereupon, the assessee filed a revised return of its income on 17-1-1964, disclosing its total income as Rs. 50,605. The ITO finalized the assessment on 19-3-1964, after taking into consideration the revised return and issued a notice to the petitioner under section 271(1)(c) for concealment of income. The ITO referred the matter to the AAC as penalty intended to imposed by him exceeded Rs. 1,000.

The Inspecting Assistant Commissioner, finding that the assessee had concealed the particular of its income, made the impugned order imposing a penalty of Rs. 25,000 on the petitioner. The petitioner then preferred an appeal before the Tribunal which was dismissed. In the instant writ petition. It was contended by the petitioner that section 297(2)(g) being violative of article 14 of the Constitution is invalid and, therefore, no penalty could be imposed on the petitioner under section 271 and, that under section 271(1) a penalty can be imposed by the Income-tax Officer or the Appellate Assistant Commissioner only if he, in the course of any proceedings under the Act of 1961, is satisfied that any person has committed any of the acts enumerated in clauses (a), (b) or (c) of section 271(1); that, as the assessment against the petitioner was made under the Act of 1922, and not under the Act of 1961, the Income-tax Officer or the Appellate Assistant Commissioner had no jurisdiction to impose any penalty under section 271(1).

HELD: The effect of clauses (a), (f) and (g) of section 297(2) is that where the assessee files a return of income before the commencement of the Act of 1961, that is before 1-4-1962, for any assessment year, then the assessment of that person for that year is under the 1922 Act; any proceeding for the imposition of a penalty in respect of any assessment completed before 1-4-1962, can be initiated and penalty can be imposed under the 1922 Act; any proceedings for the imposition of a penalty in respect of any assessment for the year ending on 31-3-1962 or any earlier year which is completed on or after 1-4-1962 can be initiated and penalty can be imposed under the 1961 Act. In the present case, the petitioner filed a return of income before 1-4-1962, but the assessment was completed on 19-3-1964, that is after 1-4-1962, therefore, clause (g) of section 297(2) was plainly attracted for the initiation of proceedings for imposition of penalty under the Act of 1961.
