The penalty under section 271(1)(c) is leviable if the Assessing Officer is satisfied in the course of any proceedings under this Act that any person has concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars of such income. [Para 11.2] Indisputedly, the assessee, instead of rebutting the statement of 'S' recorded on oath during the remand proceedings, surrendered the amount and sought to withdraw the appeal filed before the Commissioner (Appeals). Even during the penalty proceedings, the assessee did not submit any explanation at all before the Assessing Officer. In these circumstances, it does not lie in the mouth of the assessee that it did not conceal particulars of its income in the return filed originally. In the course of penalty proceedings, the assessee did not bring any material before the Assessing Officer to rebut the inference drawn by the Assessing Officer in the course of reassessment proceedings. In terms of provisions of section 271(1)(c) read with Explanation 1 thereto. It is well established that whenever there is difference between the returned and assessed income, there is inference of concealment. The Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c) raises a presumption that can be rebutted by the assessee with reference to facts of the case. Thus, the onus is on the assessee to rebut the inference of concealment. The absence of explanation itself would attract penalty. The onus laid down upon the assessee to rebut the presumption raised under Explanation 1 would not be discharged by any fantastic or fanciful explanation. It is not the law that any and every explanation has to be accepted. The provisions of clause (A) to Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c), when the assessee did not submit any explanation during penalty proceedings, is clearly attracted and the assessee has miserably failed to discharge the onus laid down in this explanation. The plea of the assessee that copy of the statement of 'S' recorded on oath was not confronted to them for rebuttal, is baseless in view of observations of the Commissioner (Appeals), wherein it is clearly mentioned that copy of the statement was supplied to the assessee and thereafter alone, the assessee surrendered the amount and sought permission to withdraw the appeal. Even otherwise, for the first time an affidavit has been filed by 'S', director of the assessee company before the Tribunal in quantum proceedings wherein it is stated that the said statement of 'S' was not made available to them. However, 'S', who appeared before the Tribunal was specifically informed that the affidavit is not of the appropriate person. Thereafter, the assessee did not file any affidavit of 'S' nor disputed the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) in quantum proceedings before the Tribunal. In penalty proceedings also, the assessee did not submit any reply before the Assessing Officer. Since the facts on record establish that the assessee was supplied a copy of the aforesaid statement recorded on oath and only thereafter, amount was surrendered during the remand proceedings and the assessee sought to withdraw their appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals), the plea made that copy of the said statement was not made available is meaningless and is not tenable. Even otherwise, since the transaction was between the assessee company and 'F' Ltd., a company controlled by 'S', all the facts were within the specific knowledge of the assessee and its Director. In fact, 'S' was confronted with the statement of 'S' recorded during the course of survey, in the reassessment proceedings. In any case, the fact remains that the said surrender was not voluntary and it is only after statement of 'S' was recorded during the remand proceedings, the assessee felt cornered and offered the amount to tax. [Para 11.3]

On reference : HELD: A consideration of the provisions of section 297( 2)(f) and (g) establishes that the completion of the assessment before 1-4-1962 or after 1-4-1962 would be determinative of the applicability of the provisions of the 1922 Act or the 1961 Act, as the case may be. In the instant case, though on the basis of the return originally submitted by the assessee, the assessment was completed on 12-8-1960, there was a reopening of the assessment and the reassessment was completed only on 29-2-1972. The word 'assessment' has been defined in section 2(8) as including reassessment and the definition provision would apply, if there is nothing repugnant in the subject or the context and there is nothing to indicate that the definition under section 2(8) cannot be read into section 297(2)( g). Thus, if reassessment for the year ending on 31-3-1962 or any earlier year, was completed on or after 1-4-1962, proceedings for penalty could be initiated and penalty also imposed or levied under the provisions of the 1961 Act. In the instant case, at the time when the assessment was completed, there was no finding nor even any possibility of a finding that there was any concealment, which would justify the initiation of proceedings for the levy of penalty and also the imposition of penalty and it was only at the stage of reassessment, it came to light that large unexplained hundi credits existed and that formed the basis of the reassessment, which was completed on 29-2-1972. Under those circumstances, there could be no question of any concealment prior to the completion of the original assessment on the basis of the original return filed by the assessee. What was, therefore, relevant for purpose of initiating action for levy of penalty was only the reassessment and not the original assessment and since the reassessment was completed only on 29-2-1972, according to section 297(2)(g ), proceedings for levy of penalty could be initiated under the 1961 Act and penalty could be levied in accordance with the provisions of section 271.

As regards the question of imposition of penalty, in the instant case, there was no dispute that the income returned by the assessee in respect of the relevant assessment year was far less than 80 per cent of the total income assessed. Therefore, the requirement of the first part of the Explanation to section 271(1)(c) was fully satisfied. Further, in the instant case, no explanation at all was offered by the assessee regarding the increase in perk of non-genuine hundi credits. No further evidence was also produced by the assessee despite the opportunities given to the assessee to prove the genuineness of the hundi credits. The Tribunal, while dealing with the appeals against the order of assessment for the assessment year in question, had also categorically found that the assessee did not place any evidence to prove that it had made any effort to obtain the particulars of the credit or had met with practical difficulties in that regxrd. Therefore, the entire facts and materials considered during the reassessment proceedings established clearly and cogently that there had been a concealment. The Explanation to section 271(1)(c) got attracted and the assessee was liable for penalty. The Tribunal was, therefore, not justified in cancelling the penalty.

wilful neglect on the part of the assessee results in discharge of the burden placed on the assessee under the Explanation and once that burden is discharged the position reverts to as it was before the insertion of the Explanation . That is to say that on a finding that return of income which is less than 80 per cent of the assessed income is not the result of fraud or gross or wilful neglect, the penalty cannot be sustained by raising a presumption of concealment of income under the Explanation. If in an appropriate case the Tribunal or fact-finding authority is satisfied that there is no fraud or gross or wilful neglect on the part of assessee in submitting his return, then in such a case the assessee cannot be found within the mischief of the Explanation. At best additions made on account of the provisions of sections 68, 69, 69A, 69B and 69C become relevant at the time of raising the presumption under the Explanation to section 271(1)(c) on account of difference between the assessed income and the returned income. Once the presumption of concealment or concealed income stands rebutted, it is for the department to establish that the income which the assessee is alleged to have concealed is, in fact, his income as distinguished from deemed income of the assessee which he failed to disclose in his returns. The contention that in view of the provisions of section 68 for treating unexplained cash credits in the books of account of the assessee as income of the previous year relevant to the assessment years in question, the further question of proving that the additions were income of the assessee of the relevant previous year for the purpose of penalty proceeding did not arise, could not be accepted.

Sections 68, 69, 69A, 69B and 69C are all part of the same scheme where certain amounts though not proved to be the income of the assessee of the previous year concerned are for the purpose of charging to tax are deemed to be so by creating legal fiction absolving the department from its initial duty to prove that any such is the income of the assessee. But for these provisions, it was for the revenue to prove that any sum, not disclosed by the assessee but which is sought to be taxed as income of the assessee, is the income of the assessee for the previous year relevant to the assessment year.

The Explanation which was inserted in section 271(1)(c) with effect from 1-4-1976 cannot be held to be retrospective in operation to govern the cases coming earlier. That fact went to show that prior to the insertion of this Explanation it was not open to the Assessing Officer to raise any presumption about specific sums added or deductions disallowed, to consider it as income in respect of which particulars of income have been concealed merely on the ground of non-submission of explanation or explanation furnished but not found satisfactory though in such an event the amount could be added or deduction disallowed by resorting to other deeming provisions. It is to be noticed that falsity of explanation was expressly put differently from mere unsatisfactory nature of explanation offered. So also a clear distinction was drawn between an explanation which is not satisfactory and which is not bona fide. The former was sufficient to include the disputed sum in the computation of income of the assessee as falsity of explanation inheres wilful non-disclosure. In the latter case, though explanation offered by the assessee in respect of such additions or disallowance may be not satisfactory in the opinion of the ITO, it may be sufficient to include it in income, but still if the assessee establishes his bona fides about the explanation submitted by him, penalty could not be imposed by invoking the Explanation.

However, as the instant case was governed by the Explanation as it existed prior to the above referred provision, the only presumption that could be raised was that in case returned income was less than 80 per cent of the assessed income, the assessee could be deemed to have concealed particulars of income. On the assessee's showing that the difference was not owing to fraud or gross or wilful neglect on his part the presumption stood rebutted.

The fiction created under sections 68, 69, 69A, 69B and 69C by itself cannot be extended to penalty proceedings to raise the presumption about concealment of such income.

The Tribunal was right in law in cancelling the penalty imposed by the ITO under section 271(1)(c).

Note - The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

In this background, the pre-amended and erstwhile Explanation 5A as it stood at the time of search applied only to non-filer assessees who were searched under section 132 at the relevant time of search. To put it differently, Explanation 5A was strangely not applicable to those assessees who had already filed their returns under section 139 prior to search howsoever may be the extent of wrong doing or concealment. [Para 9.5] The application of pre-amended Explanation was limited to non-filer assessee whereas this anomaly was corrected in substituted Explanation. To elaborate, while the original Explanation 5A introduced by the Finance Act, 2007 with effect from 1-6-2007 held the persons guilty of concealment where the return was not filed only, the substituted Explanation 5A roped in with retrospective effect from 1-6-2007 by the Finance (No.2) Act , 2009 attempted to cover both filers of return of income as well as non- filers for the purposes of penalty on undisclosed income found. Thus, when viewed the law as existing on the date of initiation of search, Explanation 5A was attracted only where the assessee failed to file return of income altogether. Hence, when seen with reference to date of search 11-2-2009 in the instant case, the provisions of erstwhile Explanation 5A were not attracted to the assessee-company as the return of income was already filed prior to search and put on record. The application of amended provisions of Explanation 5A of section 271(1)(c) which came into force by an amendment subsequent to search albeit with retrospective effect thus cannot be applied when seen with reference to cause of action i.e. date of search. It is to be borne in mind that Explanation 5A appended to section 271(1)(c) is a legal fiction for deeming concealment against the assessee in search cases. Both original return under section-139 as well as revised return under section 153C had been filed before the amended provisions were brought into force. Hence, the shelter of substituted provisions of Explanation 5A to section 271(1)(c) could not be taken to the instant case for fastening concealment penalty. The assessee having filed the return under section-139 prior to search as well as return under section 153C prior to substituted Explanation coming into force, would be governed by pre-amended Explanation 5A and thus would escape the clutches of penalty under section 271(1)(c) due to non-fulfillment of conditions of pre-amended Explanation. [Para 9.7]

, it becomes clear that because of the expression 'deliberately' the Courts were of the opinion that even if explanation of the assessee was false the burden still lies with the revenue to prove beyond doubt that the assessee has concealed particulars of income. The Parliament amended the law by omitting the expression 'deliberately' in sub-section (c) which was omitted by the Finance Act, 1964. After such omission an Explanation was also inserted. [Para 9.3] Proviso was amended by Taxation Laws (Amendment Act and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1986 with effect from 10-9-1986. [Para 9.4]

After insertion of the Explanation (1) in section 271(1)(c), the burden has been shifted to the assessee to prove that he has not concealed the particulars of income and if such explanation is found to be bona fide, then penalty cannot be levied but if no explanation is given or the explanation is found to be false then penalty consequences will follow. It may be noted that whatever doubts were there regarding requirement of mens rea or 'deliberateness' have been removed by the Supreme Court in case of Union of India v. Dharamendra Textile Processors [2008] 174 Taxman 571/306 ITR 277. In this said decision the Larger Bench held that 'the object behind the enactment of section 271(1)(c) read with the Explanations indicates that the said section has been enacted to proved for a remedy for loss of revenue. The penalty under the provision is a civil liability. Wilful concealment is not an essential ingredient for attracting civil liability as is the case in the matter of prosecution under section 276C. [Para 9.5]

Hence, keeping in view the facts and circumstances of the instant case wherein the bona fide has not been proved by the assessee and the revenue could bring about a clear case of concealment of income, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) cannot be interfered with. [Para 10]

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1996-97 - Assessee did not revise its original return on receipt of second audit report which pointed out incorrect claim of liability in original return, and was compelled to disclose second audit report when scrutiny was carried out and after being asked to explain about inflation of cost - Similarly, claim in respect of booking of expenditure payable to ‘P’ Ltd. was incorrect and on being asked by Assessing Officer, it changed its explanation though that was not substantiated - Whether assessee had consciously withheld from department revised computation as per revised audit report, and assessee having filed inaccurate particulars, instant case was covered under Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c) - Held, yes

FACT: For the assessment year 1996-97, the assessee-company was finally assessed at a loss, and the appeal filed by the assessee having been withdrawn, the quantum of loss as determined became final. In the assessment order, the Assessing Officer had mainly made two additions, one in respect of bottle support expenses and the other for bogus purchases. In the course of penalty proceedings, the Assessing Officer observed that the return was already accepted under section 143(1)(a) but when it was taken up for scrutiny and the assessee was confronted in regard to its claim of distribution related cost of Rs. 67.71 lakhs, the assessee filed a revised computation and withdrew the claim of Rs. 44.5 lakhs. Thus, according to the Assessing Officer, if the case had not been selected for scrutiny, the assessee would not have withdrawn the claim to that extent. A revised audited financial statement for the period ending 31-3-1996 was also filed with revised computation of income. The revised figures were available when the audit was also revised and the assessee could have filed the revised return up to 31-3-1998, but it chose not to file such revised return. Since the total claim was of Rs. 80 lakhs in all, the Assessing Officer came to the conclusion that the assessee was liable for penalty under section 271(1)(c) read with Explanation 1 thereunder, for furnishing inaccurate particulars of income.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the levy of penalty.

On second appeal :

HELD: The assessee had not filed accurate particulars of income regarding his income/loss, as found by the Assessing Officer and the Commissioner (Appeals) and not contested by the assessee. In penalty proceedings the assessee had filed incorrect audit report under section 44AB with the original return. The circumstances under which the assessee had to carry out second audit were not spelt out and above all the assessee could have revised its return after it received second audit report but it chose not to do so. It was compelled to disclose the second audit report when scrutiny was carried out and after being asked to explain about the inflation of cost. The assessee incorrectly made a claim of liability in the return and even after it being pointed out in the revised audit, did not revise the computation suo motu and allowed the limitation for filing revised return to expire. [Para 7]

The assessee had consciously withheld from the department the revised computation as per revised audit report which was available to it by 19-5-1997, wherein the wrong claim made in the original return and original audit report was pointed out. Similarly, in respect of booking of expenditure of Rs. 10 lakhs payable to ‘P’ Ltd., the claim was incorrect and on being asked by the Assessing Officer, it changed its explanation though it was not substantiated. Coming to the legal arguments of the assessee that the penalty cannot be levied in a case where returned income and assessed income are loss, the Supreme Court in CIT v. Prithipal Singh & Co. [2001] 249 ITR 670/ 118 Taxman 330 declined to interfere on the facts of the case and confirmed the order of the Punjab and Haryana High Court holding that penalty for concealment cannot be levied in a case where returned income and assessed income is loss. Thus, the decision in Prithipal Singh & Co.’s case (supra ) rendered by the Supreme Court did not create a binding precedent as it was rendered on a particular set of facts. The important fact in that case was the assessment year 1970-71. Therefore, that decision did not lay a binding precedent for the cases pertaining to the assessment year 1976-77 onwards. [Para 12]

FACT: The assessees filed writ petitions challenging the validity of the provisions of section 271(1B), which was brought on the statute book by the Finance Act, 2008 with retrospective effect from 1-4-1989, on the ground that it is ultra vires the Constitution of India inasmuch as apropos to its insertion in the Act, the salutary requirement of the Assessing Officer arriving at his own satisfaction during the course of assessment proceedings that the assessee has concealed the particulars of his income or has furnished inaccurate particulars of income before initiating penalty proceedings had been done away with, by a deeming fiction encapsulated therein. The assessees prayed that the impugned sub-section (1B) of section 271 may be struck down as constitutionally invalid or alternatively, it may be read down to the effect that the satisfaction should be deemed to have been recorded only where reasons are specified with respect to specific items of additions or disallowances leading to the initiation of penalty proceedings.

HELD: The provision of clause (c ) of sub-section (1) of section 271, which deals with imposition of penalty for concealment of particulars of income or furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income by the assessee, has remained untouched since the 1922 Act was enacted, except for a brief interval in 1987 when the Direct Tax Laws (Amendment) Act, 1987 was passed. However, the same was not brought into force and the original position was reverted to, with the enactment of the Direct Tax (Amendment) Act, 1989. The gap, if any, in the interregnum was sought to be filled up by insertion of sub-section (5) in section 271. [Para 8]

What was sought to be achieved by the Direct Tax Law (Amendment) Act, 1987 was restored by the Direct Tax Law (Amendment) Act, 1989, insofar as clause (c) of section 271(1) was concerned. Therefore, there was no cogent reason articulated as to why retrospectivity to the impugned provision of section 271(1B) was also with effect from 1-4-1989. It was not the case of the revenue that this had been done keeping in mind its administrative convenience or for the reason that it did not want to continue with penalty proceedings in respect of stale cases. [Para 8.1]

of section 32A dealing with the procedure in respect of unabsorbed investment allowance in connection with the cases that have opted for business re-engineering, are quite clear that the 'amalgamated company shall not exceed the period of 8 years specified' in sub-section (3) of section 32A. Thus, the Act expressly provides for restriction of 8 years for the amalgamated company, like in the case of the present assessee. [Para 5] Thus, the period of limitation in respect of the brought forward investment allowance had lapsed in the assessment year 1996-97, itself as held by the Assessing Officer and upheld by the Tribunal in the assessment proceed-ings and the assessee should not have claimed the expired brought forward investment allowance. In other words, the assessee had made a claim without any support of the law in existence or the order of the BIFR and also against the express provisions of section 72A(3) or section 32A(6). [Para 6]

On having held that the assessee had wrongly claimed the expired investment allowance in the instant assessment year against the express provisions of the Act in that regard, it was to be examined if the explanation for the said wrong claim was bona fide or otherwise. From the impugned order it was found that the Commissioner (Appeals) had deleted the penalty by holding, without qualifying, that there was nothing to suggest the gross or wilful negligence or fraud by the assessee. The assessee had also contended that it was under the bona fide belief while making the said claim. In that regard, it was examined whether there was any information in the order of the BIFR; the provision of the SICA and section 72A or section 32A or any other provision under other statutes in favour of the assessee. There was no provision or order in favour of the assessee to suggest that it was entitled to claim the said expired loss beyond 8 years. Therefore, the answer was negative and against the assessee. Thus, the claim was patently wrong and such wrong or false claim could not avoid penalty. Although every wrong claim should not attract deemed concealment penalty, yet the claim made in the instant case with an attempt to explain the same relying on the non-existent direction of the BIFR should certainly attract such a penalty. In such a situation, the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) that there was no wilful negligence by the assessee was totally misplaced. [Para 7]

Regarding the debate on the wilfulness, being the essential ingredient in matters attracting the provisions of section 271(1)(c), it is a settled law now that the Assessing Officer does not have to prove that the assessee has concealed the income or furnished the inaccurate particulars. The Explanation to section 271(1)(c) contains the provisions for deemed concealment wherever there is difference between the returned and assessed incomes and it provides for a complete code in matters of penalty. From the Explanation 1, it refers to a couple of independent groups of cases, which are the deemed cases of concealment. They are: (A) This group refers to again two types of cases and they are: (i ) the persons, who fail to offer an explanation, (ii) the persons, who have offered an explanation which is found to be outright false by the revenue authorities; or (B) This group refers to cases where the explanation offered by the person is not found false outright, but those cases which are other than such outright false explanation cases. These are diagnosed by the following symptoms : (i) such person is not able to substantiate the explanation offered; and (ii) such person not only fails to prove that the such explanation is bona fide but all the facts disclosed relating to the such explanation and material to the computation of his total income. [Para 9]

On comparison, the assessee's case was found covered by the cases of group (B) above and the onus was on the assessee to substantiate the explanation or prove the bona fide and also the responsibility of full disclosure of all the facts relating to the explanation and materials as stated above. Per contra, the Assessing Officer was not under an obligation to prove the wilful attempt of the assessee in matter of concealment or that the explanation of the assessee in that regard was not bona fide. Thus, it was the assessee's responsibility to meet the above requirements. Wilful concealment is not an essential ingredient for attracting civil liability; such as a penalty under section 271(1)(c). [Para 10]

On appeal, the Tribunal cancelled the penalty levied by the IAC on the ground that there was no material to show that the payment of commission to agent firm was bogus and merely because the assessee agreed to the inclusion of the income that firm in its own total income, the inference that it represented the concealed income of the assessee could not be drawn.

On reference : HELD: In the instant case the income returned by the assessee for the same period, was obviously much less than 80% of the income finally assessed under section 147. Consequently, by the operation of the Explanation to section 271(1)(c), the assessee would be deemed to have concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars of such income for the purposes of clause (c) of section 271(1); and the assessee could avoid this fiction only on proving that his failure to return the correct income did not arise from any fraud or any gross or wilful neglect on his part. But no evidence was tendered by the assessee in that respect. On the other hand, there was sufficient material in the case to show that "fraud" was perpetrated by the assessee. The assessee debited in the profit and loss account for the relevant period commission paid to the agent-firm. When the accounts of the agent-firm was examined, the ITO detected that in the accounts of that firm the disputed amount was shown as debt due and that the debtor was none other than the assessee-firm. There was thus no payment by the assessee and no receipt by the assessee and no receipt by the agent-firm of any commission. In the absence of the debit of the commission in the profit and loss account of the assessee-firm, that amount also would have formed part of its assessable income and hence returnable at the very outset. As correctly inferred by the IAC it was only after the ITO proved to the hilt that the agent-firm was only a bogus concern set up for the purpose of diversion of more than half the profits of the assessee, that the firm agreed to the inclusion of the income so diverted in the reassessment and that there was clearly a calculated attempt on the part of the assessee to reduce its tax liability. The presumption provided for in section 271(1)(c) applies to the facts of this case with full force and the penalty provision under section 271(1)(c) must automatically apply.

There was enough material available and the reasonings of the Tribunal were clearly erroneous. The Tribunal held that there was no material to show that the payment to the agent-firm was bogus. The order of the IAC, extracted in extenso the findings of the ITO containing the materials on the basis of which he came to the conclusion that the agent-firm was a bogus concern and that registration could be granted. If the agent-firm was a bogus concern, the alleged payment to such a firm could not stand on a better footing. The taxing authorities held further that the agent-firm did not do any work for the assessee and that actually there was no payment of any commission by the assessee to the agent-firm. It could not be held that such a conclusion was not warranted by the facts of the case. It could not be said that non-disclosure alone can constitute concealment of income for the purposes of section 271(1)(c). Explanation 2 of section 147 enjoins that production before the ITO of account books or other evidence which material evidence could with due diligence have been discovered by the ITO will not necessarily amount to disclosure within the meaning of that section. If such a statutory inference is available in the matter of assessment of escaped income, there is no reason why it should not be applied for the purpose of section 271(1)(c) also if the false entry in the accounts was deliberate and made with a view to suppress the actual income. A false inflation of expenditure or any item deductible under the Act for computing the income will undoubtedly affect the taxable income to the detriment of the revenue and to the manifest advantage of the assessee. The ITO cannot start on the presumption that every entry in the assessee's accounts is false and pursue all possible avenues for ascertaining whether the entry is true. In the instant case, the ITO had no reason to believe that the entry in the assessee's accounts relating to the payment of the commission to the agent-firm was spurious. The falsity of the entry was undoubtedly a matter kept back from the ITO; and the reasoning of the Tribunal in this respect was not convincing. Even assuming that there was no concealment as such, there could be little doubt that the conduct of the assessee, namely, placing for the acceptance of the ITO a bogus debit as genuine, would constitute the furnishing of inaccurate particulars of the assessee's income so as to attract section 271(1)(c).

The perceptions of the taxpayers and the tax authorities about the impact of this judgment are at times so diametrically opposed to each other that there is effectively no meeting ground between these two extremes. Therefore, it would be necessary to deal with the legal position regarding the scope of penalty provisions under section 271(1)(c) post Dharamendra Textile Processors' case (supra ) by the Supreme Court. [Paras 11 and 12] A plain reading of the provisions of section 271(1)(c ) and the Explanation1 thereto, as it stands now, makes it clear that so far as the scheme of penalty for concealment of income is concerned, it is like this. It is sine qua non for imposition of penalty that the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner, during the course of any proceedings before them, should be satisfied that the assessee had (i) concealed his income, or (ii) furnished inaccurate particulars of income. As regards the quantum of penalty, the penalty imposed under section 271(1)(c) can range between 100 per cent and 300 per cent of the tax sought to be avoided by the assessee, as a result of such concealment of income or furnishing of inaccurate particulars. The third and most important feature of this provision is deeming provision regarding concealment of income. Not only the penalty provisions cover the situations in which the assessee has concealed income or furnished the inaccurate particulars, but in certain situations, even without there being anything to indicate so, statutory deeming fiction for 'concealment of income' also comes into play. In addition to normal connotations of 'concealment', thus, a deeming fiction is also implicit in the scheme of penalty provisions. This deeming fiction by way of the Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c) envisages two situations - (a) first, where in respect of any facts material to the computation of total income under the provisions of the Act, the assessee fails to offer an explanation or the explanation offered by the assessee is found to be false by the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner; and (b) second, where in respect of any facts material to the computation of total income under the provisions of the Act, the assessee is not able to substantiate the explanation and fails to prove that such explanation is bona fide and that the assessee had disclosed all the facts relating to the same and material to the computation of total income. In the first situation, the deeming fiction is triggered by the inaction of the assessee by his not giving the explanation with respect to any fact material to the computation of total income, or by action of the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner by giving categorical finding to the effect that the explanation given by the assessee is false. In the second situation, the deeming fiction is triggered by the failure of the assessee leading to satisfaction of conditions laid down in clause (b) of the Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c), namely, that the assessee is not able to substantiate an explanation in respect of any fact material to the computation of total income, and in addition to this, the assessee is also not able to prove that such an explanation was given bona fide and all the facts relating to the same and material to the computation of total income have been disclosed by the assessee. When this deeming fiction comes into play, which can only happen in one of the above situations, the related addition or disallowance in computing the total income of the assessee, for the purposes of section 271(1)(c), is deemed to represent the income in respect of which inaccurate particulars have been furnished. [Para 14]

Thus, even on the first principle, a penalty under section 271(1)(c ) is not simply as a consequence of an addition being made to the income of the assessee. The penalty under section 271(1)(c) is a penalty for concealment of income or for furnishing of inaccurate particulars or under the extended definition by virtue of the Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c), for a deemed concealment of income. As a corollary to this legal position, unless it is established that there is concealment of income or furnishing of inaccurate particulars or it is established that, on the facts of the case, concealment of income can be deemed in accordance with the provisions of law, the penalty provisions cannot be invoked at all. [Para 15]

There is a school of thought, however, to the effect that to successfully impose penalty under section 271(1)(c), the burden of the revenue is not discharged simply by demonstrating that the above conditions are satisfied; the revenue must also establish mens rea on the part of the assessee. There have been significant developments with regard to this school of thought in the recent past. [Para 16]

The first significant recent development that must be taken note of is the Supreme Court's judgment in the case of Dilip N. Shroff v. Jt. CIT [2007] 291 ITR 519/161 Taxman 218. [Para 17]

On reference:

The said Explanation was referred to only while setting out the principle of the decision of Punjab and Haryana High Court in Karnail Singh V. Kaleran's case (supra ). The effect of the Explanation to section 271(1)(c) has been set out by the Supreme Court in two recent decisions in CIT v. Mussadilal Ram Bharose [1987] 165 ITR 14/30 Taxman 546H and CIT v. K.R. Sadayappan [1990] 185 ITR 49/ 51 Taxman 304 . expressions ‘has concealed the particulars of income’ and ‘has furnished inaccurate particulars of income’ have not been defined either in section 271(1)(c) or elsewhere in the Act. [Para 8]

The word ‘conceal’ is derived from the latin word concelare which implies to hide. The offence of concealment is, thus, a direct attempt to hide an item of income or a portion thereof from the knowledge of the income-tax authorities. [Para 10] It may be noted that these words ‘concealed’, ‘particulars’ and ‘inaccurate’ are with regard to income and not with regard to any other thing. In the light of above discussion it can be said that there cannot be a straitjacket formula for detection of default of concealment of particulars or furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income. It depends upon the facts of each case. In the case under consideration, there was no dispute that purchases were made, though the assessee failed to substantiate its claim to the extent that the purchases were made from that particular party. Therefore, in the case under consideration, the word ‘particulars’ used in section 271(1)(c ) would embrace the meaning of the purchases made and not the party from whom these were made. As stated above that words ‘concealed’, ‘particulars’ and ‘inaccurate’ are with regard to income and not with regard to any other thing. From which party the purchases were made is not much important while computing the income. The important aspect in computing income is purchases. In the case under consideration, the purchases were recorded regularly in the books of account on day-to-day basis. The Tribunal while deciding the quantum matter observed that the assessee must have made purchases from the market from unregistered dealers in cash and details could not be obtained from such dealers. The assessee, therefore, obtained hawala bills from ‘F’. The Tribunal further observed that the Commissioner (Appeals) was of the view that in these circumstances the assessee must have inflated the purchase bills and on that account the disallowance to the extent of 25 per cent was found to be reasonable. The case of the Assessing Officer in quantum matter was that the entire purchases were disallowable whereas the appellate authorities found that the assessee must have made the purchases but the same might not be from ‘F’. Actual purchases made by the assessee were not doubted by the appellate authorities while deciding the quantum matter. However, considering the circumstances, they confirmed the addition to the extent of 25 per cent of the relevant purchases on the basis of the facts, figures and particulars provided by the assessee. Thus, the main basis on which the Assessing Officer levied penalty was not sustained by the appellate authorities. [Para 11]

In addition to main provisions of concealment, namely, ‘has concealed the particulars of his income’ or ‘has furnished inaccurate particulars of such income’ there are those which are deemed to represent the income in respect of which particulars have been concealed. The deemed concealment is provided in the Explanations. Often a question arises whether in cases where additions or disallowances are made by the ITO, the penal provisions of section 271(1)(c) would attract. The Explanation 1 takes care of this situation. [Para 12]

A conspectus of the said Explanation makes it clear that the statute visualized the assessment proceedings and penalty proceedings to be wholly distinct and independent of each other. In essence, the Explanation is a rule of evidence. Presumptions which are rebuttable in nature are available to be drawn. The initial burden of discharging the onus of rebuttal is on the assessee. The rationale behind this view is that the basic facts are within the special knowledge of the assessee. Section 106 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, gives statutory recognition to this universally accepted rule of evidence. There is no discretion conferred on the Assessing Officer as to whether he can invoke the Explanation or not. The Explanation 1 comes into operation when, in respect of any facts material to the computation of total income of any person, there is failure to offer an explanation or an explanation is offered which is found to be false by the Assessing Officer or the first appellate authority, or an explanation is offered which is not substantiated. In such a case, the amount added or disallowed in computing the total income is deemed to represent the income in respect of which particulars have been concealed. As per the provision of the Explanation 1, the onus to establish that the explanation offered was bona fide and all facts relating to the same and material to the computation of his income have been disclosed by him will be on the person charged with concealment. The explanation of the assessee for the purpose of avoidance of penalty must be an acceptable explanation; it should not be a fantastic or fanciful one. As indicated above, the consequence follows as a matter of law. The burden is on the assessee. If he fails to discharge that burden, the presumption that he had concealed the income or furnished inaccurate particulars thereof is available to be drawn. [Para 13]

Case 4

The assessee was engaged in the business of manufacture and trading of granite blocks. It was also engaged in the business of dealing in import of ceramic tiles. The Assessing Officer, on the basis of a search conducted at the assessee's premises, held that the assessee-firm was under invoicing and mis-declaring their import of ceramic tiles by changing the invoice and description in the Bill of Entry after it was assessed by the Customs. The Assessing Officer made addition to the total income of the assessee, being the excess stock for the tiles imported by the assessee under two bills of entry during the year, treating the same as unexplained investment.

The assessee claimed that excess quantity was supplied by the foreign parties to adjust the higher value of American Dollar per square meters.

Thereafter, a show-cause notice was issued under section 271(1)(c) and penalty proceedings were initiated.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that although the claim of the assessee had not been accepted by the assessing authority, it did not outrightly reject the assessee's contention, thereby implying that there were some bona fides in the assessee's contention. There was material to indicate that the assessee had actually paid higher rate for the said consignment and it had made payment in excess of any other mode. Therefore, he held that addition to income was justifiable, but levy of penalty on such valuation of excess stock was not necessary.

The Tribunal was of the view that it was not a fit case to impose penalty under section 271(1)(c), and therefore, there was no justification to interfere with the well considered order of the Appellate Authority deleting the penalty. Aggrieved by the order the revenue preferred this appeal.

HELD: Penalty under section 271(1)(c) is a civil liability. Therefore, mens rea is not an essential element for imposing penalty for breach of such civil obligations or liabilities. Wilful concealment is not an essential ingredient for attracting civil liability. [Para 63]

Existence of conditions stipulated in section 271(1)(c) is a sine qua non for initiation of penalty proceedings under section 271. The existence of such conditions should be discernible from the assessment order or order of the Appellate Authority or Revisional Authority. Even if there is no specific finding regarding the existence of the conditions mentioned in section 271(1)(c), at least the facts set out in Explanation 1(A) and (B) should be discernible from the said order, which would, by a legal fiction, constitute concealment because of deeming provision. Even if these conditions do not exist in the assessment order passed, at least, a direction to initiate proceedings under section 271(1)(c) is a sine qua non for the Assessing Officer to initiate the proceedings because of the deeming provision contained in section 1(B). The said deeming provisions are not applicable to the orders passed by the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Commissioner. [Para 63]

HEADNOTE: Explanation to section 271(1)(c), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1959-60 - Original assessment of assessee-firm was completed oh 12-8-1960 - Subsequently assessment was reopened to consider assessment of certain spurious hundi credits - In course of reassessment proceedings and subsequently, even during penalty proceedings before IAC, assessee merely asked for adjournments and did not offer any explanation as to genuineness of aforesaid hundi credits - Whether assessee having failed to discharge presumption of concealment, by virtue of applicability of Explanation to section 271(1)(c) it was liable for penalty - Held, yes - Whether even though original assessment was made under 1922 Act, reassessment having been completed under 1961 Act, penalty proceedings could be initiated and levied under section 271(1)(c) of the 1961 Act-Held, yes

FACT: For the assessment year 1959-60, the assessment of the assessee-firm was completed on 12-8-1960. Subsequently, the assessment was reopened under section 147(a) to consider the assessment of certain spurious hundi loans. A revised return was filed by the assessee, showing the income as originally assessed. In the course of the assessment proceedings, since the assessee did not substantiate the genuineness of the hundi credits, despite a number of opportunities given, the ITO treated the amount of aforesaid hundi credits as income from undisclosed sources and also disallowed interest relating to that and completed the assessment on 29-2-1972. The Tribunal upheld the addition of aforesaid credits as well as the disallowance of interest. In the course of penalty proceedings, numerous opportunities were given to the assessee, but the assessee merely asked for adjournments and did not offer any explanation as to the genuineness of the aforesaid hundi credits. The IAC, in view of the Explanation to section 271(1)(c), imposed penalty. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the concealment was referable only to the original return filed by the assessee on 11-5-1959 and, therefore, section 28(1)(c) of the Indian Income-tax Act would be applicable and further that the filing of a revised return on 28-8-1969, could not be taken as amounting to concealment in 1959. In this reasoning the Tribunal further held that the burden of establishing that the unexplained cash credits were the income of the assessee, was on the department and as the department had not produced evidence to show that such credits were either false or represented the income of the assessee, or that the payments were fictitious, no penalty was leviable and, therefore, deleted the penalty so imposed.

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1969-70 - Assessee-firm disclosed an income of Rs. 1,172 which was revised to Rs. 1,922 - However, ITO estimated it at Rs, 95,200 and assessed it - Penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) were also initiated - In quantum appeal, Tribunal reduced income of assessee to Rs. 39,000 - Whether Explanation to section 271(1)(c) was attracted and as assessee failed to rebut presumption of concealment against it deletion of penalty by Tribunal was not justified - Held, yes

FACT: For the assessment year 1969-70, the assessee-firm, disclosed its income of Rs. 1,172. Subsequently, the assessee filed a revised return disclosing the income of Rs. 1,922. However, the ITO estimated the income at Rs. 1,15,930 and after giving certain deductions he arrived at the net taxable income of Rs. 95,200. He also initiated penalty proceedings under section 27(1)(c) against the assessee. On second appeal, the income of the assessee was reduced to Rs. 39,000 by the Tribunal in quantum appeal. As regards the penalty, the Tribunal held that the possibility of error in good faith in the estimate of income could not be entirely ruled out and no fraud or gross and wilful neglect could either be attributed to the assessee. The penalty was, therefore, deleted by the Tribunal.

On reference:

HELD: In the instant case, since the difference between the income returned and income finally assessed by the Tribunal was too large, it was doubtful whether in such a situation there was any room for 'error in good faith'. The difference in amount was not small, it was very large. Moreover, the other observation of the Tribunal that 'no fraud or gross and wilful neglect can either be attributed to the assessee' was equally misplaced in law. The difference between returned income and assessed income was more than 20 per cent. If so, the Explanationto section 271(1)(c), then in force, got attracted Once the Explanation was attracted, presumption of concealment arose and as explained by the Superme Court in CIT v. K.R. Sadayappan [1990] 185 ITR 49/51 Taxman 304, the burden of rebutting the said presumption shifted to the assessee. It might also be noticed that in the instant case the assessee had filed no explanation, whatsoever, in response to the penalty notice. In its order the Tribunal had nowhere said that the assessee had discharged the onus lying upon him by virtue of Explanation to section 271(1)(c). The Tribunal was, therefore, not justified in deleting the penalty and the matter was referred to the Tribunal to rehear the case and to dispose of the same.

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1971-72 - Whether where income assessed by ITO was more than 80 per cent of returned income and assessee by not giving any explanation, failed to discharge onus cast upon it, Tribunal was right in holding that provisions of Explanation to section 271(1)(c) were attracted and, therefore, was justified in upholding order of ITO imposing penalty - Held, yes

FACT: For the assessment year 1971-72, the assessee filed its return of income showing total income of Rs. 71,870. However, the ITO completed the assessment on a total income of Rs. 1,68,350 and initiated penalty proceed-ings under section 271(1)(c) for concealing the particulars of income. The ITO issued show-cause notices to the assessee but the latter did not file any reply. Hence, the ITO imposed a penalty under section 271(1)(c) on the ground that an item of Rs. 51,314 was debited to the purchase account which was included in entry of Rs. 2.25 lakhs thereby showing that said amount was debited twice to the purchase of goods account suppressing the profit to the said extent. No explanation was furnished except stating that it was compensatory error. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition. On revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal set aside the order of the Commissioner (Appeals).

On reference :

HELD: With the incorporation of Explanation to section 271(1) by the Finance Act, 1964 the Apex Court has held in the cases of CIT v. Mussadilal Ram Bharose [1987] 165 ITR 14/30 Taxman 546H, CIT v. K.R. Sadayappan [1990] 185 ITR 49/ 51 Taxman 304 , Addl. CIT v. Jeevan Lal Shah [1994] 205 ITR 244/ 73 Taxman 182 and B.A. Balasubramaniam & Bros. Co. v. CIT [1999] 236 ITR 977 that it is for the assessee to discharge the onus as contemplated in the said Explanation. [Para 7]

The Explanation to section 271(1)(c) was clearly attracted in the instant case inasmuch as the assessed income was more than 80 per cent of the returned income. The onus was on the applicant which, it had failed to discharge as no explanation whatsoever was given by it before the Assessing Officer. Moreover, the Tribunal had recorded a clear finding that by debiting the amount of purchase of goods twice, the profits had been reduced. Therefore, the Tribunal was justified in upholding the order of the ITO imposing the penalty. [Paras 12 and 13]

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment years 1967-68 and 1968-69 - On search at business premises, two sale deeds for purchase of properties in name of wives of assessees were recovered - Source of money for purchase of properties was stated to be loans and sate of jewellery - ITO did not agree with statements and made additions - Penalty proceedings were initiated and IAC imposed penalty - On appeal Tribunal after considering various items found that there were no incriminating materials warranting a presumption of concealment for assessment year 1967-68 but held that there was concealment in subsequent year by assessee - Whether since findings recorded by Tribunal were findings of fact, and moreover, there was no specific question challenging factual findings on ground that there was no material to support said findings, in such circumstances, it was not open to High Court to interfere with aforesaid findings of Tribunal - Held, yes - Whether, consequently, order passed by Tribunal was to be affirmed
 - Held, yes

FACT: On 12-6-1967, the Enforcement Directorate conducted a search of the business premises of the firm in which the assessees were partners. During the said search, a sale deed dated 14-7-1966, relating to a premises in favour of the wives of the two assessees jointly for a considering of Rs. 41,900 was seized. The said document showed that the stamp papers to the value of Rs. 4,100 had been used for that document. A similar sale deed dated 1-5-1967, relating to another premises purchased for a consideration of Rs. 42,000 was also recovered from the premises along with a receipt

On the question of source of funds to purchase the above mentioned properties, the assessee stated that the cost of the property in all came to Rs. 72,910 and that for that purpose the wives had provided a sum of Rs. 36,000 each by raising loans and by selling jewels.

While completing assessments, the ITO accepted the case of obtaining loans but did not accept the assessee’s case of sale of jewellery of their wives. Therefore, the ITO made certain additions as undisclosed income from other sources in the assessments of both the assessees. Thereafter, the penalty proceedings were initiated and the IAC imposed penalty under section 271(1)(c). On appeal, the Tribunal accepted the assessee’s case in its entirety so far as the assessment year 1967-68 was concerned. According to the Tribunal, there were no incriminating materials warranting a presumption of concealment for that year. As regards the assessment year 1968-69, the Tribunal sustained the levy of penalty, but reduced the amount of penalty levied.

On reference :

HELD: The Tribunal actually went into the question as to whether there was in fact concealment by the assessee in respect of both the assessment years. The Tribunal after considering the various items which formed the subject-matter of assessment, found that for the assessment year 1967-68, there was no justification for holding that there was concealment as had been done by the IAC. But there was concealment in the subsequent year by the assessees though not to the extent held by the IAC. In view of the finding given by the final fact finding authority, the Tribunal, on the question as to whether there was in fact any concealment and if so to what extent, it was not possible for this court to interfere with the said finding especially when there was no specific question challenging the factual finding on the ground that that there was no material to support that finding. The Tribunal, after having held that for the year 1967-68, there was no concealment, proceeded to hold that there was concealment mainly on the basis that even in the revised return for the assessment year 1968-69, the assessee had failed to give an explanation either before the assessing authority or before the IAC or before the Tribunal. As regards this assessment year, the Tribunal found that there were special circumstances, apart form the revised return and the resultant assessment on an agreed basis, to indicate that there was concealment. In view of the fact that the finding of the Tribunal was based on materials, the Tribunal’s findings could not be interfered with in instant reference.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1966-67 - Whether Explanation to section 271(1)(c) covers a case where best judgment assessment is made under section 144 and it is found that income returned by assessee falls short of 80 per cent of income so assessed as reduced by bona fide expenditure incurred by assessee for purpose of earning any income included in assessee's total income - Held, yes - Whether burden of showing that failure to return aggregate income correctly did not arise from any fraud or gross or wilful neglect is upon assessee - Held, yes

He also added back a sum on account of certain expenses claimed and disallowed. On appeal, the Tribunal held that mere rejection of accounts and estimation of income at a higher figure by itself could not mean that there was either fraud or gross or wilful neglect on the part of the assessee in returning its aggregate income and since the department had not brought on the record any material or evidence from which it could be reasonably or positively inferred that the assessee's books and returns were not correct and complete, it was not possible to sustain the penalty. Accordingly, the penalty order was set aside.

On reference :

In the instant case, the finding of the Tribunal was that the interest income under section 214 was liable to be assessed in the assessment year 1972-73. Therefore, the impugned income could not form part of the assessment or concealed income for the assessment year 1974-75. Even otherwise, the Tribunal had found that the assessee had disclosed the particulars of interest under section 214 both in the statement of details of interest receipts and also in the return of income filed for the assessment year 1974-75. the penalty order as to which specific particulars were furnished inaccurate or were concealed. [Para 7]

Moreover, the expressions 'has concealed the particulars of income' and 'has furnished inaccurate particulars of income' have not been defined either in section 271 or elsewhere in the Act. However, notwithstanding the difference in the two circumstances, it is now well-established that they lead to the same effect, namely, keeping off a certain portion of the income from the return. [Para 7.1] The penalty under section 271(1)(c ) is leviable if the Assessing Officer is satisfied in the course of any proceedings under the Act that any person has concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars of such income. It is well-settled that assessment proceedings and penalty proceedings are separate and distinct and the findings in the assessment proceedings cannot be regarded as conclusive for the purposes of the penalty proceedings. It is also well-settled that the criterion and yardsticks for the purpose of imposing penalty under section 271(1)(c ) are different than those applied for making or confirming the additions. It is, therefore, necessary to reappreciate and reconsider the matter so as to find out as to whether the addition or disallowance made in the quantum proceedings actually represents the concealment on the part of the assessee as envisaged in section 271(1)(c ) and whether it is a fit case to impose the penalty by invoking the said provisions. The provisions of section 271(1)(c ) stipulate that if the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner(Appeals) or the Commissioner, in the course of proceedings under the Act, is satisfied that any person has concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars thereof, he may direct that such person shall pay by way of penalty a sum which shall not be less than but which shall not exceed three times the amount of tax sought to be evaded by a reason of the concealment of particulars of his income. Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c) mentions that where in respect of any facts material to the computation of the total income of any person under the Act, such person fails to offer an explanation or offers an explanation which is found by the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner(Appeals) or the Commissioner to be false, or such person offers an explanation which he is not able to substantiate and fails to prove that such explanation is bona fide and that all the facts relating to the same and material to the computation of his total income have been disclosed by him, then the amount added or disallowed in computing the total income of such person as a result thereof shall for the purpose of clause (c) of section 271(1), be deemed to represent the income in respect of which particulars have been concealed. In other words, the necessary ingredients for attracting Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c) are that (i ) the person fails to offer the Explanation, or (ii) he offers the Explanation which is found by the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner (Appeals) or the Commissioner to be false, or (iii ) the person offers explanation which he is not able to substantiate and fails to prove that such explanation is bona fide and that all the facts relating to the same have been disclosed by him. [Para 7.3]

If the case of any assessee falls in any of these three categories, then the deeming provision provided in Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c) come into play, and the amount added or disallowed in computing the total income shall be considered as the income in respect of which particulars have been concealed, for the purposes of clause (c ) of section 271(1), and the penalty follows. On the other hand, if the assessee is able to offer an explanation, which is not found by the authorities to be false, and assessee has been able to prove that such explanation is bona fide and that all the facts relating to the same have been disclosed by him, the assessee shall be out of the clutches of Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c), and in that case, the penalty shall not be imposed. The Supreme Court in the case of Dilip N. Shroff v. Jt. CIT [2007] 291 ITR 519 / 161 Taxman 218 had considered the scope of the provisions under section 271(1)(c ). [Para 7.3]

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessee-firm was dealer in kirana goods, sugar, vanaspati ghee, etc., and, for assessment year 1978-79, it had declared certain losses - Assessee gave an explanation but same was rejected by ITO who made additions to assessee’s income - ITO then initiated penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c), read with Explanation thereto, and ultimately imposed penalty - Whether, in view of fact that there were number of Explanations to section 271(1)(c) introduced with effect from 1-4-1976 and ITO had not referred to particular Explanation which was being invoked by him, imposition of said penalty was invalid - Held, yes - Whether even assuming that Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c) was invoked by ITO, even then said penalty could not be sustained because explanation furnished by assessee was bona fide and had not been found to be false by ITO - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-firm was a dealer in kirana goods, sugar, vanaspati ghee, etc. In the relevant assessment year, namely 1978-79, the assessee had declared certain losses in sugar account as well as in ‘Dalda ghee 2 kgs. account’. The assessee stated that the loss in sugar account was due to the fact that certain bags of sugar were damaged in rain which it sold at comparatively lower price. Similar was the reply in respect of ‘Dalda ghee 2 kgs. account’ where the tin boxes were stated to have been damaged. Regarding low gross profit in respect of all the accounts except kirana goods it was stated that it was not possible to maintain day to day stock tally. It was, therefore, urged that the gross profit rate declared be accepted. The ITO did not accept the assessee’s explanation and made certain agreed addition to the assessee’s income. The ITO then initiated penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c), read with Explanation thereto. To this the assessee urged that the difference in the assessed income and declared income was due to the addition on account of low gross profit and inadmissible expenses and that it had agreed to said addition just to avoid litigation and neither the income had been concealed nor inaccurate particulars had been furnished. The ITO, however, rejected the assessee’s contentions and levied a penalty under section 271(1)(c). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld the ITO’s order imposing penalty.

On second appeal, the assessee, inter alia, contended that there were a number of Explanations introduced with effect from 1-4-1976 to section 271(1)(c) and the ITO had not referred to a particular Explanation which was being invoked by him before he assumed jurisdiction of imposition of penalty and, therefore, in the absence of mention of a particular Explanation, the finding was vague and liable to be annulled.

HELD: A perusal of the assessment order by the ITO as well as the penalty order, in the present case, revealed that he invoked the Explanation below section 271(1)(c). At the relevant time, there were four Explanations below section 271(1)(c). The ITO did not specify as to which Explanation had been invoked by him to assume jurisdiction for the levy of the penalty. Therefore, the assumption of jurisdiction by the ITO to levy penalty under section 271(1)(c) was illusory and vague and, thus, invalid.

Even on merits, the penalty imposed upon the assessee could not be sustained because out of the four Explanations below section 271(1)(c), it was only Explanation 1, which could be invoked in the present case. This Explanation provides that it would be a case of deemed concealment where a person fails to offer an explanation or offers an explanation which is found by the ITO to be false. In the present case, the explanation had been offered by the assessee and there was no finding of the ITO or the Commissioner (Appeals) that the explanation furnished by the assessee was false. Another situation under Explanation 1 where it can be a case of deemed concealment is where an explanation has been offered which the assessee is unable to substantiate. However, the proviso below Explanation 1 further provides that it would not be a case of deemed concealment if the explanation is otherwise bona fide. There was nothing in the present case, to show that the explanation furnished by the assessee was not bona fide. Therefore, the present was a mere case of estimates of income and the assessee agreed to the addition to avoid litigation.

all rules prescribing irrebuttable presumptions are rules of substantive law cannot be adopted. The question can only be answered after examining the rule and its impact on the proof of facts A and B.

In the light of the above observations let us examined as to whether the rule contained in the Explanation can be said to be a rule of substantive law or a rule of procedural law, i.e., whether it is a rule for establishing or dis-establishing a specified substantive right or a rule of evidence merely. Clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 provides for the payment of certain penalty that may be directed by the ITO or the AAC if he is satisfied that any person has concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars of such income. Thus a person becomes liable to the penalty, how much that penalty should be we are not concerned with in connection with the enquiry, if he has concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars of the same. The Explanation only provides that, in certain circumstances, the assessee will be deemed to have concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars and the burden will then be on him to establish that the failure to return the correct income did not arise from any fraud or any gross or wilful neglect on his part. The condition which raises this presumption is that where the total income returned by the assessee is less than 80% of the total income as assessed under sections 143, 144 and 147 reduced by the expenditure incurred by him for the purpose of making or earning any income included in the total income but which has been disallowed as a deduction, the presumption will arise. Thus if an assessee makes a return and that return is disbelieved and he is assessed to a higher amount than he purports to show in the return and the total income that he has shown in his return is less than 80% of the income for which he is assessed, then the law thinks, as provided by this Explanation, that he has concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars. Can it be said, in the circumstances, that the existence of the position of the return being less than 80 per cent of the total income assessed is not relevant to the concealment of the particulars of his income by the assessee or his furnishing inaccurate particulars of such income. Clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 contemplates a certain amount of penalty for concealment of the particulars of income or furnishing inaccurate particulars by an assessee. If the return of an assessee's income is found not to be correct and is less than 80 per cent of the income at which he is ultimately assessed, the Explanation in such a state of affairs provides for the raising of a presumption against the assessee for his having concealed the particulars of his income or having furnished inaccurate particulars of such income. Obviously, applying the test laid down in Izhar Ahmad Khan's case (supra ) the Explanation provides nothing more than a rule of evidence relating to the raising of a rebuttable presumption in certain circumstances. It is not a rule which creates or negatives any substantive right. Such a rule is within the competence of the legislature to create. The question, however, is as to whether by the creation of such a rule the provisions of article 14 of the Constitution have been violated.

Article 14 of the Constitution guarantees to every citizen equality before the law and for the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.

An applicant pleading that article 14 has been violated must make out that not only he had been treated differently from others, but he has been so treated from persons similarly circumstances without any reasonable basis, and such differential treatment is unjustifiably made.

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1974-75 - For relevant assessment year in profit and loss account assessee credited a sum of Rs. 1,14,212 being interest under section 214 on income-tax refund allowed to it in respect of assessment years 1967-68 and 1971-72 - Assessee claimed deduction on ground that it had been assessed in earlier years - However, in reply to ITO's queries assessee not only failed to produce any evidence but also did not raise any objection in course of hearing before IAC against disallowance of said deduction - Assessment was completed without allowing said deduction - Assessing Officer initiated penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) - Assessee contended that it had claimed deduction on bona fide belief that said amount allowed by department under section 214 was not chargeable to tax and as particulars were written in return, there was no element of concealment - Assessing Officer, however, imposed penalty - Whether assessee having disclosed particulars of interest under section 214 both in statement of details of interest received and also in return filed, charge of concealment of income or of furnishing inaccurate particulars of income had no basis and, consequently, Tribunal was right in cancelling penalty - Held, yes - Whether even otherwise when Tribunal's finding was that interest amount in question was assessable in assessment year 1972-73 there was no question of its being concealed in assessment year 1974-75 - Held, yes

FACT: In the profit and loss account attached to the return filed for the assessment year 1974-75, the assessee claimed to have credited a sum of Rs. 1,14,212 being the interest allowed under section 214 on income-tax in respect of the assessment years 1967-68 and 1971-72. The assessee also claimed deduction of same on ground that it had been assessed in earlier year. The assessee, however, could not produce any evidence of earlier assessment of the amount of interest under section 214. Thus, the Assessing Officer proposed not to allow the claim of deduction in his draft assessment order under section 144B to the IAC. The assessee did not also raise any objection in course of hearing before IAC. The assessment was, thus, completed without allowing the deduction claimed, in the assessment year 1974-75, and, consequently, the inclusion of the aforesaid amount of interest under section 214 for the assessment year 1967-68 in the assessment of the assessee for the assessment year 1974-75 had become final. The Assessing Officer initiated penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) in respect of concealment and inaccurate particulars filed in the return relating to the incorrect claim of aforesaid deduction, on the ground that the amount had been claimed to have been already assessed in earlier year. The assessee contended that it had claimed the amount as deduction on the bona fide belief that the said amount allowed by the department under section 214 was not chargeable to tax and as the particulars were written in the return, there was no element of concealment. The Assessing Officer, however, imposed penalty under section 271(1)(c) on the ground that the assessee had concealed its income and furnished inaccurate particulars in respect of the income of Rs. 1,14,212 by claiming deduction in the return stating 'assessed in earlier year'. On second appeal, the Tribunal cancelled the penalty on the ground that as the assessee had disclosed particulars of interest under section 214 both in the statement of details of interest received and also in the return filed, the assessee could not be charged with concealment of its income or furnishing inaccurate particulars of income.

On reference:

HELD: If certain income is not liable to be assessed as income of any particular assessment year, the question of concealing such income or furnishing inaccurate particulars of such income by the assessee while filing the return for the said assessment year could not arise at all. What revenue was required to do was to consider the explanation, if any, offered by the assessee and decide upon its acceptability. The burden was on the assessee to prove that there was no concealment. That is the main import of the Explanation added to section 271(1)(c) with effect from 1-4-1964.
