CONSCIOUS CONCEALMENT - Penalty under section 271(1)(c) is civil liability and for attracting such civil liability, wilful concealment is not an essential ingredient as is case in matter of prosecution under section 276C - Union of India v. Dharamendra Textile Processors [2008] 166 Taxman 65 (SC).

An order imposing penalty for failure to carry out a statutory obligation is the result of a quasi-criminal proceeding, and penalty will not ordinarily be imposed unless the party obliged either acted deliberately in defiance of law or was guilty of conduct contumacious or dishonest, or acted in conscious disregard to its obligation. Penalty will not also be imposed merely because it is lawful to do so. Whether penalty should be imposed for failure to perform a statutory obligation is a matter of discretion of the authority to be exercised judicially and on a consideration of all the relevant circumstances. Even if a minimum penalty is prescribed, the authority competent to impose the penalty will be justified in refusing to impose penalty when there is a technical or venial breach of the provision of the Act or where the breach flows from a bona fide belief that the offender is not liable to act in the manner prescribed by the statute - Hindustan Steel Ltd. v. State of Orissa [1972] 83 ITR 26 (SC).

Mere omission from the return of an item of receipt does neither amount to concealment nor deliberate furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income unless and until there is some evidence to show or some circumstances found from which it can be gathered that the omission was attributable to an intention or desire on the part of the assessee to hide or conceal the income so as to avoid the imposition of tax thereon. In order that a penalty under section 271(1)(iii) may be imposed, it has to be proved that the assessee has consciously made the concealment or furnished inaccurate particulars of his income - K.C. Builders v. Asstt. CIT [2004] 135 Taxman 461 (SC).

'Concealment' refers to a deliberate act on part of assessee; if explanation given by assessee with regard to mistake committed by him has been treated to be bona fide and it has been found as a fact that he has acted on basis of wrong legal advice, question of his failure to discharge his burden in terms of Explanation appended to section 271(1)(c) would not arise - T. Ashok Pai v. CIT [2007] 161 Taxman 340 (SC).

Primary burden of proof is on revenue; even when burden is required to be discharged by an assessee, it would not be as heavy as in prosecution cases; before a penalty can be imposed, the entirety of circumstances must reasonably point to conclusion that disputed amount represented income and that assessee had consciously concealed the particulars of his income or had furnished inaccurate particulars thereof - Dilip N. Shroff v. Jt. CIT [2007] 161 Taxman 218 (SC).

Penalty under section 271(1)(c) is civil liability and for attracting such civil liability, wilful concealment is not an essential ingredient as is case in matter of prosecution under section 276C - Union of India v. Dharamendra Textile Processors [2008] 166 Taxman 65 (SC).

Supreme Court judgment in case of Dilip N.Shroff v. Jt. CIT [2007] 291 ITR 519 requires reconsideration; Explanations added to section 271(1)(c) in their entirety also indicate element of strict liability on assessee for concealment or for giving inaccurate particulars while filing returns - Union of India v. Dharamendra Textile Processors [2007] 295 ITR 244 (SC). [See also Union of India v. Rajasthan Spg. & Wvg. Mills [2009] 180 Taxman 609 (SC)].

Only those persons will be liable to penalty who do not have good and sufficient reason for not deducting tax and burden, of course, is on such person to prove such good and sufficient reason - CIT v. Eli Lilly & Co. (India) (P.) Ltd. [2009] 178 Taxman 505 (SC).

Onkar Saran & Sons [1992] 195 ITR 1 (SC).

Committee Report. Earlier the concealment penalty was based on the quantum of income concealed and there was an Explanation that in case the returned income is less than 80 per cent of the assessed income, then the burden of proving that concealment was on the assessee. Wanchoo Committee recommended that the penalty should be based on the amount of tax sought to be evaded. What is meant by tax sought to be evaded was mentioned in the Explanation 4. [Para 3.20] From the judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Dharamendra Textile Processors [2008] 306 ITR 277/ 174 Taxman 571, it was clear that the object behind enactment of section 271(1)(c ) was to provide a remedy for loss of revenue. Wilful concealment is not an essential ingredient for imposing penalty, as that is the requirement in case a prosecution is launched. However, in the instant case, the assessee was fully aware of the fact of unaccounted sales. He was fully aware of the income from such sales. He had not given any explanation to say as to why such sales were not disclosed in the original return. The explanation for not disclosing such sales was not forthcoming. Only explanation given was that the income had been surrendered to purchase peace and to avoid litigation. [Para 3.21]

The assessee had not agreed to an item to be included in the income, which was being reflected in the books of account. This was a case where unaccounted sales were found during the course of search and amount outstanding on account of such sales were found. Even in respect of accounted sales, the assessee was preparing the purchase vouchers as actual purchases were made from hawkers and no purchase bills were obtained from them. [Para 3.22]

In the original return, the assessee had not disclosed the entire sales. That fact was material to the computation of the total income. No explanation had been offered as to why such sales were not reflected in the original return. The only explanation submitted was that the assessee agreed to the addition to purchase peace. Such explanation could not be considered as bona fide because the documents relating to such unaccounted sales were found. It was also found that the assessee was having unaccounted debtors to the extent of Rs. 93.54 lakhs as on 31-3-2004. Hence, in the instant case, the Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c) was squarely applicable for imposition of penalty. [Para 3.24]

As per section 271(1B), there is deemed satisfaction in respect of additions made. The Assessing Officer had imposed penalty not only on the addition made to the income returned under section 153A but also on the difference between the original returned income and the income returned in response to the notice under section 153A. The Act does not require any specific form of satisfaction to be recorded. The satisfaction can be inferred from the assessment order. [Para 4.1]

From the observations of the Assessing Officer recorded in the assessment order it was clear that the Assessing Officer was satisfied that the additional income being offered was the concealed income. The narration of the facts in the assessment order and mentioning of incriminating documents found during the course of search showing unaccounted sales clearly indicated that the Assessing Officer was satisfied during the course of proceedings that penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) were required to be initiated. The satisfaction was evident and it could not be held that the proceedings had been initiated without recording satisfaction. [Para 4.2]

Relying on the decision of the Tribunal in Asstt. CIT v. Goutham Public School [2004] 88 ITD 31 (Visakhapatnam) and considering the facts as mentioned above, it was to be held that the Assessing Officer was satisfied before initiating the proceedings under section 271(1)(c). [Para 4.3]

It was true that the show-cause notice did not contain the specific allegation, i.e., whether it was in respect of concealment of income or furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income. The notice was to be read along with the assessment order during the course of which proceedings had been initiated. The proceedings had been initiated for concealment of income. The assessee in his reply had understood the spirit in which notice had been issued. In his reply, it had been mentioned that he had offered additional income to buy peace and to have an end to the proceedings. If the notice in substance and effect is in conformity with or according to the intent and purpose of the Act, then such notice cannot be held as invalid as per section 292B. The purpose of issuing the show-cause notice is to give the assessee an adequate opportunity in respect of default, which is detected and alleged against him. From the nature of the assessment proceedings and the fact mentioned in the assessment order, it was clear that there was a specific charge of concealment of income and the assessee got adequate opportunity in rebutting such charge. Hence, it could not be said that penalty proceedings were invalid because the Assessing Officer had not struck off the column for which the assessee was not required to give reply. Hence, on that ground, penalty proceedings could not be cancelled. [Para 5.1]

24.1 Penalty provisions

24.1-1 Penalty for concealment of income [Section 271(1)(c)]

Under the existing provision contained in clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 of the Act penalty for concealment of income or furnishing inaccurate particulars of income is levied on the "amount of tax sought to be evaded", which has been defined, inter alia, as the difference between the tax due on the income assessed and the tax which would have been chargeable had such total income been reduced by the amount of concealed income. Courts have held that penalty under clause (c) of sub- section (1) of section 271 cannot be levied in cases where the concealment of income occurs under the income computed under general provisions and the tax is paid under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC of the Act.

In CIT v. Nalwa Sons Investment Ltd. [2012] 21 taxmann.com 184 (SC), it was held that when assessment was made on income computed under section 115JB and tax had been paid on income so computed, penalty under section 271(1)(c) would not be imposed with reference to additions that would have been made taking into account concealment made by assessee while making assessment under normal procedure.

In CIT v. Jindal Polyester & Steel Ltd. [2014] 52 taxmann.com 259 (All.) the High Court held that book profit disclosed by assessee for purpose of tax liability under MAT provision was relevant and not income determined under provisions of the Income-tax Act. When concealment of income did not lead to tax evasion under MAT provisions, no penalty would be levied.

In Unison Hotels Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2013] 40 taxmann.com 237 (Delhi) it was held that when taxable income is computed on book profits under section 115JB, there cannot be imposition of penalty under section 271(1)(c) for additions made under normal provisions.

Tax paid under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC over and above the tax liability arising under general provisions is available as credit for set off against future tax liability. Understatement of income and the tax liability thereon under general provisions results in larger amount of such credit becoming available to the assessee for set off in future years. Therefore, where concealment of income, as computed under the general provisions, has taken place, penalty under clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 should be leviable even if the tax liability of the assessee for the year has been determined under provisions of section 115JB or 115JC of the Act.

Section 271 of the Act has been amended so as to provide that the amount of tax sought to be evaded shall be the summation of tax sought to be evaded under the general provisions and the tax sought to be evaded under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC. However, if an amount of concealment of income on any issue is considered both under the general provisions and provisions of section 115JB or 115JC then such amount shall not be considered in computing tax sought to be evaded under provisions of section 115JB or 115JC. Further, in a case where the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC are not applicable, the computation of tax sought to be evaded under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC shall be ignored. This amendment will take effect from 1-4-2016 and will accordingly apply, in relation to the assessment year 2016-17 and subsequent assessment years.

(A-B) + (C-D)

FACT: The question that arose for decision in reference application under section 256(2) was whether the law applicable for the purpose of imposing penalty under section 271(1)(c) was the law applicable as on date of filing of return or the law that was obtainable on the date of passing of the penalty order. The Division Bench of the High Court pointing out that the two Bench cases of the Court in CIT v. Bihar Cotton Mills Ltd. [1988] 170 ITR 290 and CIT v. M.N. Chatterjee [1988] 170 ITR 87 had taken a view contrary to the Supreme Court judgment in Brij Mohan v. CIT [1979] 120 ITR 1 by placing reliance on two other Supreme Court cases in Jain Brothers. Union of India [1970] 77 ITR 107 and Maya Rani Punj v. CIT [1986] 157 ITR 330, opined that the decisions of the Supreme Court rendered in relation to section 271(1)(a) have no bearing on the question of quantum of penalty leviable under section 271(1)(c), and referred the matter before the Full Bench.

On reference:

HELD: The issue in question stood concluded by a decision of the Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. Onkar Saran Sons [1992] 195 ITR 1 wherein it was held that even in a case where a return filed under section 148 involves an element of concealment, the law applicable for imposition of penalty will be the law as in force at the time of filing of the original return for the assessment year in question and not the law as it stands on the date on which the return in response to the notice under section 148 was filed.

Therefore, the Tribunal was justified in law in holding that the law applicable was as it stood on the date of filing of the return and not on the date of passing the penalty order for concealment of income or satisfaction about the concealment of income for the purpose of imposing penalty.

The proceedings under section 271(1)(c ) can be initiated only if the Assessing Officer or the first appellate authority is satisfied in the course of any proceedings under the Act as per clause (c) of the section 271(1) that any person has concealed the particulars of his income or has furnished inaccurate particulars of such income, he may direct that such person shall pay by way of penalty the sum mentioned in sub-clause (iii ) of clause (c) of the section 271(1). The expression used in clause (c) of the section 271(1) is ‘has concealed the particulars of his income’ or ‘furnished inaccurate particulars of such income’. The expressions ‘has concealed the particulars of income’ and ‘has furnished inaccurate particulars of income’ have not been defined either in section 271(1)(c) or elsewhere in the Act. Two words are important words for considering a matter for levy of penalty under section 271(1)(c). These words are ‘conceal’ and ‘inaccurate particulars’ The word ‘conceal’ is derived from the latin word ‘concelare’ which implies con+celare to hide. The offence of concealment is thus a direct attempt to hide an item of income or a portion thereof from the knowledge of the income-tax authorities. [Para 9]

In addition to main provisions of concealment ‘has concealed the particulars of his income’ or ‘has furnished inaccurate particulars of such income’ there are deemed to represent the income in respect of which particulars have been concealed. The deemed concealment is provided in Explanations. The penalty under the said section is a civil liability. Wilful concealment is not an essential ingredient for attracting the civil liability. [Para 9.1]

While considering an appeal against an order made under section 271(1)(c) what is required to be examined is the record which the officer imposing the penalty had before him and if that record can sustain the finding about concealment, that would be sufficient to sustain the penalty. The Explanations added to section 271(1)(c) in that entirety also indicate the element of strict liability on the assessee for concealment or for giving inaccurate particulars while filing returns. It is obvious that the penal provisions would operate when there is concealment of particulars of income or a failure of duty to disclose fully and truly particulars of income, imposed under the Act and the Rules thereunder. The duty is enjoined upon a person to make a correct and complete disclosure of particulars of his income and it is only when he fails in his duty by not disclosing particulars of his income or part thereof, he conceals the particulars of his income. The duty is enjoined upon him to make a complete disclosure of particulars of his income as well as a correct disclosure. Therefore, if the disclosure made of the particulars of income is incorrect, then also he commits breach of his duty. Such defaults entail the penal consequences contemplated by section 271(1)(c). [Para 9.2]

24.1 Penalty provisions

24.1-1 Penalty for concealment of income [Section 271(1)(c)]

Under the existing provision contained in clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 of the Act penalty for concealment of income or furnishing inaccurate particulars of income is levied on the "amount of tax sought to be evaded", which has been defined, inter alia, as the difference between the tax due on the income assessed and the tax which would have been chargeable had such total income been reduced by the amount of concealed income. Courts have held that penalty under clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 cannot be levied in cases where the concealment of income occurs under the income computed under general provisions and the tax is paid under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC of the Act.

In CIT v. Nalwa Sons Investment Ltd. [2012] 21 taxmann.com 184 (SC), it was held that when assessment was made on income computed under section 115JB and tax had been paid on income so computed, penalty under section 271(1)(c) would not be imposed with reference to additions that would have been made taking into account concealment made by assessee while making assessment under normal procedure.

In CIT v. Jindal Polyester & Steel Ltd. [2014] 52 taxmann.com 259 (All.) the High Court held that book profit disclosed by assessee for purpose of tax liability under MAT provision was relevant and not income determined under provisions of the Income-tax Act. When concealment of income did not lead to tax evasion under MAT provisions, no penalty would be levied.

In Unison Hotels Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2013] 40 taxmann.com 237 (Delhi) it was held that when taxable income is computed on book profits under section 115JB, there cannot be imposition of penalty under section 271(1)(c) for additions made under normal provisions.

Tax paid under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC over and above the tax liability arising under general provisions is available as credit for set off against future tax liability. Understatement of income and the tax liability thereon under general provisions results in larger amount of such credit becoming available to the assessee for set off in future years. Therefore, where concealment of income, as computed under the general provisions, has taken place, penalty under clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 271 should be leviable even if the tax liability of the assessee for the year has been determined under provisions of section 115JB or 115JC of the Act.

Section 271 of the Act has been amended so as to provide that the amount of tax sought to be evaded shall be the summation of tax sought to be evaded under the general provisions and the tax sought to be evaded under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC. However, if an amount of concealment of income on any issue is considered both under the general provisions and provisions of section 115JB or 115JC then such amount shall not be considered in computing tax sought to be evaded under provisions of section 115JB or 115JC. Further, in a case where the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC are not applicable, the computation of tax sought to be evaded under the provisions of section 115JB or 115JC shall be ignored. This amendment will take effect from 1-4-2016 and will accordingly apply, in relation to the assessment year 2016-17 and subsequent assessment years.

To give effect to the above, Explanation 4 to section 271(1)(c) has been substituted Explanation 4 provides that the amount of tax sought to be evaded shall be determined in accordance with the following formula—

(A-B) + (C-D)

where,

A = amount of tax on the total income assessed as per the provisions other than the provisions contained in section 115JB or section 115JC (herein called general provisions);

B = amount of tax that would have been chargeable had the total income assessed as per the general provisions been reduced by the amount of income in respect of which particulars have been concealed or inaccurate particulars have been furnished;

C = amount of tax on the total income assessed as per the provisions contained in section 115JB or section 115JC;

D = amount of tax that would have been chargeable had the total income assessed as per the provisions contained in section 115JB or section 115JC been reduced by the amount of income in respect of which particulars have been concealed or inaccurate particulars have been furnished:

FACT: The assessee-firm filed a return showing an income. The ITO completed the assessment on the higher income. The penalty proceedings were initiated under section 271(1)(c) in respect of unexplained cash credit and unexplained investment. The case was referred by the ITO to the IAC who issued a show-cause under section 274 in response to the notice the assessee filed a written reply which was not accepted by the IAC and he found that the assessee interpolated the entries in the cash book with regard to the credit of certain amount. He further recorded a finding that the assessee tried to evade taxes by claiming the business as a separate unit and that the explanation given regarding the cash credit was not even probable. The assessee filed an appeal and the Tribunal set aside both these findings and held that in the absence of finding that the assessee made any attempt to conceal the facts, it would be difficult to give a finding that merely because the assessee failed in his device to illegally avoid taxes he could be held guilty within the provisions of section 271(1)(c)

HELD: No questions had been raised on behalf of the department on the findings recorded by the Tribunal.

In the decision of the Supreme Court in Karnani Properties Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax [1971] 82 ITR 547 (SC) it was held that when the question referred to the High Court speaks of 'on the facts and circumstances of the case', it means 'on the facts and circumstances found by the Tribunal' and not 'facts and circumstances' that may be found by the High Court on a reappraisal of the evidence. In view of that pronouncement of law, it was held that the findings recorded by the Tribunal could not be gone into.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

Section 271(1)(c) is attracted where, in the course of any proceedings under the Act, the Assessing Officer or the first appellate authority is satisfied that (a) any person has concealed the particulars of his income, or (b) has furnished inaccurate particulars of such income. The expression "has concealed" and "has furnished inaccurate particulars" have not been defined either in the section or elsewhere in the Act. However, notwithstanding differences in the two circumstances, they lead to the same effect, viz., keeping off a certain portion of the income. The former is direct while the latter may be indirect in its execution. The word 'conceal' is derived from the Latin word 'concelare' which implies 'to hide'. In Webster's New International Dictionary, the word has been equated with : 'to hide or withdraw from observation; to cover or keep from sight; to prevent discovery of; to withhold knowledge of'; the meaning of word 'concealment' as found in Shorter Oxford English Dictionary is : "In law, the intentional suppression of truth or fact known, to the injury or prejudice of another". There may be cases where the facts may attract both the offences and in some cases there may be overlapping of the two offences.

If, in the facts and circumstances of a particular case, and on the materials before it, the Tribunal reaches a conclusion that concealment was not proved, it is a question of fact and no question of law arises from such order. Similarly, whether the burden in a given case has been discharged on a set of facts or not is a question of fact. Where a finding of fact arrived at by the Tribunal is based on no material or is perverse or is based on irrelevant, extraneous or inadmissible considerations or is arrived at by the application of wrong principles of law, a question of law arises. Where the Tribunal fails to arrive at its own conclusion of fact after due and proper consideration of the entire materials for and against the assessee and cancels the penalty, a question of law arises. Similar is the case where conclusions of the Tribunal suffer from infirmity on account of relevant materials and evidence being ignored.

A conspectus of the Explanation added by the Finance Act, 1964, and the subsequent substituted Explanations makes it clear that the statute visualized assessment proceedings and penalty proceedings to be wholly distinct and independent of each other. In essence, the Explanation (after 1964) is a rule of evidence. Presumptions which are rebuttable in nature are available to be drawn. The initial burden of discharging the onus of rebuttal is on assessee. The rationale behind this view is that the basic facts are within the special knowledge of the assessee. Section 106 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 gives statutory recognition to this universally accepted rule of evidence. There is no discretion conferred on the Assessing Officer as to whether he can invoke the Explanation or not. Explanation 1 , which primarily concerned the case at hand, automatically comes into operation when, in respect of any facts material to the computation of the total income of any person, there is failure to offer an explanation or the explanation is offered which is found to be false by the Assessing Officer or the first appellate authority, or an explanation is offered which is not substantiated. In such a case, the amount added or disallowed in computing the total income is deemed to represent the income in respect of which the particulars have been concealed. As per the proviso to Explanation 1, the onus to establish that the explanation offered was bona fide and all facts relating to the same and material on the computation of his income have been disclosed by him will be on the person charged with concealment. Mere failure to substantiate the explanation is not enough to warrant penalty. The revenue has to establish that the explanation offered was not substantiated.

The principal logical import of the Explanation is to shift the burden of proof from the revenue on to the assessee. Rebuttal must be on materials relevant and cogent. It is for the fact-finding body to judge the relevancy and sufficiency of the materials. If such a fact-finding body, bearing the aforesaid principles in mind, comes to a conclusion that the assessee has discharged the onus, it becomes a conclusion of fact, and no question of law arises. The initial burden is on the assessee. Once the initial burden is discharged, the assessee would be out of mischief unless further evidence is adduced. It is plain on principle that it is not the law that the moment any fantastic or unacceptable explanation is offered, the burden placed would be discharged and the presumption rebutted.

Section 271(1)(c) imposes penalty for concealment of particulars of the income or furnishing inaccurate particulars thereof. This obviously means that the act o f concealment is an overt act and stems from the return of income filed by the assessee. If an assessee does not file a return at all, action is contemplated under section 277(7)(a). But when a return is filed and particulars of income are conceale d, action is contemplated under section 271(1)(c) . Hence, the very basis for an imposition of the penalty under section 271(1)(c) is not the assessment year in respect of which the return of income has been filed but the return itself. The question is as to when the act of concealment occurred. If an act of concealment is the basis for applying the law, then the date of filing the return will be the crucial date and the law in force on that date will be applicable for deciding the quantum of penalty.

Accordingly, in the instant case, the penalty was leviable in accordance with the amended provisions of section 271(1)( c) which came into force on 1-4-1968.

In essence, the Explanation (both after 1964 and 1976) is a rule of evidence. Presumptions which are rebuttable in nature are available to be drawn. As per the provision of Explanation 1, the onus to establish that the explanation offered was bona fide and all facts relating to the same and material to the computation of his income have been disclosed by him will be on the person charged with concealment.

Mere failure to substantiate the explanation is not enough to warrant penalty. The revenue has to establish that the explanation offered is not substantiated. The provision of Explanation 1 is concerned only with cases coming under clause (B) of the Explanation, where the assessee has offered an explanation which he is not able to substantiate. The explanation of the assessee for the purpose of avoidance of penalty must be an acceptable explanation; it should not be a fantastic or fanciful one. As indicated above, the consequence follows as a matter of law. The burden is on the assessee. If he fails to discharge that burden, the presumption that he has concealed the income or furnished inaccurate particulars thereof is available to be drawn.

In the case at hand, no explanation worth the name was offered by the assessee. Statement was to the effect that hand loans were obtained which were intended to be refunded immediately and, therefore, the entries were not made. But, later on, the arrangement did not work out and, therefore, the amount was offered for taxation. There was clear admission that entries were not made on the relevant dates. It was not a case where entries were made on the relevant dates, and the source of money was omitted. The entries on the contrary were made on dates when there was sufficient cash balance. The intention to hide the actual state of affairs was clear. The explanation offered had no semblance of acceptability, was fanciful and vague. The Tribunal clearly erred in law by misreading the position of law stated in Sir Shadilal Sugar & General Mills Ltd. v. CIT [1987] 168 ITR 705/33 Taxman 460A (SC). Its conclusion that the assessment having been made on the basis of addition offered by the assessee, no penalty was imposable, was not correct.

IT : Where search and seizure was conducted by Central Excise Department, penalty under section 271(1)(c) was not to be levied by Income Tax Officer as concealment was not conducted by Income-tax Department

Section 271(1)(c)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 1996-97 - Assessee did not revise its original return on receipt of second audit report which pointed out incorrect claim of liability in original return, and was compelled to disclose second audit report when scrutiny was carried out and after being asked to explain about inflation of cost - Similarly, claim in respect of booking of expenditure payable to ‘P’ Ltd. was incorrect and on being asked by Assessing Officer, it changed its explanation though that was not substantiated - Whether assessee had consciously withheld from department revised computation as per revised audit report, and assessee having filed inaccurate particulars, instant case was covered under Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c) - Held, yes

The issue for consideration was whether penalty for concealment of particulars of income can be levied under section 271(1)(c ) where it is shown that assessee would not have filed the returns but for the issue of notice under section 148. In other words whether non-furnishing of return within the stipulated period under section 139 tantamounts to concealment of the particulars of income. The words "concealment" or "conceal" have not been defined in the Income-tax Act, 1961.

The words ‘conceal’ and ‘concealment’, according to their dictionary meaning, can be used by the Legislature in the widest possible sense. It may include the act of commission as well as the act of omission. But it is a well settled legal position that words in a given statute are to be construed in the context in which they are used. The word ‘concealment’ is qualified by the words ‘of particulars of income’. So one can be said to have concealed the particulars of income if he is under an obligation to disclose the same. The reason is obvious. Penal provisions are to be construed very strictly. No person can be penalised unless he is found guilty on account of his failure to perform his statutory obligation.

Section 139 casts an obligation on the assessee to furnish the particulars of income in the return to be filed by him. Particulars of income are required to be furnished by the assessee in the return or along with the return. No other manner is prescribed by the statute for disclosing the particulars of income.

The context in which language is used by the Legislature shows that it is the act of commission of default which is subject to penalty and not the act of omission. Therefore, concealment of particulars of income, if any, has to be seen with reference to the return of income and not in any other manner. If the assessee files the return without disclosing the particulars of income, then it can be said that assessee had concealed the particulars of income. But where no return is filed, it is difficult to hold that assessee had concealed the particulars of income.

This view is fortified by the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Brij Mohan v.CIT [1979] 120 ITR 1/ 2 Taxman 209 wherein it was held that the concealment of the particulars of income was effected by the assessee when he filed the return of total income and, therefore, the law as prevailed on that date would be applicable for the levy of penalty for concealment of particulars of income. The only other judicial opinion available directly on the point disputed in the instant case, was the decision of Madras High Court in the case of S. Santhosa Nadar v. First Addl. ITO [1962] 46 ITR 411 (Mad.) wherein it has been held "where no return is filed, the case could not fall under section 28(1)(c)". The provisions of section 271(1)(c) are in pari materia with the provisions of section 28(1)(c ) of the 1922 Act. Therefore, the ratio laid down by the Madras High Court would be applicable to the case falling under section 271(1)(c). The aforesaid view has been accepted with reference to section 271(1)(c) of 1961 Act by the Karnataka High Court in the case of Addl. CIT v. C.V. Bagalkoti & Sons [1978] 115 ITR 131 .

The aforesaid judicial opinion remained undisturbed till 1-4-1989 when Explanation 3 was inserted by the Legislature. So, prior to 1-4-1989 this judicial opinion should be given full respect and cannot be discarded by any authority giving one or the other reasons. The only question now remained whether by insertion of Explanation 3, the aforesaid judicial opinion was nullified.

Explanation 3 to section 271(1)(c ), inserted with effect from 1-4-1989, is not applicable to the existing assessees. Had the Legislature intended to raise such presumption in respect of the existing assessees, it would have specifically provided so. Therefore, even after 1-4-1989, it could not be said that non-furnishing of return within the stipulated period under section 139 by the existing assessees would tantamount to concealment of the particulars of income.

Explanation is applied and the onus is placed on the assessee, because the returned income is less than 80 per cent of the assessed income, to rebut the presumption raised against the assessee. The matter of raising presumptions against the assessee on the given facts is also covered by the following decisions of the Punjab & Haryana High Court :

1.Vishwakarma Industries v. CIT [1982] 135 ITR 652 (Punj. & Har.) (FB) 2.Rajeswar Singh’s case (supra), and

3.CIT v. Surinder Singh [1986] 160 ITR 456 (Punj. & Har.)

The Full Bench judgment of the Punjab & Haryana High Court in the case of Vishwakarma Industries (supra) has been approved by the Supreme Court in the cases of CIT v. Mussadilal Ram Bharose [1987] 165 ITR 14 /30 Taxman 546 H and Chuharmal v. CIT [1988] 172 ITR 250 / 38 Taxman 190 .

I find that the decisions of the Gujarat High Court, Kerala High Court and the Punjab & Haryana High Court referred to earlier, were not brought to the notice of the Hon’ble Mumbai High Court while deciding the cases of P.M. Shah and Dharamchand L. Shah ( supra), wherein it was held that old Explanation to section 271(1)(c) (which was operative upto assessment year 1975-1976) could be considered by the Tribunal even for the first time. Therefore, merely because the Explanation has not been referrd to in the show-cause notices, etc. there is no legal bar against invoking the said Explanation during the course of penalty proceedings. In the present case, penalty under section 271(1)(c ) was imposed because the Assessing Officer was satisfied that the assessee had concealed particulars of his income. Whether the failure of the assessee in this regard was due to fraud, or the failure to return the correct income was due to gross or wilful neglect of his part, is not relevant in the case of the assessee. On appeal the first appellate authority considered that Explanation to section 271(1)(c) is appliacble in the assessee’s case for the assessment year under consideration i.e. 1983-84. It cannot, therefore, be said that the Income-tax Authorities have not invoked the Explanation to section 271(1)(c). The nature of the Explanation to section 271(1)(c) upto assessment year 1975-76 was different, i.e. penalty is leviable when the income returned by an assessee was less then 80% of the income assessed and the Explanation was attracted. But as already stated the nature of the Explanation inserted by Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 1975 w.e.f. 1-4-1976 is different from the earlier Explanation which was operative upto assessment year 1975-76. Under the newly substituted Explanation applicable w.e.f. 1-4-1976, where in respect of any facts material to the computation of income, if the assessee gives no explanation at all, or the explanation is found to be false, or such person offers an explanation which is not bona fide, then the amount added or disallowed in the assessment arising out of such facts shall be deemed to be the concealed income. Therefore, the scope and nature of the Explanation to section 271(1)(c) upto the assessment year 1975-76 and the scope and nature of Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c) w.e.f. 1-4-1976 are different totally. In view of the decisions of the Gujarat High Court referred in para 11 above and the decisions of the Punjab & Haryana High Court referred to in the immediately preceding paragraph, which were in respect of old Explanation upto the assessment year 1976-1976, and in view of the nature and scope of new Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c), I am of the considered opinion that the decisions of the Mumbai High Court in the case of P.M. Shah’s case (supra) and Dharamchand L. Shah’s case (supra) relied on by the assessee’s counsel, are not applicable to the present case.

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessee-firm was dealer in kirana goods, sugar, vanaspati ghee, etc., and, for assessment year 1978-79, it had declared certain losses - Assessee gave an explanation but same was rejected by ITO who made additions to assessee’s income - ITO then initiated penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c), read with Explanation thereto, and ultimately imposed penalty - Whether, in view of fact that there were number of Explanations to section 271(1)(c) introduced with effect from 1-4-1976 and ITO had not referred to particular Explanation which was being invoked by him, imposition of said penalty was invalid - Held, yes - Whether even assuming that Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c) was invoked by ITO, even then said penalty could not be sustained because explanation furnished by assessee was bona fide and had not been found to be false by ITO - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-firm was a dealer in kirana goods, sugar, vanaspati ghee, etc. In the relevant assessment year, namely 1978-79, the assessee had declared certain losses in sugar account as well as in ‘Dalda ghee 2 kgs. account’. The assessee stated that the loss in sugar account was due to the fact that certain bags of sugar were damaged in rain which it sold at comparatively lower price. Similar was the reply in respect of ‘Dalda ghee 2 kgs. account’ where the tin boxes were stated to have been damaged. Regarding low gross profit in respect of all the accounts except kirana goods it was stated that it was not possible to maintain day to day stock tally. It was, therefore, urged that the gross profit rate declared be accepted. The ITO did not accept the assessee’s explanation and made certain agreed addition to the assessee’s income. The ITO then initiated penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c), read with Explanation thereto. To this the assessee urged that the difference in the assessed income and declared income was due to the addition on account of low gross profit and inadmissible expenses and that it had agreed to said addition just to avoid litigation and neither the income had been concealed nor inaccurate particulars had been furnished. The ITO, however, rejected the assessee’s contentions and levied a penalty under section 271(1)(c). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld the ITO’s order imposing penalty.

On second appeal, the assessee, inter alia, contended that there were a number of Explanations introduced with effect from 1-4-1976 to section 271(1)(c) and the ITO had not referred to a particular Explanation which was being invoked by him before he assumed jurisdiction of imposition of penalty and, therefore, in the absence of mention of a particular Explanation, the finding was vague and liable to be annulled.

HELD: A perusal of the assessment order by the ITO as well as the penalty order, in the present case, revealed that he invoked the Explanation below section 271(1)(c). At the relevant time, there were four Explanations below section 271(1)(c). The ITO did not specify as to which Explanation had been invoked by him to assume jurisdiction for the levy of the penalty. Therefore, the assumption of jurisdiction by the ITO to levy penalty under section 271(1)(c) was illusory and vague and, thus, invalid.

Even on merits, the penalty imposed upon the assessee could not be sustained because out of the four Explanations below section 271(1)(c), it was only Explanation 1, which could be invoked in the present case. This Explanation provides that it would be a case of deemed concealment where a person fails to offer an explanation or offers an explanation which is found by the ITO to be false. In the present case, the explanation had been offered by the assessee and there was no finding of the ITO or the Commissioner (Appeals) that the explanation furnished by the assessee was false. Another situation under Explanation 1 where it can be a case of deemed concealment is where an explanation has been offered which the assessee is unable to substantiate. However, the proviso below Explanation 1 further provides that it would not be a case of deemed concealment if the explanation is otherwise bona fide. There was nothing in the present case, to show that the explanation furnished by the assessee was not bona fide. Therefore, the present was a mere case of estimates of income and the assessee agreed to the addition to avoid litigation.

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment years 1967-68 and 1968-69 - On search at business premises, two sale deeds for purchase of properties in name of wives of assessees were recovered - Source of money for purchase of properties was stated to be loans and sate of jewellery - ITO did not agree with statements and made additions - Penalty proceedings were initiated and IAC imposed penalty - On appeal Tribunal after considering various items found that there were no incriminating materials warranting a presumption of concealment for assessment year 1967-68 but held that there was concealment in subsequent year by assessee - Whether since findings recorded by Tribunal were findings of fact, and moreover, there was no specific question challenging factual findings on ground that there was no material to support said findings, in such circumstances, it was not open to High Court to interfere with aforesaid findings of Tribunal - Held, yes - Whether, consequently, order passed by Tribunal was to be affirmed
 - Held, yes

FACT: On 12-6-1967, the Enforcement Directorate conducted a search of the business premises of the firm in which the assessees were partners. During the said search, a sale deed dated 14-7-1966, relating to a premises in favour of the wives of the two assessees jointly for a considering of Rs. 41,900 was seized. The said document showed that the stamp papers to the value of Rs. 4,100 had been used for that document. A similar sale deed dated 1-5-1967, relating to another premises purchased for a consideration of Rs. 42,000 was also recovered from the premises along with a receipt

On the question of source of funds to purchase the above mentioned properties, the assessee stated that the cost of the property in all came to Rs. 72,910 and that for that purpose the wives had provided a sum of Rs. 36,000 each by raising loans and by selling jewels.

While completing assessments, the ITO accepted the case of obtaining loans but did not accept the assessee’s case of sale of jewellery of their wives. Therefore, the ITO made certain additions as undisclosed income from other sources in the assessments of both the assessees. Thereafter, the penalty proceedings were initiated and the IAC imposed penalty under section 271(1)(c). On appeal, the Tribunal accepted the assessee’s case in its entirety so far as the assessment year 1967-68 was concerned. According to the Tribunal, there were no incriminating materials warranting a presumption of concealment for that year. As regards the assessment year 1968-69, the Tribunal sustained the levy of penalty, but reduced the amount of penalty levied.

On reference :

HELD: The Tribunal actually went into the question as to whether there was in fact concealment by the assessee in respect of both the assessment years. The Tribunal after considering the various items which formed the subject-matter of assessment, found that for the assessment year 1967-68, there was no justification for holding that there was concealment as had been done by the IAC. But there was concealment in the subsequent year by the assessees though not to the extent held by the IAC. In view of the finding given by the final fact finding authority, the Tribunal, on the question as to whether there was in fact any concealment and if so to what extent, it was not possible for this court to interfere with the said finding especially when there was no specific question challenging the factual finding on the ground that that there was no material to support that finding. The Tribunal, after having held that for the year 1967-68, there was no concealment, proceeded to hold that there was concealment mainly on the basis that even in the revised return for the assessment year 1968-69, the assessee had failed to give an explanation either before the assessing authority or before the IAC or before the Tribunal. As regards this assessment year, the Tribunal found that there were special circumstances, apart form the revised return and the resultant assessment on an agreed basis, to indicate that there was concealment. In view of the fact that the finding of the Tribunal was based on materials, the Tribunal’s findings could not be interfered with in instant reference.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of the assessee.

Nowhere the Tribunal gave a specific finding that the explanation of the assessee by itself could be accepted The Tribunal had nowhere referred to the Explanation introduced in section 271(1)(c) in the year 1964. It did not say that the failure of the assessee to produce any evidence, apart from his own statement, by itself was sufficient in the circumstances of the case to dislodge the presumption arising in view of the aforesaid Explanation.

Under section 271(1)(c) penalty is attracted when there is concealment of particulars of the assessee's income. The Explanation states that when there is a particular difference in the total income and the income returned by the assessee, unless the assessee proves that the failure to return the correct income did not arise from any fraud or any gross or wilful neglect on his part, he shall be deemed to have concealed the particulars of his income, etc. A fiction is created by this Explanation that the assessee has concealed the particulars of his income unless he discharges the earlier burden imposed on him to prove that the income returned was not for the reasons stated therein. Therefore, whenever there is failure on the part of the assessee in the circumstances referred to in the Explanation to section 271(1)(c), the statutory presumption automatically follows and it shall have to be deemed that the assessee had concealed the particulars of his income. No doubt, the presumption could be rebutted. The main section 271(1)(c) by itself does not refer to any fraud or gross or wilful neglect. The penalty is attracted as and when there has been a concealment of the particulars of income and if the Explanation compels the authorities to draw a particular presumption, such a presumption shall have to be drawn and burden will certainly be on the assessee to have the presumption rebutted. In Jeevan Lal Sah's case (supra), the Supreme Court pointed out that the law had undergone a change after the introduction of the Explanation to section 271(1)(c) in the year 1964 and the rule regarding burden of proof enunciated in Anwar Ali's case (supra) was no longer valid.

In the instant case, it was clear that the Tribunal had not placed before it the correct principles; instead it applied the ratio of Anwar Ali's case (supra) which is not longer good law.

Therefore, on the facts and in the circumstances of the instant case, the Tribunal was not justified in cancelling the penalty under section 271(1) (c) read with the Explanation to the said section.

But as already stated the nature of the Explanation inserted by Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 1975, w.e.f. 1-4-1976 is different from the earlier Explanation which was operative upto assessment year 1975-76. Under the newly substituted Explanation applicable w.e.f. 1-4-1976, where in respect of any facts material to the computation of income, if the assessee gives no explanation at all, or the explanation is found to be false, or such person offers an explanation which is not bona fide, then the amount added or disallowed in the assessment arising out of such facts shall be deemed to be the concealed income. It does not cover a case where an assessee has filed return of income for any previous year and income found during search related thereto was not disclosed in such return.

To include the same within the scope of deemed concealment in search cases as provided by Explanation 5A, the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2009 recasts the Explanation to provide that where the return of income for such previous year has been furnished before search but such income has not been declared in such return, then, although, such income is declared in any return of income furnished on or after date of search, it would be deemed that the assessee concealed the particulars of such income entailing concealment penalty.

As is evident from clause (c ) of section 271(1), the words used are 'has concealed the particulars of his income' or furnished 'inaccurate particulars of such income'. Thus, both in case of concealment and inaccuracy, the phrase 'particulars of income' has been used. The Legislature has not used the words 'concealed his income'. From this it would be apparent that penal provision would operate when there is a failure to disclose fully or truly all the particulars. The words 'particulars of income' refer to the facts which lead to the correct computation of income in accordance with the provisions of the Act. So, when any fact material to the determination of an item as income or material to the correct computation is not filed or that which is filed is not accurate, then the assessee would be liable to penalty under section 271(1)(c ). If the income has to be assessed under section 145, then the presumption would be that the income was not properly returned. In the instant case also , the assessee was not maintaining the accounts during the course of the business year after year and, in fact, the assessee was writing the accounts after the close of the year and inflating the expenses so as to show the income at his will. In these circumstances, it did not lie in the mouth of the assessee that he was not concealing his income by furnishing inaccurate particulars thereof, as concluded by the Assessing Officer and the Commissioner (Appeals). 271(1)(c) may be issued for concealment of income. During the course of penalty proceedings, apart from issuing a formal show-cause notice under section 271(1)(c ), the Assessing Officer had specifically confronted the assessee with the facts pertaining to diversion of profits through the instrumentality of sham sale transactions with the sister concerns and called upon the assessee to explain why penalty for concealing the particulars of income may not be levied. The assessee furnished its reply. The Assessing Officer after elaborate discussion of the facts and circumstances of case came to the conclusion that the assessee had concealed the income by diverting the profits to its sister concerns. The Assessing Officer had further observed that the assessee had furnished inaccurate particulars of its income. On these facts the charge of concealment had been specifically and unambiguously brought out by the Assessing Officer in the show-cause notice issued to the assessee as well as in the penalty order passed by the Assessing Officer. In the show-cause notice, the Assessing Officer had clearly indicated the default of concealing the particulars of income. The satisfaction recorded in the assessment order using the words ‘concealment of income’ clearly brought out the charge that the penalty was proposed to be levied for concealing the particulars of income. The income could be concealed obviously by concealing the particulars thereof. Looking to the fact that the penalty proceedings before the Assessing Officer do not have formal trappings of a criminal trial and nuances of criminality cannot be imported into such proceedings, strict procedural requirements of a criminal trial like issue of the formal charge-sheet are not necessary in such proceedings. The assessee had been allowed appropriate opportunity of being heard as per the provisions of section 274. The basic requirement had been duly complied with by the Assessing Officer inasmuch as the Assessing Officer had indicated that the penalty under section 271(1)(c) was proposed to be levied for concealing the particulars of income represented by diversion of profits through sham transactions with the sister concerns. No prejudice, therefore, had been caused to the assessee in the matter of rebutting the case against it.

The assessee had taken resort to routing its sales through sham or unreal transactions which were merely paper transactions, with its sister concerns for the sole purpose of diverting its profits. There were tell tale signs in ample measure starting from the record which indicated that these sale transactions with the sister concerns were illusory transactions. The transactions with the sister concerns were admittedly at rates much lower than the prevailing market rates. The assessee had obviously resorted to a make believe arrangement whereunder the sister concerns had been used as conduits for siphoning off of its profits. The Assessing Officer had brought out in the penalty order the close inter-connection of the assessee with the sister concerns. Five partners of the assessee-firm were also partners in the three sister concerns utilised for profit diversion. The substantiated chunk of sham transactions were routed through one of the firms. Thus, 70 per cent of profits in the sister concerns was held by the five partners of the assessee firm who were common. The other partners also were closely related family members. These facts provided irrefutable evidence that the transactions with the sister concerns were merely a ruse to divert the profits; in fact the sale transactions of the assessee with the sister concerns and the subsequent transactions of the sister concerns with the outside parties formed an integral and indivisible part of the composite scheme of tax planning of the assessee. Hence, the assessee-firm had adopted non-genuine and artificial device of showing paper transactions with the sister concerns with the objective of reducing its tax liabilities. These transactions were commercially inert and had been entered into as part of tax saving scheme. The penalty for concealment levied under section 271(1)(c) was, therefore, liable to be upheld.

Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c ) incorporates a rule of evidence and shifts the onus on the shoulders of the assessee in furnishing the explanation before the Assessing Officer. The Explanation does not constitute an ingredient of the offence and it lays down only a rule of evidence. The Explanation does not confer any discretion on the assessing authority to invoke it or not. It automatically applies to cases where penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) for the offence of concealing the particulars of income have been initiated. The consequences from the applicability of Explanation 1 follow as a matter of law. If the assessee fails to offer explanation or the explanation is found to be false or the assessee is not able to substantiate the explanation, the presumption that he concealed the particulars of income is bound to be drawn. In the instant case there was no infirmity in the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) in invoking the Explanation 1 for the purpose of considering the exigibility of the penalty under section 271(1)(c).

The assessee's contention that Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c) had no application at all in the instant case because no explanation from the assessee was sought regarding concealment at the time of completing the assessment and this was put to the assessee only at the stage of the penalty proceedings, could not be accepted on the basis of section 69 under which the addition was made while completing the assessment. It was also a fact that the assessee accepted the addition made under section 69 and did not challenge it in any appeal. It was, therefore, clear that the circumstances were put to the assessee even while completing the assessment or must be deemed to have been put to the assessee while completing the assessment in terms of section 69. Therefore, the argument that it was only at the time of the imposition of penalty that explanation of the assessee was sought, could not be accepted.

It was clear that the burden to explain the alleged concealment was on the assessee. The assessee contended that he had received money from his father-in-law who was employed in a foreign country. Obviously no money from a foreign country could come into his hands legally except through a bank. The amount could be paid over to the assessee by the father-in-law only by way of a cheque or only after withdrawing the same from the bank. The assessee did not produce any material in support of his case that the amount was something received from his father-in-law who was employed abroad. In fact in his explanation before the Assessing Officer he had clearly stated that no documentary evidence was available in respect of the said receipt from his father-in-law. In that situation, it was clear that he had failed to substantiate his explanation and, hence, in terms of Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c), there was concealment of income by the assessee making him liable to penalty under section 271(1)(c).

The crux of the matter to be examined was whether penalty under section 271(1)(c), read with the Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c ) was applicable to the facts of the instant case. The proceedings under section 271(1)(c ) can be initiated only if the Assessing Officer or the first appellate authority is satisfied in the course of any proceedings under the Act that any person has concealed the particulars of his income or has furnished inaccurate particulars of such income and he may direct that such person shall pay by way of penalty the sum mentioned in sub-clause (iii) of clause (c) of section 271(1)(c). The expression used in clause (c) is ‘has concealed the particulars of his income’ or ‘furnished inaccurate particulars of such income’. Therefore, in both cases of concealment and inaccuracy the phrase ‘particulars of income’ is used. The expressions ‘has concealed the particulars of income’ and ‘has furnished inaccurate particulars of income’ have not been defined either in section 271(1)(c) or elsewhere in the Act. [Para 8]

The word ‘conceal’ is derived from the latin word concelare which implies to hide. The offence of concealment is, thus, a direct attempt to hide an item of income or a portion thereof from the knowledge of the income-tax authorities. [Para 10]

It may be noted that these words ‘concealed’, ‘particulars’ and ‘inaccurate’ are with regard to income and not with regard to any other thing. In the light of above discussion it can be said that there cannot be a straitjacket formula for detection of default of concealment of particulars or furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income. It depends upon the facts of each case. In the case under consideration, there was no dispute that purchases were made, though the assessee failed to substantiate its claim to the extent that the purchases were made from that particular party. Therefore, in the case under consideration, the word ‘particulars’ used in section 271(1)(c ) would embrace the meaning of the purchases made and not the party from whom these were made. As stated above that words ‘concealed’, ‘particulars’ and ‘inaccurate’ are with regard to income and not with regard to any other thing. From which party the purchases were made is not much important while computing the income. The important aspect in computing income is purchases. In the case under consideration, the purchases were recorded regularly in the books of account on day-to-day basis. The Tribunal while deciding the quantum matter observed that the assessee must have made purchases from the market from unregistered dealers in cash and details could not be obtained from such dealers. The assessee, therefore, obtained hawala bills from ‘F’. The Tribunal further observed that the Commissioner (Appeals) was of the view that in these circumstances the assessee must have inflated the purchase bills and on that account the disallowance to the extent of 25 per cent was found to be reasonable. The case of the Assessing Officer in quantum matter was that the entire purchases were disallowable whereas the appellate authorities found that the assessee must have made the purchases but the same might not be from ‘F’. Actual purchases made by the assessee were not doubted by the appellate authorities while deciding the quantum matter. However, considering the circumstances, they confirmed the addition to the extent of 25 per cent of the relevant purchases on the basis of the facts, figures and particulars provided by the assessee. Thus, the main basis on which the Assessing Officer levied penalty was not sustained by the appellate authorities. [Para 11]

In addition to main provisions of concealment, namely, ‘has concealed the particulars of his income’ or ‘has furnished inaccurate particulars of such income’ there are those which are deemed to represent the income in respect of which particulars have been concealed. The deemed concealment is provided in the Explanations. Often a question arises whether in cases where additions or disallowances are made by the ITO, the penal provisions of section 271(1)(c) would attract. The Explanation 1 takes care of this situation. The Tribunal had ignored the amendment made in Explanation to section 271(1)(c) which came into effect from 1-4-1976. The relevant part of the said Explanation was inserted by the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 1975 and the amendment has prospective effect and not retrospective effect. After this amendment, whether there is a case of penalty or not, that has to be considered in the light of the amended Explanation. After this Explanation if the Assessing Officer or the first appellate authority is satisfied that (a) any person has concealed the particulars of his income, or (b) has furnished inaccurate particulars of such income, the penalty under section 271(1)(c) should be imposed.

The expressions ‘has concealed’ and ‘has furnished inaccurate particulars’ have not been defined anywhere else in the Act but that makes no difference. The word ‘conceal’ is derived from the Latin word ‘concelare’ which implies ‘to hide’. In the Webster’s New International Dictionary, the word has been equated to hide or withdraw from observation, to cover or keep from sight; to prevent discovery of; to withhold knowledge of.

Once the Assessing Officer is satisfied and found that the assessee has offered ‘no explanation’ or offers an explanation which is not substantiated by the assessee, that represents the concealed income and in that case, that income should be deemed to have been concealed by the assessee for the purpose of section 271(1)(c).

In the instant case, the basis of addition of income was some papers found at the time of search. The author of those papers, a son of one of the partners, had admitted in the statement before the ITO that he had prepared those papers, and those papers were related to the business of the assessee-firm. On these facts and circumstances, the addition had been made on account of the concealed income that had been finally sustained by the Tribunal. That addition had not been challenged by the assessee. In these circumstances, this was a fit case for penalty. There was no reason for cancelling the penalty imposed by the Assessing Officer and sustained by the Commissioner (Appeals).

The provisions of section 271(1)(c ) stipulate that if the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner(Appeals) or the Commissioner, in the course of proceedings under the Act, is satisfied that any person has concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars thereof, he may direct that such person shall pay by way of penalty a sum which shall not be less than but which shall not exceed three times the amount of tax sought to be evaded by a reason of the concealment of particulars of his income. Section 271(1)(c ) is attracted where, in the course of any proceedings under the Act, the Assessing Officer or the first appellate authority is satisfied that (a) any person has concealed particulars or his income or (b) has furnished inaccurate particulars of such income. The expressions ‘has concealed’ and ‘has furnished inaccurate particulars’ have not been defined either in the section or elsewhere in the Act. However, notwithstanding differences in the two circumstances, they lead to the same effect, viz., keeping off a certain portion of the income. The former is direct while the latter may be indirect in its execution. The word ‘conceal’ is derived from the Latin word ‘concelare’ which implies ‘to hide’. In Webster’s New International Dictionary, the word has been equated ‘to hide or withdraw from observation; to cover or keep from side, to prevent discovery of; to withhold knowledge of’. There may be cases where the facts may attract both the offences, and in some cases there may be overlapping of the two offences.

If on the facts and in the circumstances of a particular case and on the materials before it, the Tribunal reaches a conclusion that the concealment was not proved, it is a question of fact and no question of law arises from such order. Similarly, whether the burden in a given case has been discharged on a set of facts or not is a question of fact. Where a finding of fact arrived at by the Tribunal is based on no material or is perverse or is based on irrelevant, extraneous or inadmissible considerations or is arrived at by application of wrong principle of law, a question of law arises. Where the Tribunal fails to arrive at its own conclusion of fact after due and proper consideration of the entire materials for and against the assessee and cancels the penalty, a question of law arises. Similar is the case where conclusions of the Tribunal suffer from infirmity on account of relevant materials and evidence being ignored.

A conspectus of the Explanation added by the Finance Act, 1964, and the subsequent substituted Explanations make it clear that the statute visualised assessment proceedings and penalty proceedings to be wholly distinct and independent of each other. In essence, the Explanation (both after 1964 and 1976) is a rule of evidence. Presumptions which are rebuttable in nature are available to be drawn. The initial burden of discharging the onus of rebuttal is on the assessee. The rationale behind this view is that basic facts are within the special knowledge of the assessee. Section 106 of Indian Evidence Act, 1872, gives statutory recognition to this universally accepted rule of evidence. There is no discretion conferred on the Assessing Officer as to whether he can invoke the Explanation or not. Explanation 1, which primarily concerns the case at hand, automatically comes into operation when, in respect of any facts material to computation of total income of any person, there is failure to offer an explanation or an explanation is offered which is found to be false by the Assessing Officer or first appellate authority, or an explanation is offered which is not substantiated. In such a case, amount added or disallowed in computing total income is deemed to represent the income in respect of which particulars have been concealed. As per the provision of Explanation 1, the onus to establish that explanation offered was bona fide and all facts relating to the same and material to the computation of his income have been disclosed by him will be on person charged with concealment. Mere failure to substantiate explanation is not enough to warrant penalty. The revenue has to establish that explanation offered was not substantiated. The provision of Explanation 1 is concerned only with cases coming under clause (b) of the Explanation , where the assessee offered an explanation which he was not able to substantiate. The explanation of the assessee for purpose of avoidance of penalty must be an acceptable explanation; it should not be a fantastic or fanciful one. Consequence follows as a matter of law. Burden is the on assessee. If he fails to discharge that burden, presumption that he had concealed income or furnished inaccurate particulars thereof is available to be drawn.

The principal logical import of the Explanation is to shift burden of proof from the revenue on to the assessee. Rebuttal must be on materials relevant and cogent. It is for the fact-finding body to judge relevancy and sufficieny of materials. If such a fact-finding body, bearing the aforesaid principles in mind, comes to the conclusion that the assessee has discharged the onus, it becomes a conclusion of fact and no question of law arises. As observed earlier, initial burden is on the assessee. Once initial burden is discharged, the assessee would be out of mischief unless further evidence is adduced. It is plain on principle that it is not law that the moment any fantastic or unacceptable explanation is offered, burden placed would be discharged and the presumption rebutted.

On reading the Explanation to section 271(1) (c) it has to be presumed that if the total income returned by any person is less than 80 per cent of the total income, such person shall, unless he proves that the failure to return correct income did not suffer from any fraud or any gross or wilful neglect on his part, he is deemed to have concealed the particulars of his income. In the instant case, the Tribunal fell into error of law in not relying on the Explanation and rather merely depending upon the substantive provision of section 271 (1) (c). Further, the decision relied upon by the Tribunal had been overruled by a subsequent Full Bench decision of the Patna High Court in CIT v. Nathulal Agrawala & Sons [1985] 153 ITR 292/ 22 Taxman 199. Therefore, the Tribunal was not legally correct in cancelling the impugned penalty.

The word ‘concealed’ as used in section 271(1)(c ) has not been defined in the Income-tax Act. Its ordinary dictionary meaning is ‘to hide or withdraw from observation, to cover or keep from sight, to prevent discovery of, to withhold knowledge of.’ The meaning of the word ‘concealment’ as found in the Shorter Oxford English Dictionary, 3rd edn., Vol. I, is as below: ‘In law, the intentional suppression of fact or truth of fact done to the injury or prejudice of another’. It is thus clear that the expression, when used in law, must imply an injury or prejudice to another, which in a tax case must mean the revenue. The connotation of ‘concealment’ must, therefore, cover a mental act to hide some thing with the purpose of reducing the income of the assessee, thereby defrauding the revenue. Hence, although the expression ‘deliberately’ was omitted from the relevant section by the Finance Act, 1964 with effect from 1-4-1964, even then it has got to be said that in order to constitute the offence of concealment, play of the mind towards evasion of tax in a designed manner has got to be present. Conversely, therefore, if there be understatement of income in a very haphazard manner and if strong indications be there that there was no conscious effort on the part of the assessee to show his income at a lower figure, the assessee, in such a case, cannot be considered to be guilty of concealment of income.

The expression ‘furnishing inaccurate particulars of income’ in its simple form assumes a very wide character and can take into its compass any act of submission of particulars which may be inaccurate in any way. The inaccuracy in the particulars of income may be towards advantage or disadvantage of the assessee. Since this particular expression has also not been defined in the Act, it is necessary to have a proper interpretation of the same suiting the context. The principle of ‘noscitur a sociis’ may be applied herein to come to the conclusion that the expression is required to be used in this particular context in conjunction with or as an appendix to the earlier expression ‘concealed’. Common sense would tell one that an assessee cannot be visited with penalty under section 271(1)(c ) if he has furnished inaccurate particulars of his income in a manner so as to depict a higher figure of income than what it should be. One, therefore, has to circumscribe the meaning of the expression furnishing inaccurate particulars of income’ to limited situations where the assessee has furnished in accurate particulars of his income in a conscious manner so as to understate his income for the purpose of defrauding the revenue.

10.3 Section 271(1) of the Act empowers the Assessing Officer to levy penalty for the following offences :

Failure to comply with notice for assessment (of total income or fringe benefits); or
