5. Section 80 of the Act provides that penalty should not be imposed if the assessee proves that he has reasonable cause for failure. Earlier, section 80 comprised of only one part. It was broken into two parts, comprising of sub-sections (1) & (2) w.e.f. 28-5-2012. Sub-section (1) of section 80, inter alia, provides that notwithstanding anything contained in the first proviso to sub-section (1) of section78, no penalty shall be imposable on an assessee if he proves that there was reasonable cause for the alleged failure.

Meaning of reasonable cause

6. In S. Raghbir Singh Sandhawalia v. CIT AIR 1958 Punj. 250, it was held that the expression 'reasonable' means 'rational' according to the dictates of reason and not excessive or immoderate. An act is reasonable when it is comfortable or agreeable to reasons, having regard to the facts of the particular controversy.

This phrase has been interpreted in a number of decisions, including under the I.T. Act. In the case of Municipal Corpn. of Delhi v. Jagan Nath Ashok Kumar, AIR 1987 SC 2316, the SC interpreted the expression 'reasonable cause' as follows:—

"…Stroud's Judicial Dictionary, Fourth Edition, page 2258, states that it would be unreasonable to expect an exact definition of the word 'reasonable'. Reason varies in its conclusions according to the idiosyncrasy of the individual, and the times and circumstances in which he thinks. The reasoning, which built up the old scholastic logic sounds now like the jingling of a child's toy. But mankind must be satisfied with the reasonableness within reach and in cases not covered by authority, the verdict of a jury or the decision of a judge sitting as a jury usually determines what is 'reasonable'…."

Reasonable cause can be reasonably said to be a cause which prevents a man of average intelligence and ordinary prudence, acting under normal circumstances, without negligence or inaction or want of bona fides [Azadi Bachao Andolan v. Union of India [2001] 116 Taxman 249/252 ITR 471 (Delhi)].

Lack of funds or financial crisis has not been held to tantamount to reasonable cause. In Trans (India) Shipping (P) Ltd. v. CCE [2005] 2 STT 82 (Chennai), it has been observed that a delay in payment or non-payment of service tax within the prescribed time due to the cash crisis or financial hardship is generally not approved as falling within the scope of 'reasonable cause'.

Briefly speaking, reasonable cause means an honest belief founded upon reasonable grounds of the existence of a state of circumstances, which (assuming them to be true) would reasonably lead any ordinary prudent and cautious man (placed in the position of the person concerned) to come to the conclusion that the same was the right thing to do. The cause shown has to be considered and only if it is found to be frivolous, without substance or foundation, the aforesaid penalty can be imposed [see Woodward Governors India (P) Ltd. v. CIT [2001] 118 Taxman 433 (Delhi)].

'Under reported income' in consequence of 'Misreporting of income'

There are sub section (8) and (9) of section 270A which prescribe that if 'under reported income is in consequence of misreporting of income', penalty would be 200% of the tax payable on such 'under reported income'. Six cases where such 'under reported income' can be said to be 'in consequence of misreporting of income' are given under sub section (9) which are numbered from clause (a) to (f) under that sub section.

There are however following issues which merit attention:

(a)

In a given case, even if there was a case of 'misreporting of income' due to which the addition/disallowance was made in the assessment order, the difference between the assessed income and processed income would nonetheless continue to be termed as 'under reported income' or at best 'under reported income in consequence to misreporting of income'.

This appears to have been done consciously by the legislature to avoid negotiate the possible argument coming at any stage that since assessing officer has failed to use the expression 'misreporting of income', jurisdiction to levy penalty under sub section (8) read with sub section (9) ought to fail. We have already opined that such stand of the Revenue may not stand to the test of law for the reasons elaborated by us in the earlier part of this article.

(b)

Burden to prove that the 'under reported income' includes such cases of income which can be called as 'under reported income in consequence to misreporting of income', would rest on the shoulders of the assessing officer. This situation is akin and identical to the old Explanation (1A) to section 271(1)(c) whereby also the burden to prove that the explanation furnished by the assessee in the matter of facts material to the computation of income was false, was rested on the shoulders of the assessing officer. It would therefore be incumbent for the assessing officer here also in the new penalty provision of sub section (9) of section 270A, to bring the case of the assessee under any of the clauses (a) to (f) of sub section (9) before penalty @ 200% of the tax payable is imposed. Show cause notice which would be issued by the assessing officer for eliciting the reply defence of the assessee, and the penalty order passed must clearly mention under which clause or clauses of sub section (9) of section 270A case of the 'under reported income' falls.

(c)

These clauses as mentioned in (a) to (f) of sub section (9) are exhaustive, meaning thereby that any situation other than the listed six would not make the addition/disallowance as 'misreporting of income'. This is different matter that hardly would there be any other situation which has been left out to be covered under these exhaustive six clauses except the ones discussed hereinafter.

(d)

These clauses (a) to (f) of sub section (9) are at times overlapping, meaning thereby that one situation of 'misreporting of income' may be covered under more than one such clauses/cases. 'Misreporting of income' may be due to 'suppression of facts' or 'misrepresentation of facts' or may result due to 'recording of false entry in the books of accounts', or due to 'claim of expenditure not substantiated by any evidence'. There may at times not exist any water tight compartments between various clauses enshrined under sub section (9).

For instance, an expense on account of commission on sale may remain unsubstantiated for want of evidence and at the same time, it may be found that such commission was in fact a 'false entry' recorded in the books of accounts as such. This too may have been done by 'misrepresenting the facts' and it is very well possible that it was on account of rather 'suppressing the correct facts'.

From the impugned order it was found that the Commissioner (Appeals) had deleted the penalty by holding, without qualifying, that there was nothing to suggest the gross or wilful negligence or fraud by the assessee. The assessee had also contended that it was under the bona fide belief while making the said claim. In that regard, it was examined whether there was any information in the order of the BIFR; the provision of the SICA and section 72A or section 32A or any other provision under other statutes in favour of the assessee. Regarding the debate on the wilfulness, being the essential ingredient in matters attracting the provisions of section 271(1)(c), it is a settled law now that the Assessing Officer does not have to prove that the assessee has concealed the income or furnished the inaccurate particulars. The Explanation to section 271(1)(c) contains the provisions for deemed concealment wherever there is difference between the returned and assessed incomes and it provides for a complete code in matters of penalty. From the Explanation 1, it refers to a couple of independent groups of cases, which are the deemed cases of concealment. They are: (A) This group refers to again two types of cases and they are: (i ) the persons, who fail to offer an explanation, (ii) the persons, who have offered an explanation which is found to be outright false by the revenue authorities; or (B) This group refers to cases where the explanation offered by the person is not found false outright, but those cases which are other than such outright false explanation cases. These are diagnosed by the following symptoms : (i) such person is not able to substantiate the explanation offered; and (ii) such person not only fails to prove that the such explanation is bona fide but all the facts disclosed relating to the such explanation and material to the computation of his total income. [Para 9]

On comparison, the assessee's case was found covered by the cases of group (B) above and the onus was on the assessee to substantiate the explanation or prove the bona fide and also the responsibility of full disclosure of all the facts relating to the explanation and materials as stated above. Per contra, the Assessing Officer was not under an obligation to prove the wilful attempt of the assessee in matter of concealment or that the explanation of the assessee in that regard was not bona fide. Thus, it was the assessee's responsibility to meet the above requirements. Wilful concealment is not an essential ingredient for attracting civil liability; such as a penalty under section 271(1)(c). [Para 10]

However, Clause (B) of explanation 1 to section 271 is accommodated in section 270A(6) and the comparative table is given below: Thus, under section 270A(6) the income-tax authority must record his satisfaction or dissatisfaction before dropping or slapping penalty, as the case may be. The taxpayer can use section 270A(6)(a) to press his stand that he has offered bona fide explanation and it is for the income-tax authority to record why he is not satisfied with the explanation of the taxpayer.

(b) Placement of section 270A(6):Section 270A(1) gives the overall scope of the provision empowering the income-tax authorities to levy penalty for under-reported income which could include under-reported income as such or due to misreporting of income. Sub-section (6) is meant for the entire section 270A and not for under-reported income simpliciter. Unfortunately, it is placed after describing the under-reported income simpliciter but much before the misreporting of income dealt with in sections 270A(8) and 270A(9). Ideally, section 270A(6) must have been placed after explaining both under-reported and misreported incomes so that its applicability / coverage would not have created confusion and ambiguity.

(c) Misrepresentation or suppression of facts: Under-reporting of income due to misreporting of income is one of the instances covered in section 270A(9). The expression 'misrepresentation' could be found in section 245D(6) (relating to settlement of cases) and in section 245T (relating to advance ruling). In both, settlement of cases and in advance ruling the taxpayer is given opportunity of being heard. Only on representing the case before the prescribed authority, there could be a possibility of misrepresentation.

Where there is no query from the income-tax authority and no reply from the taxpayer, any addition made could not be called as 'misrepresentation'. It could be argued that misrepresentation is implicit by submitting incorrect ITR with details of income chargeable to tax and thus when wrong claims in the ITR when negatived, it amounts to misrepresentation of income.

The other aspect 'suppression of facts' entails a deliberate act of not revealing the facts and not necessarily twisting of facts. Not furnishing the facts could amount to suppression of facts.

The expression "misrepresentation and suppression of facts" could create great hardship to the taxpayers as any addition made otherwise than by way of estimated addition would be construed as misrepresentation or suppression of facts by the tax authorities.

(d) Failure to record investments in the books of account: This expression would cover unrecorded investments of the taxpayers chargeable to tax as income. But usage of the expression "recording investments in the books of account" seems to provide a leeway in cases where the investments do not belong to the business. Obviously, in such cases, the unrecorded investment would belong to the family of incomes which are chargeable to tax under section 115BBE with resultant penal consequence under section 271AAC of 10% of the unrecorded investments, which is less severe than 200% penalty envisaged in section 270A(8) read with section 270A(9).

(e) Claim of expenditure not substantiated by any evidence: Where the assessee incurs expenditure, which is not substantiated would be treated as misreporting of income. For example, if the assessee has incurred expenditure by way of salary to employees and did not maintain vouchers or the payment was not incurred through banking channel a confirmation from the employees would be adequate for allowance of claim. Where the expenditure claim is not substantiated by any evidence that could only lead to the claim of expenditure treated as misreporting of income.

(f) Recording of false entry in the books of account: This would cover making of accounting entries in the books of account for the purpose of under-reporting of income through misreporting. Where the income is not impacted even if the entry is a false entry for example a journal entry between two suppliers account or inter se customers accounts will not fall in this category. Further one has to take notice of section 271AAD which penalizes false entry in the books of account and which is independent of any other provision in the Act. It includes not only a false entry but also omission of any entry which can impact the total income chargeable to tax under the Act. For example, purchase not recorded in the books of account is not a false entry but it is an omission of entry which is covered by section 271AAD.

Thus recording false entry /omission of entry in the books of account would attract penalty under section 270A(8) @ 200% plus penalty under section 271AAD @ 100%.

2.6-3 Preliminary Objection - It would be pertinent to note that a preliminary legal objection may be raised before the Court that the Income-tax Department should first supply a copy of the satisfaction note, if any, recorded by them before assuming jurisdiction under section 92C(3) and before making a reference to the TPO under section 92CA. It may also be raised by way of a preliminary objection that since the reference to TPO was made without providing any prior opportunity, the same is patently invalid and should be quashed on this ground alone.1 4 The expression ‘having regard to’ used under various provisions of the Act including section 92(1) in this context assumes substantial significance. It implies that an opinion must be formed strictly in terms of the factors enumerated therein. The expression indicates that in exercising the power regard must be had also to the factors enumerated therein together with all factors relevant for exercise of that power.1 5

2.6-4 Search, Seizure, Authorization and Penalty - ‘Reason to believe’ also constitutes an important pre-requisite for the AO when it comes to search and seizure authorization under section 132(1)1 6 or reassessment under section 147(a).1 7 In fact, a similar approach must also be taken for levying penalty for concealment of income under section 271(1)(c) where the burden shall lie on the department to establish that the assessee had concealed his income.1 8

2.6-5 Objectivity in the context of judicial review - The formation of opinion is a quasi judicial act and, therefore, such opinion must be objective one and not merely subjective, i.e., there must be some material or information in his possession having nexus for formation of such opinion. Since prior approval has to be obtained from the Commissioner, the Assessing Officer must record his reasons so that the Commissioner may apply his mind to satisfy himself that the Assessing Officer has exercised his discretion correctly. Further, the exercise of discretion by the Assessing Officer is the subject-matter of judicial review which cannot be made, unless the appellate authorities or the Courts have these reasons before them. Therefore, the recording of reasons is necessary, in law, being part of the principles of natural justice. Similar thoughts were also echoed in the case of Rajesh Kumar v. Dy. CIT 19.

2.7 Unacceptable approach - Thus to marginalize the aspect of forming a reasoned opinion by the AO prior to reference not only makes him a redundant cog in the wheel but also seems to be patently opposite to the fundamental scheme of the Act where sound adjudication forms an integral part in the development of fiscal jurisprudence. Equally strange is the approach adopted by the ITAT in discounting natural justice by not affording the assessee a reasonable opportunity of being heared prior to the impugned reference. It has been observed that procedure to determine ALP in section 92CA is different from the one provided in section 92C. Under section 92C, the Assessing Officer has himself to determine the ALP whereas under section 92CA, he can refer the matter to TPO. There is nothing in the section to suggest that the AO should hear the assessee or record reasons before making reference to TPO or to suggest that the AO should ask the assessee whether he should himself proceed to determine ALP or should involve TPO for this purpose.20 The view is substantially based on the fact that to hold otherwise might totally defeat/jeopardize the purpose of the whole assessment and bring to a halt the entire machinery. However, a brief glance at some of the provisions of the Act would clearly suggest that the scheme of this legislation does not subscribe to such a narrow interpretation.

1.3 The Supreme Court approved the following propositions of law:

u Mens rea is an essential or sine qua non for criminal offence. A straitjacket formula of mens rea cannot be blindly followed in each and every case. The scheme of a particular statute may be diluted in a given case. If, from the scheme, object and words used in the statute, it appears that the proceedings for imposition of the penalty are adjudicatory in nature, in contradistinction to criminal or quasi-criminal proceedings, the determination is of the breach of the civil obligation by the offender. The word ‘penalty’ by itself will not be determinative to conclude the nature of proceedings being criminal or quasi-criminal. The relevant considerations are the nature of the functions being discharged by the authority and the determination of the liability of the contravenor and the delinquency.

u Mens rea is not essential element for imposing penalty for breach of civil obligations or liabilities.

u Two principles of construction - one relating to casus omissus and the other in regard to reading the statute as a whole, appear to be well-settled. Under the first principle a casus omissus cannot be supplied by the court except in the case of clear necessity and when reason for it is found in the four corners of the statute itself but at the same time a casus omissus should not be readily inferred and for that purpose all the parts of a statute or section must be construed together and every clause of a section should be construed with reference to the context and other clauses thereof so that the construction to be put on a particular provision makes a consistent enactment of the whole statute. This would be more so if literal construction of a particular clause leads to manifestly absurd or anomalous results which could not have been intended by the Legislature.

In Fakir Mohmed Haji Hasan v. CIT [2002] 120 Taxman 11 (Guj.), the Gujarat High Court laid down the following propositions:

The scheme of sections 69, 69A, 69B and 69C of the Act would show that in cases where the nature and source of investments made by the assessee or the nature and source of acquisition of money, bullion, etc., owned by the assessee or the source of expenditure incurred by the assessee are not explained at all, or not satisfactorily explained, then the value of such investments and money, or value of articles not recorded in the books of account or the unexplained expenditure may be deemed to be the income of such assessee.

It follows that the moment a satisfactory explanation is given about such nature and source by the assessee, then the source would stand disclosed and will, therefore, be known and the income would be treated under the appropriate head of income for assessment as per the provisions of the Act.

However, when these provisions apply because no source is disclosed at all on the basis of which the income can be classified under one of the heads of income under section 14 of the Act, it would not be possible to classify such deemed income under any of these heads including 'Income from other sources' which have to be sources known or explained.

When the income cannot be so classified under any one of the heads of income under section 14, it follows that the question of giving any deductions under the provisions which correspond to such heads of income will not arise.

If it is possible to peg the income under any one of those heads by virtue of a satisfactory explanation being given, then these provisions of sections 69, 69A, 69B and 69C will not apply, in which event the provisions regarding deductions, etc., applicable to the relevant head of income under which such income falls will automatically be attracted.

The opening words of section 14 'Save as otherwise provided by this Act' clearly leave scope for 'deemed income' of the nature covered under the scheme of sections 69, 69A, 69B and 69C being treated separately, because such deemed income is not income from salary, house property, profits and gains of business or profession, or capital gains, nor is it income from 'other sources' because the provisions of sections 69, 69A, 69B, and 69C treat unexplained investments, unexplained money, bullion, etc., and unexplained expenditure as deemed income where the nature and source of investment, acquisition or expenditure, as the case may be, have not been explained or satisfactorily explained. Therefore, in these cases, the source not being known, such deemed income will not fall even under the head 'Income from other sources'.

Therefore, the corresponding deductions, which are applicable to the incomes under any of these various heads, will not be attracted in case of deemed incomes which are covered under the provisions of sections 69, 69A, 69B and 69C in view of the scheme of those provisions.

Exceptions to or Exclusions from the 'Under reported Income' Proceeding further from the stage that there was difference between the assessed income and processed income and thus there was 'under reported income', it would be open for the assessee to explain on the parameters of clauses (a) to (e) of sub section (6) that despite such difference and ostensible 'under reported income', there is in fact no or lower' under reported income' in the sense that the addition/disallowance made in the assessment order is covered under one or more of such clauses of sub section (6).

(a)

As to the exception or exclusion carved under clause (a) of sub section (6), if an assessee offers an explanation about any addition or disallowance made in the assessment order, which is found bona fide by the assessing officer and assessee has disclosed all the material facts to substantiate the explanation offered, such amount of addition or disallowance in that situation would not be treated as 'under-reported income'. Burden envisaged under this clause is akin identical to the burden placed under Explanation 1(B) of section 271(1)(c) on the shoulders of the assessee.

Therefore, for instance, a disallowance was made under section 40A(2) in the assessment order on the ground that the expenditure paid to the related person was excessive having regard to the fair market value of goods or services. If the assessee gives explanation in respect of payment made to the related person, which is found bona fide by the assessing officer and all the material facts in this regard were disclosed substantiated by the assessee by producing evidence, say, comparative rates to prove fair market value their evidences, such disallowance though made in the assessment would nonetheless be excluded from the purview of 'under reported income'.

(b)

Further, under clause (b) of sub section (6), if such amount of addition or disallowance made in the assessment order has been determined on the basis of an estimate on the ground that method employed by the assessee is such that the income cannot be properly deduced in spite of the books of account of the assessee having been found correct and complete, such addition/disallowance made in the assessment order would nonetheless be excluded from the purview of 'under-reported income'.

For instance, in case a builder-assessee was following Completed Contract Method whereas Percentage Completion Method ought to have been followed and no defect in the books of account is found in the assessment, addition made on estimate by the assessing officer in the assessment would fall under clause (b) of sub section (6) such addition would therefore not partake the character of 'under reported income'.

(c)

'Under-reported income' under clause (c) of sub section (6) would not include such income if addition/disallowance was made on the basis of estimate as against the lower estimated addition/disallowance made by the assessee on the same issue in the return of income and assessee has disclosed all the facts material to such addition/disallowance.

Example of this case may be taken where disallowance on account of personal user of the car etc. is estimated if some disallowance was already made by the assessee in the return of income under this head by disclosing all material facts. Such enhanced estimated disallowance would not be treated as part of 'under reported income.'

(d)

Going further and dealing with clause (d) of sub section (6), addition made in the assessment order on the basis of arms' length price determined by Transfer Pricing Officer whereas assessee had maintained information and documents as prescribed under section 92D, declared international transaction and disclosed all material facts relating to the transaction, would not be part of 'under reported income'.

For instance, where addition/adjustment has been made by the Transfer Pricing Officer/assessing officer due to the application of different method of transfer pricing analysis, or due to application of additional filters or rejection of filters applied by the assessee for making comparative analysis, or acceptance or rejection of comparable(s) so on and so forth, such addition/adjustment made in the assessment order in such circumstance would not be 'under reported income'. In fact, earlier there was Explanation 7 to section 271(1)(c) in respect of addition/disallowance made as a result of the order of the Transfer Pricing Officer which in the opinion of the authors was somewhat more onerous for the assessee.

(e)

Lastly, any amount of 'undisclosed income' as referred to in explained through the Explanation (c) to section 271AAB would also not become 'under-reported income' as there is separate penalty provision under that section to deal with the penalty on the amount of such 'undisclosed income'.

(a)

The plain meaning of the expression 'furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income' implies furnishing of details or information about income which are not in conformity with the facts or truth. The details or information about income deal with the factual details of income and this cannot be extended to areas which are subjective such as the status of taxability of an income, admissibility of a deduction and interpretation of law. 3.32 TDS

Chapter XVII-B requires a payer to deduct tax in respect of specified payments/credits. Does he have to consider the GAAR for making a deduction? This is explained below separately for section 195 and other sections. Section 195 - Section 195 provides that any person responsible for paying to a non-resident any sum chargeable under the provisions of the Act shall at the time of credit or payment deduct income-tax. The provision applies to a sum chargeable under the provisions of the Act and hence, if a sum is not chargeable the payer is not required to deduct tax. It may happen that on application of general principles of the Act and the relevant Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement, the income is not chargeable to tax, but upon application of GAAR it becomes chargeable to tax. A question that arises is, what is the exact responsibility of the payer in this connection? On a literal reading, the payer has to deduct tax on a sum chargeable under the provisions of the Act which would include the provisions of GAAR and hence a payer is required to deduct tax on the sum that could be taxable after considering the provisions of GAAR.

The other view is that a payer is not required to take cognizance of GAAR at the time of payment. The expression 'chargeable under provision of the Act' in section 195 should mean chargeable after following the procedure laid down under the Act for charging a particular sum to tax. Now, GAAR is not merely a computational provision which would result in taxation of a particular sum. GAAR involves a detailed process and steps before an amount can be taxed as income. To illustrate, as explained in para 3.22 :

♦

the AO should consider it necessary to invoke provision of Chapter XA.

♦

the AO should refer the matter to the Commissioner.

♦

the Commissioner should be of the opinion that the provisions of the Chapter XA are required to be invoked.

♦

the Commissioner should issue notice to the assessee.

♦

the Commissioner should provide an opportunity have been heard.

♦

♦

the Approving Panel should give an opportunity of being heard.

♦

the Approving Panel should issues directions and make a declaration that an arrangement is an IAA.

♦

the AO should determine the consequences of the IAA.

♦

the AO obtains prior approval of the Commissioner before passing the assessment order.

Thus, there is an elaborate procedure to be followed before tax consequences are determined under GAAR. If the payer has to determine the chargeability it would mean that the payer occupies the position of the AO, Commissioner and the Approving Panel and decides whether GAAR is applicable or not. Such an interpretation is not warranted.

Again, GAAR can be invoked only during assessment or reassessment proceedings [see section 144BA(1)]; hence, it cannot be invoked in TDS proceedings which are neither assessment nor reassessment proceedings.

A further question that arises is that whether GAAR has to be considered by the officer while issuing certificate under section 195(2)/(7) or 197(1). In view of the reasons given above, it appears that the officer cannot consider GAAR while issuing the certificate.

Interesting Situations in which whether penalty under section 270A may be levied?

(a)

This is quite surprising that section 270A does not envisage any penalty on account of additions/disallowances/adjustments made to the returned income under section 143(1)(a). It may be recalled that section 143(1)(a) contains 6 different types of adjustments which can be made while processing the return. Such additions/disallowances/adjustments may be on account of any arithmetical error in the return, any incorrect claim if such incorrectness is apparent from any information in the return, disallowance of loss brought forward from earlier year and set off in this year which was not allowed to be carried forward as the return for that year was filed beyond the due date prescribed under section 139(1), disallowance of expenditures indicated in the audit report but not disallowed in the return, disallowance of deduction under section 10AA, 80IA, 80IAB, 80IB, 80IC, 80ID, 80IE if the return is furnished beyond the due date as prescribed under section 139(1). Legislature has not created any disincentive in the form of any additional tax on the lines of erstwhile section 143(1A), or any penalty under section 270A on account of the difference between the returned income and the processed income. Under section 271(1)(c), there was 'Explanation 6' which provided that no penalty under section 271(1)(c) would be levied in respect of prima facie adjustments made if as per the then existing provision under section 143(1A), additional tax had been charged which was equal to 20% of the tax payable on such adjustments. Under the existing provisions, there is no concept of additional tax on such adjustments except the normal tax levied on such difference. There does not seem to be any justification for not envisaging any disincentive or penalty in respect of such adjustments. Rationale for not envisaging the penalty under section 270A or some other disincentive on account of these adjustments seems to be that when such additions/disallowances are made in the intimation under section 143(1)(a) based on the information contained in the return of income itself, it means that there was no attempt to hide anything on the part of the assessee. But, if this is the rationale, it may not sound well. Contrarily, such additions/disallowances/adjustments made on account of patent and blatant errors in the return of income ultimately lead to under-reporting of income for no good reason or justification.

The dictionary meaning of these terms are:

Duhaime's law dictionary defines "misrepresentation" as a "false and material statement which induces a party to enter into a contract". Further, it also defines "suppression" as "the intentional non-disclosure by the prosecution of evidence favorable to an accused and asked for by the accused, where that evidence is material either to guilt or punishment". Based on the trends of past transfer pricing assessments, a common scenario which comes to mind is a case where the tax authorities may seek information/documents not in the possession of the taxpayer. For example, ultimate selling price of goods by the associated enterprise or financial statements of Associated Enterprises, etc. Non-furnishing of these, typically leads to an adverse inference being drawn while determining the arm's length price, thereby leading to a transfer pricing adjustment. The appellate authorities may be called upon to decide if such cases can be classified as "misrepresentation" or "suppression of fact" attracting a levy of penalty.

(v)

Section 273B of the Act – Shelter of "reasonable cause" not available for penalties under Section 270A of the Act

As we are aware, section 273B of the Act provides for non-levy of penalty, levied under the specific provisions mentioned therein, if the taxpayer proves that there was a reasonable cause for the failure.

Interestingly and to an extent even surprisingly, the said shelter of "reasonable cause" has not been made available for penalty levied under section 270A of the Act.

(vi)

Immunity under Section 270AA of the Act not available for misreporting of income

To reduce instances of levy of penalty inter-alia in cases where the addition(s) made in the assessment /re-assessment proceedings (leading to the levy of penalty) has(ve) been accepted, section 270AA of the Act has been introduced by the Finance Act, 2017 to provide the taxpayer an opportunity to seek, from the Assessing Officer, immunity from imposition of penalty under section 270A of the Act.

This is subject to fulfillment of the following conditions:

(a)

Payment of tax and interest within the specified time.

(b)

Non filing of any appeal against the order of assessment/reassessment.

An important point to note here is that the aforesaid immunity provisions are applicable for penalty levied/sought to be levied under section 270A only vis-à-vis cases related to "underreporting of income". In other words, no immunity can be sought in cases of "misreporting of income".

In addition to above, the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT), vide Circular No. 05/2018 dated 16 August 2018, has clarified that an application made by an assessee under section 270AA of the Act seeking immunity, will not bar the assessee from contesting the same issue in any earlier assessment year. This circular also clarifies that the tax authority shall not take an adverse view in penalty proceedings for earlier assessment year(s) under the old penalty regime merely because the taxpayer has applied for immunity under the new penalty regime.

(vii)

Interplay between Section 271G of the Act and Section 270A of the Act – Double blow?

Section 270A of the Act inter-alia provides for the levy of penalty for underreporting of the income, if information prescribed under Section 92D of the Act is not maintained.

Section 271G of the Act seeks to levy a penalty of 2 percent of the value of international transaction for failure to furnish any information as required under section 92D (3) of the Act. The said section is an independent section.

Accordingly, a literal interpretation of the above sections may seemingly lead to a double blow to taxpayer by levy of the penalty in both the sections. However, one point of difference could be that penalty under section 270A of the Act may only be sustained if the transfer pricing adjustment is upheld before the higher authorities whereas the penalty under section 271G of the Act is usually independent of the fate of transfer pricing adjustments; though there are contradicting decisions on the subject.

(viii)

Thin line of difference exists between the term 'suppression of fact' (misreporting of income) and 'disclosure of material facts' (underreporting of income)

There is a thin line of difference between the term 'suppression of fact' as mentioned under misreporting of income and 'disclosure of material facts' as contemplated under underreporting of income. Given that either of the terms are not defined under the Act, it may open up the doors for prolonged litigation as penalty under the head 'underreporting' is lower than what is contemplated under 'misreporting of income'.

D. To sum up

Taxpayers and professionals, need to gear up for the new penalty regime which will have its own set of propositions to be laid out and tested at the appellate fora. It will be interesting to see how they shape up specifically in the transfer pricing world which is more a fact driven exercise. Indeed, there are exciting times ahead!

3. Quantifying under-reported income: Where income is assessed for the first time and ITR was furnished by the assessee the difference between the income assessed and income determined under section 143(1)(a) would be the under-reported income.

Where no ITR is furnished or where it is furnished in response to notice under section 148 then (i) the amount of income assessed would be treated as under-reported income in the case of company, firm or local authority; and (ii) the difference between the income assessed and the basic exemption limit would be the under-reported income for other taxpayers.

Where it is not a case of the income being assessed for the first time the difference between the income reassessed or recomputed less the amount of income assessed or reassessed or recomputed previously would be the quantum of under-reported income.

4. Instances where it is not under-reporting of income: Section 270A(6) says that the following shall not be treated as under-reported income:

(i)

Where the assessee offers an explanation and the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner (Appeals) or the Commissioner or the Principal Commissioner, as the case may be, is satisfied that the explanation is bona fide and the assessee has disclosed all material facts to substantiate the explanation offered by him, the income so enhanced shall not be treated as under-reporting of income.

(ii)

The amount of under-reported income determined on the basis of an estimate shall not be treated as under-reported income if the accounts are correct and complete to the satisfaction of the Assessing Officer or Commissioner (Appeals) or the Commissioner or the Principal Commissioner provided the method employed is such that the income cannot properly be deduced therefrom.

(iii)

The amount of under-reported income determined on the basis of estimate and the assessee on his own estimated a lower amount of addition or disallowance of the same but has included such amount in the computation of his income and has disclosed all the facts material to the addition or disallowance.

The amount of under-reported income represented by any addition made with reference to ALP determined by the TPO in case where the assessee has maintained information and documents prescribed under section 92E and declared the international transaction under Chapter X and disclosed all the material facts relating to the transaction.

The amount of undisclosed income which is dealt with in section 271AAB.

For instance, an expense on account of commission on sale may remain unsubstantiated for want of evidence and at the same time, it may be found that such commission was in fact a 'false entry' recorded in the books of accounts as such. This too may have been done by 'misrepresenting the facts' and it is very well possible that it was on account of rather 'suppressing the correct facts'.

(e) 'Misrepresentation of facts' as per its natural meaning would cover within its ambit the cases where facts were something else but have been presented differently, thus leading to 'misreporting of income'. For example, income of a minor child which was to be included in the total income of the parent under section 64 was not so included and shown to have been earned by the child as if the child was major.

'Suppression of facts' would cover such cases where facts itself have been withheld, thus leading to 'misreporting of income'. For example, factum of some income though earned but was withheld from offering to tax.

If we closely examine 'Misrepresentation' and 'Suppression', we would end up in reaching traversing through the old concepts of 'furnishing inaccurately' 'concealment' of particulars of income. 'Suppression' is concealment whereas 'misrepresentation' is something, may not be concealing but 'furnishing inaccurately'. In fact, if we examine further, we would find that all the clauses covered by (b) to (f) may be covered under the clause (a) as every other clause would be a case of either misrepresentation of facts or of suppression of facts.

(f)

All cases viz. clause (a) to (f) of sub section (9) ought to lead to addition to income or disallowance of a claim resulting into the difference between assessed income and processed income. This is so because if there is no such difference, that would mean that there is no 'under reported income' and when there is no 'under reported income', there would not be 'under reported income in consequence to 'misreporting of income'. In other words, this can be put like this that even if 'charge' is there but if quantification or machinery fails, no pecuniary consequence in the form of penalty under section 270A would follow.

For instance, even if there was 'failure to report international transaction' or 'specified domestic transaction' but during the course of assessment, there may not result any addition/adjustment on this account as assessee may have proved that such transaction was entered into at arm's length price. In that situation, 'failure to report' such transaction was though ostensibly a case of 'misreporting of income' under clause (f) of subsection (9), yet in so far as the penalty under section 270A is concerned, no penalty can be imposed under that section since there was no addition/adjustment made in the assessment order and thus there was no difference on that account resulting between the assessed income and processed income and accordingly, there was thus no 'under reported income'. Since, there was no 'under reported income' resulting, there was no question of penalty under section 270A.This may be an altogether different matter that there may be other consequence for such non-disclosure, for instance, levy of penalty u/s 271AA for failure to report the international transaction or specified domestic transaction under section 92B/92BA. But, there is certainly no case of penalty under section/s 270A.

(g)

Similarly, not all the 'misrepresentation' or 'suppression' of facts as mentioned in clause (a) of sub section (9) may lead to the addition of income or disallowance of a claim, which means that in the absence of such addition or disallowance made in the assessment order to the returned income, there would not be 'under reported income' and since there would be no 'under reported income' in such a case, there would be no question of penalty under section 270A.

For instance, if a closely-held company having accumulated profits had given a loan to a shareholder who was holding more than 10% shareholding. But in order to camouflage real character of this transaction so that it can avoid the glare of applicability of section 2(22)(e), such company misrepresented this fact by terming and showing this transaction as not in the nature of loan but in the nature of advance in the course of business. Such transaction its real nature when exposed in the assessment of the company would obviously not lead to the addition of income in the hands of the company as the deemed dividend can be taxed in the hands of the shareholder. The fact of the matter is that there would be no addition in the hands of the company on this score. There would thus be no difference between the assessed income and processed income on this account in the hands of the company and thus, there would be no 'under reported income' and accordingly, there would be no penalty on the company under section 270A. Therefore, this is a classic case where despite such rank 'misrepresentation of facts', there may not be 'under reported income' in the hands of the company with no penal consequence under section 270A.

Taxation Avoidance Agreement, the income is not chargeable to tax, but upon application of GAAR it becomes chargeable to tax. A question that arises is, what is the exact responsibility of the payer in this connection? On a literal reading, the payer has to deduct tax on a sum chargeable under the provisions of the Act which would include the provisions of GAAR and hence a payer is required to deduct tax on the sum that could be taxable after considering the provisions of GAAR. The other view is that a payer is not required to take cognizance of GAAR at the time of payment. The expression 'chargeable under provision of the Act' in section 195 should mean chargeable after following the procedure laid down under the Act for charging a particular sum to tax. Now, GAAR is not merely a computational provision which would result in taxation of a particular sum. GAAR involves a detailed process and steps before an amount can be taxed as income. To illustrate, as explained in para 1.20 :

♦

the AO should consider it necessary to invoke provision of Chapter XA.

♦

the AO should refer the matter to the Commissioner.

♦

the Commissioner should be of the opinion that the provisions of the Chapter XA are required to be invoked.

♦

the Commissioner should issue notice to the assessee.

♦

the Commissioner should provide an opportunity have been heard.

♦

where the Commissioner is not satisfied with the reply, he should refer the matter to an Approving Panel

♦

the Approving Panel should give an opportunity of being heard.

♦

the Approving Panel should issues directions and make a declaration that an arrangement is an IAA.

♦

the AO should determine the consequences of the IAA.

♦

the AO obtains prior approval of the Commissioner before passing the assessment order.

Thus, there is an elaborate procedure to be followed before tax consequences are determined under GAAR. If the payer has to determine the chargeability it would mean that the payer occupies the position of the AO, Commissioner and the Approving Panel and decides whether GAAR is applicable or not. Such an interpretation is not warranted.

Again, GAAR can be invoked only during assessment or reassessment proceedings [see section 144BA(1)]; hence, it cannot be invoked in TDS proceedings which are neither assessment nor reassessment proceedings.

A further question that arises is that whether GAAR has to be considered by the officer while issuing certificate under section 195(2)/(7) or 197(1). In view of the reasons given above, it appears that the officer cannot consider GAAR while issuing the certificate.

1.23.14.2 Other sections - So far as other sections are concerned, apart from the arguments given above, section 192, section 193, section 194A, section 194C, section 194D etc., do not refer to any sum chargeable under the provisions of the Act; they require deduction of the amount paid (section 192), or amount credited/paid (section 193) or income credited/paid (section 194A) or any sum paid/credited (section 194C/section 194J); in other words, they would apply to the amount of credit/payment to the payee and it is not relevant as to whether the sum is chargeable in his hands or not or whether it is chargeable in another person's hands or what is the extent of income embedded in such credit/payment. Hence, it could be argued that in respect of these sections the payer is required to be governed by these provisions alone and he does not have to take into cognizance the effect of GAAR.

Presently where a search/requisition has been made, the Assessing Officer is bound to assess the undisclosed income found as a result of such search/requisition under Chapter XIV-B for a block period. The amendment has done away with this form of block assessment in respect of searches or requisitions initiated on or after June 1, 2003. Three new sections 153A to 153C are to be inserted to provide for an assessment to be made after a search/requisition. Under the new scheme of assessment, the following procedure is to be followed for assessment after a search/requisition :

u The Assessing Officer must issue a notice requiring the assessee to furnish a return of income for the six assessment years immediately preceding the assessment year relevant to the previous year of search/requisition.

u The assessee is required to furnish a return for the said six assessment years within such time as may be allowed by the Assessing Officer.

u Such a return filed is deemed to have been filed under section 139 and all the provisions of the Act shall apply accordingly.

u The Assessing Officer shall thereafter proceed to assess or reassess the total income in respect of each of the assessment years.

u All proceedings of assessment or reassessment on the date of initiation of the search/requisition shall abate.

u The income is to be charged to tax at the rates applicable to the relevant assessment years.

The following points are worth noting in this connection :

(1)Though a return filed in response to a notice under section 153A will be deemed to be a return under section 139, it may not be possible to revise the same for a revised return can be furnished under section 139(5) only where a return has been furnished under section 139(1) or in response to a notice under section 142(1).

(2)Where the income is assessed after a search/requisition the benefit of basic exemption will not be denied like in the case of a block assessment.

(3)It has been held in the context of section 153 that an assessment includes the determination of tax for the provisions of sections 143(3) and 144 require that the Assessing Officer must determine the income and sum payable by the assessee. This view that the income and the sum payable must be determined within the time-limit specified under section 153 has been taken in CIT v. Purshottamdas T.Patel [1994] 209 ITR 52 (Guj.). The language used in section 153A however only proposes that the Assessing Officer determine the total income. Therefore it may be possible to take a view that even in a case where the total income is determined within the time-limit stipulated under section 153B but where the tax is determined after the time-limit stipulated under section 153B the assessment would be a valid one and would not be one which is barred by time.

(4)As a result of such assessment, interest can be levied under sections 234A, 234B and 234C and further penalty can be imposed under section 271(1)(c) for concealment. False entry is an inclusive explanation - It includes, use or intention to use forged or falsified documents such as a false invoice, false piece of documentary evidence (challan, Dispatch proof, vouchers, confirmation, debit and credit notes, etc.), false invoice without actual supply or receipt of such goods or services or to or from a person who does not exist (hawala). Shankar Industries AIR 1993 SCW 762 *Tamil Nadu Kalyana Mandapam Association v. UOI [2004] 267 ITR 9/136 Taxman 596/4 STT 308 (SC)* CCT v. TTK Health Care Ltd. [2007] 11 SCC 796 (SC).

Since it is an inclusive explanation, it means the explanation is not exhaustive and will also cover its ordinary, popular and natural meaning - Lucknow Development Authority v. M. K. Gupta [1994] 1 SCC 243 & Black Diamond Beverages v. CTO [1998] 1 SCC 458.

So, as per the above judicial view scope of false entry is not restricted to the situations given in explanation to section 271AAD(2), but it can be extended by assessing officer to give natural and ordinary meaning during any proceedings.

No deduction under section 10A, 10AA, 10B or Chapter VI-A is admissible in respect of addition consequent to adoption of the arm’s length price. There is no immunity from penalty leviable against deemed concealment on the difference between reported and assessed income, unless justified by reasonable cause under section 273B. Failure to keep accounts and documents as required under section 92D will merit penalty under section 271AA. Failure to get audit certificate will attract penalty under section 271BA.

It has been held that the burden to prove that declared rate is the transfer price under the rules is placed on the assessee as decided by the Tribunal in Aztec Software Technology Services Ltd.’s case (supra). In fact, that is also the view taken in the countries, where transfer pricing rules are in vogue. To take an example, Australian rulings would not discredit findings of the tax authorities unless bad faith could be shown as decided in San Remo Macaroni Co. v. Commissioner of Taxation [1999] FCA 1468. Deficiency of information is a fault, which could not be attributed to revenue, so that burden of proving arm’s length price lay on the taxpayer. New Business Tax System (Thin Capitalisation and Other Measures) Bill, 2000 would seek to place even greater responsibility on foreign investors with significant interest in Australian ventures.

The seriousness of transfer pricing is highlighted by a recent Instruction indicating the effect of transfer pricing exercise undertaken by tax administration in India. The resort can now be made to Mutual Agreement Procedure under Indo-U.S. Double Tax Avoidance Agreement in respect of taxes, inter alia, imposed by application of Transfer Pricing Rule vide Instruction No. 10 of 2007, dated October 23, 2007. It provides for stay on demand subject to pendency of reference for availing MAP on confirmation from Foreign Tax and Tax Research Division of the CBDT and bank guarantee for the amount due and interest thereon.

Therefore, this is a classic case where despite such rank 'misrepresentation of facts', there may not be 'under reported income' in the hands of the company with no penal consequence under section 270A. Another instance can be one where 'misrepresentation' and/or 'suppression' of facts was made by the assessee in as much as it had received amount in violation of section 269ST but gave a different shape, colour or texture to the said transaction so that it could not be caught on the parameters of section 269ST. Even if this transaction is discovered in assessment, it may not lead or result into any addition of income due to the fact of such transaction otherwise proved to be genuine. Such brazen 'misrepresentation' and/or 'suppression' of facts may be saddled with other adverse consequences, for instance, penalty under section 271DA but certainly since it is not giving rise to increase in the assessed income, this would not result into 'under reported income' and hence, there would be no penalty under section 270A.

(h)

Interestingly, clause (b) of subsection (9) of section 270A speaks of a case where there is 'failure to record investment in the books of account'. But, such 'failure to record any investment in the books of account' may result into addition under section 69 which would though result into 'under reported income' but since income under section 69 is subject to higher tax rate under section 115BBE, penalty provision as prescribed under section 271AAC would come into being not penalty provision under section 270A. Section 271AAC specifically mentions that penalty under section 270A shall not be imposed where penalty under section 271AAC is imposed. Therefore, there may be a case of 'misreporting' of such income resulting into 'under reported income' yet it is outside the scope of penalty under section 270A.

This situation would in fact emerge in all such cases where addition to the income is made in the assessment order under section 68,69, 69A to 69D, as in all such cases, penalty can be levied under section 271AAC and not under section 270A. Question arises as to when in such cases penalty under section 270A cannot be imposed, where was the necessity of enacting clause (b) to sub section (9) of section 270A.

In fact, this anomaly seems to have crept in the statute due to the reason that penalty provision of section 270A was brought into effect by the Finance Act, 2016 whereas section 271AAC was brought subsequently by the Taxation Laws (Second Amendment) Act, 2016 and legislature seems to have glossed over this 'lapse' creptor resulted subsequently in section 270A(9)(b). Therefore, when there is no such penalty that can be levied for such a situation as mentioned in clause (b) of sub section (9) under section 270A, there is no justification for continuing to retain clause (b) under subsection (9) of section 270A.

Also, it may be noted that though there is clause (b) in subsection (9) to cover the 'failure to record investment in the books of account' but there is no clause enacted as to the 'failure to record expenditure in the books of account' on similar lines. Though even if, had such clause been there under sub section (9), then also that would have led to addition under section 69C, on which penalty under section 271AAC alone could have been imposed not the one prescribed under section 270A for the reason explained in preceding paragraph. But, absence of such clause i.e. 'failure to record expenditure in the books of account' in sub section (9) on the lines of clause (b) is astonishing.

(i)

Clause (c) of subsection (9) covers claim of such 'expenditure which are not substantiated by any evidence' but despite existence of such unsubstantiated expenditure, there may not be a case of penalty under section 270A qua such expenditure.

As explained by us in the preceding paragraphs that if disallowance of an expenditure does not lead to the 'under reported income', it would not result into penalty. It may so happen in certain situations in case of unsubstantiated expenditure also.

For instance, any disallowance of expense on account of non-substantiation in case of 100% tax-exempt units would go on to swell the business profits of that unit, thus resulting into no addition to the returned income. Since there would not be 'under reported income' in such a situation, there would be no case of penalty under section 270A.

THE ARM’S LENGTH PRINCIPLE

5. As a result of such illegitimate transfers depriving countries of huge amounts, which they would have otherwise received as taxes, the international community brought the ‘Arm’s Length Principle’ into being. The underlying concept of this principle is that the pricing of goods, services or costs that are transferred or shared, as the case may be, should be equivalent or at ‘Arm’s length’ to the price prevailing in an open, competitive market rather than at a price which is determined solely by tax considerations. In other words, the pricing of intra-group transactions within a Multinational Enterprise, operating from two or more countries, should be the same that would have been applied to unrelated parties in similar transactions, under similar circumstances in the open market. Transfer pricing rules in tax laws, therefore, are intended to counter the underpayment of tax.

The ‘Arm’s length principle’ was first incorporated in the tax treaties concluded by the USA, the UK and France in 1920s and 1930s. This principle was later formulated in Article VI of the League of Nations Draft Convention on the Allocation of Profits and Property of International Enterprises in 1936. This article is similar to article 9 of the 1963 OECD Draft Convention as also article 9 of the Present OECD and UN Models of Tax Convention.

Invoking extended period 3. Section 73 of the Act, as discussed earlier, gives power to the Central Excise Officer to invoke the extended period of limitation in case of non-levy or non-payment or short-levy or short-payment of service tax or erroneous refund if the same is caused by reason of suppression of facts. In such cases, the Central Excise Officer has to indicate in the show-cause notice about the suppression of facts. It is for the department to prove that there is the suppression of facts.

In Sridhar & Santhanam v. CST [2009] 19 STT 357 (Chennai - CESTAT), the Tribunal held that the demand is barred by limitation in the absence of charge of suppression of facts.

In Habitat Technology Group v. CCE&C [Stay Order No. 815 (Bang.) of 2008, dated 13-8-2008], the Tribunal held that the prima facie the appellants had made out a case in their favour on the ground that there was no allegation of suppression of facts, etc., and the intention to evade payment of duty. In view of this position, the Tribunal granted full waiver of pre-deposit and stayed the recovery till the disposal of the appeal.

In CCE v. Metal Engineering & Forging Co. [2009] 21 STT 180 (New Delhi - CESTAT), the revenue filed the appeal challenging the order of the Commissioner (Appeals), whereby it was held that the demand was time-barred. The earlier show-cause notice was issued as the respondent had not filed any return and it also paid service tax late. The respondent never disclosed to the revenue that it was not paying service tax in respect of handling charges. There was suppression of facts and the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was not sustainable and, hence, the Tribunal allowed the appeal of the revenue.

In Himatshu Bimet Ltd. v. CST [Final Order A/212 (Ahd.) of 2007-WZB, dated 15-1-2007], the Tribunal held that there was no allegation of suppression specifically made in the show-cause notice and intention to evade tax. The appellant had made out a reasonable cause under section 80 for the waiver of penalties.

Introductory Remarks

1. The procedure for assessment is streamlined in Chapter XIV of the Income-tax Act (the Act). The provisions of sections 147 to 153 of the Income-tax Act (the Act) deal with assessments covering escapement of income, time limit for issuance of notice etc. The corresponding provision in the Indian Income-tax Act 1922 (the 1922 Act) was covered in section 34 of the 1922 Act. Virtually section 147 of the Act corresponds to section 34(1) and Explanation of the 1922 Act.

However, with regard to service of notice, the Supreme Court in the case of R.K. Upadhyaya v. Shanabhai P. Patel [1987] 33 Taxman 229/166 ITR 163 succinctly explained the difference between the Act and the 1922 Act.

"The scheme of the Act so far as notice for reassessment is concerned, is quite different. What used to be contained in section 34 of the 1922 Act has been spread out into three sections, being sections 147, 148 and 149 in the 1961 Act (as the Act stood then). A clear distinction has been made out between 'issue of notice' and 'service of notice' under the 1961 Act. Section 34 of the 1922 Act conferred jurisdiction on the Assessing Officer to reopen an assessment subject to service of notice within the prescribed period. Section 149 prescribes the period of limitation. It categorically prescribes that no notice under section 148 shall be issued after the prescribed limitation has lapsed. Section 148(1) provides for service of notice as a condition precedent to making the order of assessment. Once a notice is issued within the period of limitation, jurisdiction becomes vested in the Assessing Officer to proceed to reassess. The mandate of section 148(1) is that reassessment shall not be made until there has been service. The requirement of issue of notice is satisfied when a notice is actually issued. In the present case, admittedly, the notice was issued within the prescribed period of limitation, as 31-3-1970 was the last day of that period. Service under the 1961 Act is not a condition precedent to conferment of jurisdiction in the Assessing Officer to deal with the matter but it is a condition precedent to making of the order of assessment. As the Assessing Officer in the instant case had issued notice within limitations, the appeal was to be allowed and the order of the High Court was vacated."

The Finance Bill, 2021 proposes to insert a new section 148A which contains provisions for conducting an inquiry and providing an opportunity before issuance of notice under new section 148 of the Act. However, this procedure of enquiry, providing opportunity and passing an order, before issuing notice under new section 148 of the Act, shall not be applicable in search or requisition cases.

Section 149 of the Act is proposed to be amended with regard to time limit for issuance of notice.

7. Difference between Underreporting and Misreporting

Underreporting of income entails ignoring or just partially declaring the real income obtained, and misreporting of income refers to knowingly submitting inaccurate or misleading information regarding income.

| Particulars | Under reporting of Income | Misreporting of Income |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nature | While underreporting of income entails ignoring or just partially declaring the real income obtained | Misreporting of income refers to knowingly submitting inaccurate or misleading information regarding income |
| Intent | While underreporting may result from ignorance, negligence, or a failure to understand the reporting requirements, | Misreporting suggests an intentional act of submitting inaccurate data to deceive or manipulate. |
| Scope of Inaccuracy | underreporting entails an inadequate or partial income statement with/without any manipulation. | Misreporting sometimes entails falsifying income projections or inflating deductions to reduce tax payments significantly. |
| Penalties | While underreporting can result in penalties that are usually 50% of the tax due | Penalties for misreporting are typically more severe., income reporting errors can result in larger fines of up to 200% of the tax due. |
| Legal Treatment | Tax authorities usually handle underreporting as a civil tax concern and levy penalties and fines. | Misreporting is often considered a more severe offense and may occasionally be subject to criminal prosecution. |
| Detection | underreporting can make it difficult for tax officials to spot differences between reported and real income. | Misreporting might be harder to spot since it includes deliberate manipulation and the fabrication of misleading records. |

9. 'Bitumen' is not a 'valuable article'; No Section 69A addition if transporter does not deliver it to Govt.: SC

[D. N. Singh v. CIT, [2023] 150 taxmann.com 301 (SC)]

The assessee carried on business as a carriage contractor for bitumen. It was involved in a scam of misappropriating the bitumen and not delivering the quantity lifted to the various divisions of the Road Construction Department of the Government of Bihar. Finding out that the actual quantity was not delivered, the AO invoked Section 69A and made additions due to the short supply of bitumen.

The matter reached the Supreme Court of India.

The Supreme Court held that the assessee at any point did not claim ownership over the bitumen not delivered to the authorities. It was also not a case where the assessee exercised rights available in law, entitling it to possess goods as of right or pass on the title to another under law as permitted. At best, the assessee's possession was a shade better than that of a thief as the possession had its origin under a contract of bailment.

It would be straining the law beyond justification if the Court recognised a thief as the property owner within the meaning of Section 69A. Recognising a thief as the property owner would also mean that the owner would cease to be recognised as the owner, which would indeed be the most startling result.

When the facts are clear that the assessee is not the owner and somebody else is the owner, then treating the assessee as the owner may produce the most illegal results apart from being unjust.

The intention behind introducing Section 69A was to get at income not reflected in the books of account but found to belong to the assessee. Not only must it belong to the assessee, but it must be other valuable articles.

Applying the Principle of Ejusdem Generis, bitumen would stand out as a strange bedfellow in the company of its immediate predecessor words, viz., money, bullion, and jewellery. Bitumen is a clear misfit and could not have been the legislative intention to treat it as another valuable article.

Bitumen is a residual product in petroleum refineries and is usually used in road construction. It may be found in small quantities or large quantities. If the 'article' is to be found 'valuable', then in small quantity, it must not just have some value, but it must be 'worth a good price' or 'worth a great deal of money'. If this is so, Section 69A would then stand attracted.

But if treating it as a 'valuable article' requires ownership in large quantity and multiplying the value in large quantity, a 'good price' or a 'great deal of money' is arrived at, then it would not be valuable.

Thus, the AO acted illegally in holding that the assessee was the 'owner' and made the addition under Section 69A on the said basis.

10. AO rightly imposed a penalty under the Black Money Act for non-disclosure of foreign assets in Schedule FA of ITR: ITAT

[Ms. Shobha Harish Thawani v. Jt. CIT [2023] 154 taxmann.com 564 (Mumbai - Trib.)]

The Mumbai Tribunal has confirmed the imposition of a penalty on the taxpayer for failing to disclose foreign assets in the Schedule FA of ITR. The tribunal stated that reporting interest income in the ITR from said foreign asset does not exempt the taxpayer from the obligation to disclose the assets in Schedule FA.

The assessee and her husband jointly invested in Global Dynamic Opportunity Fund Ltd. The assessee's share in the said investment was 40%. The assessee invested out of funds transferred from India to HSBC Bank in Jersey.

The assessee declared interest income from the foreign investment in AY 2016-17. Said asset was sold, and capital gain was offered to tax in AY 2019-20. However, the assessee did not disclose foreign assets while filing the return of income (ITR) for AY 2016-17 to AY 2018-19 under Schedule FA.

The AO levied a penalty towards the non-disclosure under Section 43 of the Black Money Act 2015 (BMA) for each of the assessment years. On appeal, the CIT(A) upheld the levy of penalty. The aggrieved assessee filed the instant appeal before the tribunal.

CLARIFICATION TWO

Prior to 1989, taxpayers who had failed to furnish the return of income within the specified time-limit or had paid inadequate or not paid advance tax within the stipulated time-limit were charged penal interest for such defaults and also subjected to penalty proceedings. The Direct Tax Laws (Amendment) Act, 1987 inserted new sections 234A, 234B and 234C in the Income-tax Act from assessment year 1989-90 to provide for penal interest at higher rates for the defaults in late furnishing of the return of income, defaults in payment of advance tax and for deferment of advance tax respectively and omitted separate penalty provisions for these defaults. The interest payable under these sections was mandatory and there was no provision for reduction or waiver of the penal interest, as was provided specifically in this behalf prior to 1989. As a result, several taxpayers faced unintended hardships in certain circumstances.

2. The Central Board of Direct Taxes, in exercise of powers, specified in section 119(2)(a) has decided to authorise Chief Commissioners and Directors-General (Investigation) to reduce or waive penal interest charged under the aforesaid sections in the following circumstances, namely:—

(i ) where, in the course of search and seizure operation, books of account have been taken over by the Department and were not available to the taxpayer to prepare his return of income;

(ii ) where, in the course of search and seizure operation, cash had been seized which was not permitted to be adjusted against arrears of tax or payment of advance tax instalments falling due after the date of the search;

(iii ) any income other than "Capital gains" which was received or accrued after the date of first or subsequent instalment of advance tax, which was neither anticipated nor contemplated by the taxpayers and on which advance tax was paid by the taxpayer after the receipt of such income;

(iv ) where, as a result of any retrospective amendment of law or the decision of the Supreme Court after the end of the relevant previous year, certain receipts which were hitherto treated as exempt, become taxable. Since no advance tax would normally be paid in respect of such receipts during the relevant financial year, penal interest is levied for the default in payment of advance tax;

(v ) where return of income is filed voluntarily without detection by the Income-tax Department and due to circumstances beyond control of the taxpayer such return of income was not filed within the stipulated time-limit or advance tax was not paid at the relevant time.

3. The Chief Commissioners and Directors-General are being authorised to reduce or waive penal interest under sections 234A, 234B and 234C with reference to assessment year 1989-90 and any subsequent assessment year subject to certain specified conditions. This is a major step taken by the Central Board of Direct Taxes to mitigate the hardships in deserving cases.

54. Non-residents should be excluded from mandatory ITR filing where they incur on foreign travel

Section 139 lays down the provisions relating to furnishing the return of income. It prescribes that every person other than a company or firm shall furnish the return of income if his total revenue during the previous year exceeds the maximum amount not chargeable to income tax. The proviso to Section 139(1) prescribes various conditions under which the assessee is required to furnish the return of income even if the total income during the previous year does not exceed the maximum amount not chargeable to tax. The following conditions are prescribed:

(a)

He has deposited an amount or aggregate of the amounts exceeding one crore rupees in one or more current accounts maintained with a banking company or a cooperative bank,

(b)

He has incurred expenditure of an amount or aggregate of the amounts exceeding two lakh rupees for himself or any other person for travel to a foreign country,

(c)

He has incurred expenditure of an amount or aggregate of the amounts exceeding one lakh rupees towards consumption of electricity,

(d)

He fulfils such other conditions as may be prescribed.

Since these conditions apply to everyone except a company or firm, such conditions will also apply to non-residents. Consequently, where the non-residents do not have income exceeding Rs. 2.5 lakh but has foreign travel exceeding Rs. 2 lakhs could be held liable to furnish the return of income even if their income during the previous year is below the maximum amount, which is not chargeable to tax.

Therefore, an amendment to Section 139 is recommended to exclude non-residents from the applicability of these provisions.

56. Delay in handing over seized material beyond 60 days should not invalidate search

Section 132(9A) provides that if the authorised officer lacks jurisdiction, seized assets are required to be handed over to the relevant Assessing Officer within 60 days, who will then exercise the powers under subsections (8) or (9) to section 132.

There is no clarity under the statute regarding the consequences in case seized material is not handed over by the authorised officer to the Assessing Officer within 60 days.

The Gujarat High Court ruled that8 the limitation period prescribed by section 132(9A) should be interpreted to be an administrative direction and not a judicial one, and non-compliance cannot make the search vitiated.

Thus, a suitable amendment should be made to clarify that the search shall not be invalidated even if the seized assets are not handed over to the relevant Assessing Officer within 60 days.

57. Time limit should be provided within which the seized documents should be provided to the assessee

Section 132(10) provides that if a person entitled to seized documents objects to the approval given by the authorities under Section 132(8), he can apply to the Board with reasons for the objection and request the return of the documents. After hearing the applicant, the Board may pass suitable orders.

Though the Act specifically provides for supplying copies of books of account or other documents seized during the search, no time limit has been prescribed.

In the absence of a prescribed time limit, it has been observed that the authorised officer seldom gives the assessee copies of the books of account and documents seized during the search. Therefore, to achieve the desired objective, the provisions regarding the time limit for supplying copies of documents and papers seized need to be rationalised.
